The Buddha practices giving and other such actions with the correct path; he is therefore named Sugata.
Having attained these five qualities, the Tathāgata's own merit is complete.
Because of attaining correct wisdom, he is able to cognize all the mental states (citta-saṃkalpa) in the world. Having cognized what is thought, he teaches the Dharma for them; he is thus named the Unsurpassed Tamer (Anuttara-puruṣa-damyasārathi). Those who are to be tamed are invariably subdued, and those who have been subdued will never backslide. Those who are tamed are gods (devas) and humans; thus, he is named Teacher of Gods and Humans (Śāstṛdeva-manuṣyāṇām). Someone may have a doubt: "How is it that, having been born a human, he is able to transform gods?" It is for this reason that he says, "I am the Teacher of Gods and Humans."
Buddha (Awakened One) means that, at the time of sitting at the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), with respect to all dharmas—past, future, and present; conditioned (saṃskṛta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); exhaustible and inexhaustible; coarse and subtle—he dispelled the sleep of ignorance (avidyā) and, attaining omniscience (sarvajñatā), was radiantly and greatly awakened. Thus, he is named 'the Awakened One'.
Being endowed with these nine meritorious qualities, he is honored throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions. He is thus named Bhagavān (World-Honored One).
Because the Buddha is complete in the ten titles, his own [benefit] is perfected and others' [benefit] is also perfected. He benefits himself and benefits others; for this reason, he should be venerated.
content.pt:
Décimo Título, Quarta Seção

Além disso, os sūtras explicam as dez qualidades meritórias [de um Buda], a saber: Tathāgata (Assim Ido/Vindo), Arhat (Digno de Oferendas), Samyaksaṃbuddha (Perfeitamente e Completamente Desperto), Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna (Perfeito em Conhecimento e Conduta), Sugata (Bem Ido), Lokavid (Conhecedor do Mundo), Anuttara-puruṣa-damyasārathi (Insuperável Domador de Seres), Śāstṛdeva-manuṣyāṇām (Professor de Deuses e Humanos), Buda (O Desperto), e Bhagavān (Honrado pelo Mundo).
Um Tathāgata é assim chamado porque ele veio trilhando o caminho da realidade (yathābhūta) para atingir o despertar perfeito (samyaksaṃbodhi). O que ele diz é invariavelmente verdadeiro e não falso. Como o Buda perguntou a Ānanda: "A fala do Tathāgata contém alguma dualidade?" "Não contém, Honrado pelo Mundo!" Assim, ele é nomeado 'Aquele Que Fala de Acordo com a Realidade' (yathāvādin).

Além disso, desde a noite em que atingiu o Caminho até a noite do parinirvāṇa, tudo o que o Tathāgata falou nesse ínterim é verdadeiro e não pode ser refutado; daí, ele ser nomeado 'Aquele Que Fala de Acordo com a Realidade'. Também, porque ele fala apenas depois de ter cognicido os períodos de tempo anterior e posterior com onisciência (sarvajñatā), todas as suas declarações são verdadeiras.

Ademais, a memória de todos os Budas, os Honrados pelo Mundo, é firme e sem falhas. Algumas pessoas podem fazer afirmações baseadas na cognição inferencial (anumāna-jñāna), outras podem falar de acordo com as escrituras, e ainda outras podem falar sem ter apreendido claramente um objeto do momento presente. As declarações de tais pessoas podem ser corretas ou incorretas. Como é dito em um sūtra: "As declarações de alguém que confia na inferência podem ser corretas ou incorretas." O Buda fala sobre os dharmas apenas depois de os ter cognicido diretamente (pratyakṣa-jñāna); por esta razão, suas declarações são irrefutáveis. Ele é chamado 'Aquele Que Fala a Verdade'.

Ademais, o que o Buda fala é sempre o significado real. Ao contrário de outras pessoas cujas falas podem ser reais ou irreais, a sua é, portanto, irrefutável. Também, a sua fala é oportuna. Como é dito em um sūtra, o Buda cognosce os estados mentais (citta) alegres e satisfeitos dos seres sencientes e apenas então ensina o caminho do Dharma. Daí, ele ser nomeado 'Aquele Que Fala de Acordo com a Realidade'.

Ademais, ele ensina precisamente para aquele que deve ser ensinado, como declarado no Sūtra Kiṃśuka. Ele também ensina o Dharma que deve ser ensinado — seja ele conciso ou extenso, tratando dos agregados (skandhas), esferas dos sentidos (āyatanas), elementos (dhātus), etc. — portanto, nada do que ele diz é outra coisa senão verdadeiro.

Além disso, existem dois modos de discurso: um se baseia na verdade convencional (saṃvṛti-satya), e o segundo se baseia na verdade última (paramārtha-satya). Porque o Tathāgata fala com base nestas duas verdades, todas as suas declarações são verdadeiras.

Ademais, o Buda não diz que a verdade convencional é a verdade última, nem diz que a verdade última é a verdade convencional. Por esta razão, estas duas formas de fala não são mutuamente contraditórias.

Além disso, quando o Tathāgata proíbe ou permite, estas ações também não são mutuamente contraditórias. De acordo com a matéria em questão, ele proíbe; ele não permite essa mesma matéria. De acordo com a matéria em questão, ele permite; ele não proíbe essa mesma matéria. Por esta razão, suas declarações não são mutuamente contraditórias.
Há também três tipos de formulação verbal: uma surgindo de visões (dṛṣṭi), uma segunda surgindo de presunção (māna), e uma terceira surgindo de designação provisória (prajñapti). O Buda está desprovido dos dois primeiros tipos de fala e, no que diz respeito ao terceiro tipo, é puro e imaculado.
Há também quatro tipos de formulação verbal concernentes aos dharmas: o de ver, ouvir, sentir e cognicir. No que diz respeito a estes quatro, as declarações do Buda são puras, e sua mente (citta) está sem ganância ou apego.
Há também cinco tipos de formulação verbal concernentes: ao passado, ao futuro, ao presente, ao incondicionado (asaṃskṛta), e ao inefável. O Buda penetrou completamente em todas essas cinco categorias e apenas fala depois de tê-las cognicido claramente. Assim, ele é nomeado 'Aquele Que Fala de Acordo com a Realidade'. Porque ele é capaz de falar de acordo com a realidade, ele é nomeado Tathāgata.
Esta qualidade é atingida porque as aflições (kleśas) estão exauridas. Ganância (rāga), aversão (dveṣa) e ilusão (moha) são a raiz da fala falsa. Tendo extinguido estes grilhões (saṃyojana), ele é, portanto, um Arhat (Digno de Oferendas).

Além disso, o Tathāgata ensina o Dharma que conduz ao estado de um Arhat; este é o Dharma de extinguir os grilhões, que surge do conhecimento correto (samyak-jñāna). Porque todas as aflições são exauridas através da contemplação correta dos dharmas com a percepção (prajñā) da impermanência (anityatā) e assim por diante, o estado de um Arhat surge com base no conhecimento correto.
Este conhecimento correto (samyak-jñāna) surge do conhecimento e da conduta (vidyācaraṇa). Alguém é nomeado como possuindo o conhecimento correto por causa da excelente penetração nos períodos de tempo anteriores e posteriores e naquilo que não é um mero contínuo. Por cumprir as perfeições (pāramitās) da doação (dāna), etc., todos os conhecimentos e condutas são aperfeiçoados (vidyācaraṇa-sampanna). Outras pessoas também praticaram a doação e outros dharmas através do saṃsāra sem começo, mas por lhes faltar a prática correta (samyak-ācāra), não são chamadas de Sugata (Bem Ido). O Buda pratica a doação e outras ações desse tipo com o caminho correto; ele é, portanto, nomeado Sugata.
Tendo atingido estas cinco qualidades, o próprio mérito do Tathāgata está completo.
Por atingir o conhecimento correto, ele é capaz de cognicir todos os estados mentais (citta-saṃkalpa) no mundo. Tendo cognicido o que é pensado, ele ensina o Dharma para eles; ele é assim nomeado o Insuperável Domador (Anuttara-puruṣa-damyasārathi). Aqueles que devem ser domados são invariavelmente subjugados, e aqueles que foram subjugados nunca retrocederão. Aqueles que são domados são deuses (devas) e humanos; assim, ele é nomeado Professor de Deuses e Humanos (Śāstṛdeva-manuṣyāṇām). Alguém pode ter uma dúvida: "Como é que, tendo nascido um humano, ele é capaz de transformar deuses?" É por esta razão que ele diz: "Eu sou o Professor de Deuses e Humanos."
Buda (O Desperto) significa que, no momento de sentar no local do despertar (bodhimaṇḍa), no que diz respeito a todos os dharmas — passados, futuros e presentes; condicionados (saṃskṛta) e incondicionados (asaṃskṛta); exauríveis e inexauríveis; grosseiros e sutis — ele dissipou o sono da ignorância (avidyā) e, atingindo a onisciência (sarvajñatā), foi radiante e grandemente desperto. Assim, ele é nomeado 'o Desperto'.
Sendo dotado destas nove qualidades meritórias, ele é honrado ao longo dos três períodos de tempo e das dez direções. Ele é assim nomeado Bhagavān (Honrado pelo Mundo).
Porque o Buda está completo nos dez títulos, o seu próprio [benefício] é aperfeiçoado e o [benefício] dos outros é também aperfeiçoado. Ele beneficia a si mesmo e beneficia aos outros; por esta razão, ele deve ser venerado.

segments.label: 5 三不護品 (The Three Non-Guardings | As Três Não-Proteções)

content.zh:
佛身口意業不護。

所以者何？佛無不淨身口意業欲令他人不見不
知。又諸餘人或有無記，似如不淨身口意業，智者所呵。佛亦無
也。

所以者何？如來一切身口意業，皆由智慧正憶念起，若諸妄念
少智之人無如是業。又世間人或卒誤語，佛無此等。又佛善修身戒
心慧如是等法，以善修故，一切不善及似不善業皆悉除滅。

復次世
尊從久遠來修行善法，不適今也，是故諸業性淨不護。又佛常樂戒
行，不以怖畏墮惡道等。又佛一切身口意業，皆為利人故無不善，
以無不善故不須護以淨，不護業是故應禮。又佛成就三念處故，所
以應禮。若說法時，聽者一心不以為喜，若不一心不以為憂，常行
捨心。

所以者何？佛貪恚習無有餘故。又知諸法畢竟空故，無憂無
喜。又佛善集大悲心故，於善不善，心無憂喜等起大悲。又佛深知
眾生各各性故，若善心聽不以為喜，不善心聽不以為憂，以性爾故
常行捨心。又佛心堅固猶如大地，去重不高，若置重物亦復不下；
餘凡夫人其心如稱，少增而下、少減而高。又佛世尊名大悲者，是
故天人皆應敬禮。又捨深禪定，樂為人說法。餘人悲心無所成辦，
世尊大悲能濟眾生，故名有果。又以大悲成無上道，更無餘緣。復
次佛無我心，少欲知足最為第一，以大悲故自歎己身。又佛性柔
和，以大悲故有苦切言，起大方便受諸勤苦，為度眾生。又佛以大
悲度眾生故，住於世間受五陰身，如熱鐵丸於須臾頃不可堪忍。又
佛世尊善修捨心，捨此捨心常行大悲，故可尊敬。又佛為善人善中
之善。

所以者何？自得大利亦利他人，自利利人故名善人。又佛為
眾生真善知識，

如經中說：我是眾生真善知識，是憐愍者、利益者
等。又佛世尊有精進等諸功德聚，如和利以百句讚佛。有此功德，
是故應禮。

又佛自說功德，如《增一阿含．如來品》中自說：我是
人中師子、人華人象，於沙門中第一沙門，婆羅門中亦是第一，眾
聖中王。行無錯謬，不隨苦樂者，我身是也。
問曰：佛以何故自讚其身？自讚身者是愚人相。

答曰：世尊不求名
利，但為他故自歎己身。又佛無我心，為利人故自歎無咎。又以因
緣少多自讚，於佛功德不能說盡，是故不墮愚人相中，不自高故。
又如《清淨經》中，舍利弗住於佛前讚佛功德，是故應禮。又少欲
知足等無量功德皆在佛身。

所以者何？佛集一切諸功德故。以是等
緣應敬禮佛。

法寶論初
content.en:
Fifth Section: The Three Unguarded Qualities
The Buddha's bodily, verbal, and mental actions (kāyavāgmanas-karman) are unguarded.

Why is this? The Buddha has no impure bodily, verbal, or mental actions that he would wish others not to see or cognize.

Furthermore, other people may have indeterminate (avyākṛta) actions that resemble impure bodily, verbal, or mental actions and are censured by the wise. The Buddha is also without these.

Why is this? All the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Tathāgaṭa arise from wisdom (prajñā) and right mindfulness (samyak-smṛti); those with deluded thoughts and little wisdom do not have such actions.

Moreover, worldly people may occasionally misspeak, but the Buddha is without such faults.
Also, the Buddha has well-cultivated such dharmas as the body (kāya), moral discipline (śīla), mind (citta), and wisdom (prajñā). Because of this excellent cultivation, all unwholesome actions (akuśala-karman) and actions that resemble the unwholesome are entirely extinguished.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One has cultivated wholesome dharmas since the distant past, not just now. For this reason, his actions are intrinsically pure and do not require guarding. Also, the Buddha constantly delights in the practice of moral discipline, not out of fear of falling into bad destinies (durgati) and the like. Also, all the Buddha's bodily, verbal, and mental actions are for the benefit of others and are therefore without unwholesomeness. Because they are without unwholesomeness, they do not need to be guarded to be pure. Because his actions are unguarded, he is therefore worthy of veneration.

Furthermore, because the Buddha has accomplished the three stations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), he is therefore worthy of veneration. When he teaches the Dharma, if the audience listens with a unified mind, he does not take it as a cause for joy; if they do not listen with a unified mind, he does not take it as a cause for sorrow. He constantly abides in equanimity (upekṣā).

Why is this? Because the Buddha's latent tendencies (vāsanā) for greed (rāga) and aversion (dveṣa) have been eliminated without remainder. Also, because he cognizes all dharmas as ultimately empty (śūnya), there is no sorrow and no joy.

Moreover, because the Buddha has well-amassed a mind (citta) of great compassion (mahākaruṇā), with respect to the wholesome and the unwholesome, his mind does not give rise to sorrow or joy, but instead gives rise to great compassion.

Furthermore, because the Buddha deeply cognizes the individual natures of sentient beings, if they listen with a wholesome mind (citta), he does not take it as a cause for joy; if they listen with an unwholesome mind (citta), he does not take it as a cause for sorrow. Because their natures are just so, he constantly abides in equanimity (upekṣā).
Also, the Buddha's mind (citta) is firm like the great earth: it does not rise up when a weight is removed, nor does it sink down when a heavy object is placed upon it. The minds of other, ordinary beings are like a balance scale, sinking with a small addition and rising with a small subtraction.

Moreover, the World-Honored One is called 'The Greatly Compassionate One'. For this reason, gods and humans should all venerate him. Also, he relinquishes deep meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and delights in teaching the Dharma for the sake of beings. The compassionate minds of other people do not accomplish anything. The great compassion of the World-Honored One is able to save sentient beings; thus, it is called 'fruitful'.

Moreover, it is through great compassion that the unsurpassed path is accomplished; there is no other condition.

Furthermore, the Buddha has a mind free of ātman and is foremost in having few desires (alpecchatā) and being content (saṃtuṣṭi). It is for the sake of great compassion that he praises his own person. Also, the Buddha's nature is gentle. For the sake of great compassion, he speaks harsh words, employs great skillful means (upāya), and endures various hardships to liberate sentient beings. Also, because the Buddha liberates sentient beings through great compassion, he abides in the world and accepts a body of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), which is as unbearable as a red-hot iron ball, even for a single moment (kṣaṇa).

Moreover, the World-Honored One has well-cultivated a mind of equanimity (upekṣā-citta). Relinquishing this mind of equanimity, he constantly practices great compassion; therefore, he is worthy of respect.

Furthermore, the Buddha is, among good people, the best of the good.

Why is this? He has attained great benefit for himself and also benefits others. Because he benefits himself and benefits others, he is called a good person.

Moreover, the Buddha is the true good friend (kalyāṇa-mitra) for sentient beings. As it is said in a sūtra: "I am the true good friend for sentient beings, the one who is compassionate, the one who brings benefit," etc.

Moreover, the World-Honored One possesses a collection of merits such as diligence (vīrya), etc., as when Vāgīśa praised the Buddha with a hundred verses. Possessing these merits, he is therefore worthy of veneration.
Also, the Buddha himself spoke of his merits. As he stated in the Tathāgata section of the Ekottarika Āgama (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Catukka Nipāta): "I am the lion among men, the flower among men, the elephant among men. Among ascetics (śramaṇa), I am the foremost ascetic. Among brahmins (brāhmaṇa), I am also the foremost. I am the king among the host of sages. The one whose conduct is unerring, who is not swayed by suffering (duḥkha) or pleasure (sukha)—that one is I."

Question: For what reason does the Buddha praise his own person? To praise oneself is a mark of a foolish person.

Answer: The World-Honored One does not seek fame or gain; it is only for the sake of others that he extols his own person.

Moreover, the Buddha has a mind free of ātman. To extol himself for the benefit of others is without fault. Also, he praises himself to a small extent due to specific causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya), but he cannot fully describe the Buddha's merits. Therefore, this does not fall into the category of a foolish person's mark, as he is not exalting himself.

Furthermore, as in the Prasādanīya Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 28 or Dīrgha Āgama 18), Śāriputra stood before the Buddha and praised his merits. For this reason, he is worthy of veneration.

Moreover, immeasurable merits such as having few desires, being content, and so forth, are all present in the Buddha's person.

Why is this? Because the Buddha has amassed all merits. For these and other reasons, one should venerate the Buddha.

content.pt:
Quinta Seção: As Três Qualidades Não Guardadas
As ações corporais, verbais e mentais (kāyavāgmanas-karman) do Buda são não guardadas.

Por que isto é assim? O Buda não tem ações corporais, verbais ou mentais impuras que ele desejaria que outros não vissem ou não cognicissem.

Além disso, outras pessoas podem ter ações indeterminadas (avyākṛta) que se assemelham a ações corporais, verbais ou mentais impuras e são censuradas pelos sábios. O Buda também está desprovido destas.

Por que isto é assim? Todas as ações corporais, verbais e mentais do Tathāgaṭa surgem da sabedoria (prajñā) e da atenção plena correta (samyak-smṛti); aqueles com pensamentos iludidos e pouca sabedoria não têm tais ações.

Ademais, pessoas mundanas podem ocasionalmente falar mal, mas o Buda está desprovido de tais falhas.

Além disso, o Buda cultivou bem tais dharmas como o corpo (kāya), disciplina moral (śīla), mente (citta), e sabedoria (prajñā). Por causa deste excelente cultivo, todas as ações prejudiciais (akuśala-karman) e ações que se assemelham ao prejudicial estão inteiramente extintas.

Além disso, o Honrado pelo Mundo cultivou dharmas salutares desde o passado distante, não apenas agora. Por esta razão, suas ações são intrinsecamente puras e não requerem guarda. Também, o Buda deleita-se constantemente na prática da disciplina moral, não por medo de cair em maus destinos (durgati) e afins. Também, todas as ações corporais, verbais e mentais do Buda são para o benefício de outros e são, portanto, sem estado prejudicial. Porque são sem estado prejudicial, elas não precisam ser guardadas para serem puras. Porque suas ações são não guardadas, ele é portanto digno de veneração.

Além disso, porque o Buda realizou as três estações de atenção plena (smṛtyupasthāna), ele é portanto digno de veneração. Quando ele ensina o Dharma, se o público escuta com uma mente unificada, ele não toma isso como causa de alegria; se eles não escutam com uma mente unificada, ele não toma isso como causa de tristeza. Ele habita constantemente em equanimidade (upekṣā).

Por que isto é assim? Porque as tendências latentes (vāsanā) do Buda para a ganância (rāga) e aversão (dveṣa) foram eliminadas sem remanescente. Também, porque ele cognosce todos os dharmas como em última análise vazios (śūnya), não há tristeza nem alegria.

Ademais, porque o Buda acumulou bem uma mente (citta) de grande compaixão (mahākaruṇā), no que diz respeito ao salutar e ao prejudicial, sua mente não dá origem à tristeza ou alegria, mas em vez disso dá origem à grande compaixão.

Além disso, porque o Buda cognosce profundamente as naturezas individuais dos seres sencientes, se eles escutam com uma mente salutar (citta), ele não toma isso como causa de alegria; se eles escutam com uma mente prejudicial (citta), ele não toma isso como causa de tristeza. Porque suas naturezas são exatamente assim, ele habita constantemente em equanimidade (upekṣā).
Também, a mente do Buda (citta) é firme como a grande terra: não se levanta quando um peso é removido, nem afunda quando um objeto pesado é colocado sobre ela. As mentes de outros, seres comuns, são como uma balança, afundando com uma pequena adição e subindo com uma pequena subtração.

Ademais, o Honrado pelo Mundo é chamado 'O Grandemente Compassivo'. Por esta razão, deuses e humanos devem todos venerá-lo.

Além disso, ele renuncia a absorções meditativas profundas (dhyāna) e se deleita em ensinar o Dharma para o bem dos seres. As mentes compassivas de outras pessoas não realizam nada. A grande compaixão do Honrado pelo Mundo é capaz de salvar os seres sencientes; assim, é chamada 'frutífera'.

Ademais, é através da grande compaixão que o caminho insuperável é alcançado; não há outra condição.

Além disso, o Buda tem uma mente livre de ātman e é primordial em ter poucos desejos (alpecchatā) e estar contente (saṃtuṣṭi). É por causa da grande compaixão que ele elogia a sua própria pessoa.

Além disso, a natureza do Buda é gentil. Pelo bem da grande compaixão, ele fala palavras duras, emprega grandes meios hábeis (upāya), e suporta várias dificuldades para libertar os seres sencientes. Também, porque o Buda liberta os seres sencientes através da grande compaixão, ele habita no mundo e aceita um corpo dos cinco agregados (pañca-skandha), que é tão insuportável quanto uma bola de ferro incandescente, mesmo por um único momento (kṣaṇa).

Ademais, o Honrado pelo Mundo cultivou bem uma mente de equanimidade (upekṣā-citta). Renunciando a esta mente de equanimidade, ele pratica constantemente a grande compaixão; portanto, ele é digno de respeito.

Além disso, o Buda é, entre as pessoas boas, o melhor dos bons.

Por que isto é assim? Ele alcançou um grande benefício para si mesmo e também beneficia outros. Porque ele beneficia a si mesmo e beneficia aos outros, ele é chamado uma boa pessoa.

Ademais, o Buda é o verdadeiro bom amigo (kalyāṇa-mitra) para os seres sencientes. Como é dito em um sūtra: "Eu sou o verdadeiro bom amigo para os seres sencientes, aquele que é compassivo, aquele que traz benefício", etc.

Ademais, o Honrado pelo Mundo possui uma coleção de méritos como a diligência (vīrya), etc., como quando Vāgīśa elogiou o Buda com cem versos. Possuindo esses méritos, ele é portanto digno de veneração.

Além disso, o próprio Buda falou de seus méritos. Como ele declarou na seção Tathāgata do Ekottarika Āgama: "Eu sou o leão entre os homens, a flor entre os homens, o elefante entre os homens. Entre os ascetas (śramaṇa), eu sou o principal asceta. Entre os brâmanes (brāhmaṇa), eu sou também o principal. Eu sou o rei entre a hoste dos sábios. Aquele cuja conduta é sem erro, que não é movido pelo sofrimento (duḥkha) ou prazer (sukha) — esse sou eu."

Pergunta: Por qual razão o Buda elogia a sua própria pessoa? Elogiar a si mesmo é uma marca de uma pessoa tola.

Resposta: O Honrado pelo Mundo não busca fama ou ganho; é apenas para o bem dos outros que ele exalta a sua própria pessoa.

Ademais, o Buda tem uma mente livre de ātman. Exaltar-se para o benefício de outros é sem falha.

Além disso, ele se elogia um pouco devido a causas e condições específicas (hetu-pratyaya), mas ele não pode descrever completamente os méritos do Buda. Portanto, isto não cai na categoria da marca de uma pessoa tola, já que ele não está exaltando a si mesmo.

Além disso, como no Sūtra Prasādanīya, Śāriputra colocou-se diante do Buda e louvou seus méritos. Por esta razão, ele é digno de veneração.

Ademais, méritos imensuráveis como ter poucos desejos, estar contente, e assim por diante, estão todos presentes na pessoa do Buda.

Por que isto é assim? Porque o Buda acumulou todos os méritos. Por estas e outras razões, deve-se venerar o Buda.

segments.label: 6 三善品 (The Three Goods | Os Três Bens)

content.zh:
問曰：汝言應禮法，以何功德故應禮耶？

答曰：佛自讚言：我所說
法，初中後善，義善、語善。獨法具足清淨調柔、隨順梵行。初中
後善者，佛法無時不善，於少壯老三時皆善，入時行時出時亦善。
又初止惡、中捨福報、後一切捨，是名三善。又佛三時常說正法，
不雜非法如餘外道。又初中後時常為智者之所愛樂。又於三時一切
甚深，不如餘經初麁、中細、後則微末。以是等緣故名三善。義善
者，佛法義有深利益，得今世利及後世利、出世道利，不如外典願
增天眼。語善者，隨方俗語能示正義，故名語善。

所以者何？言說
之果所謂義也。是故諸所言，說能辯義理，是名語善。

復次佛法貴
如說行、非但言說，是故隨方俗語能令得道，名為語善；不如外典
但貴語言，若失語言、若失音聲辭主得罪。

復次善說真諦故名義
善，善說世諦故名語善。獨法者，佛但說正法，不為戲論說往古
事，亦不雜說法及非法。又獨法者，但為無餘涅槃故說。又獨佛能
說，故曰獨法。
問曰：有聲聞部經但聲聞說，又有餘經諸天神說，汝何故言獨佛說
耶？

答曰：是法根本皆從佛出，是諸聲聞及天神等皆傳佛語。如比
尼中說：佛法名佛所說、弟子所說、變化所說、諸天所說。取要言
之，一切世間所有善語皆是佛說，故名獨法。具足者，佛所說法無
所減少，如《欝陀伽經》中說具足相。又佛法者，不待餘經而得成
也。如和伽羅那經待五種經然後得成，佛法不爾，於一偈中其義具
足，如說諸惡莫作、諸善奉行、自淨其意、是諸佛教，故名具足。
清淨調柔者，二種清淨故，名清淨調柔。語清淨故名曰清淨，義清
淨故名曰調柔。又佛聽於正義中置隨義語，於正語中置隨語義，不
如外道隨經而取。又佛法中依法不依人，法亦分別依了義經不依不
了義經，是名淨法，非但隨經。又佛法中有三法印，一切無我、有
為諸法念念無常、寂滅涅槃。是三法印，一切論者所不能壞，以真
實故，名清淨調柔。隨梵行者，八直聖道名為梵行。梵名涅槃，是
道能到，故名梵行。法寶成就如是功德，是故應禮。
content.en:
Question: You state that one should venerate the Dharma. Due to what meritorious qualities should it be venerated?

Answer: The Buddha himself praised it, saying: "The Dharma I have taught is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end. It is excellent in its meaning (artha) and excellent in its expression (vyañjana). It is a unique Dharma, complete, pure, and supple, conducive to the holy life (brahmacarya)."
"Excellent in the beginning, middle, and end" means that the Buddha-Dharma is never not excellent. It is excellent in the three periods of youth, maturity, and old age. It is also excellent at the time of entry, the time of practice, and the time of emergence.

Furthermore, "beginning" is ceasing evil, "middle" is relinquishing meritorious reward, and "end" is relinquishing everything. This is what is meant by the three excellences.

Moreover, at all three times, the Buddha constantly teaches the true Dharma, not mixing it with non-Dharma, unlike other non-Buddhists (tīrthika). Also, in the beginning, middle, and end, it is always cherished by the wise. And at all three times, it is entirely profound, unlike other scriptures that are coarse at the beginning, subtle in the middle, and then trivial at the end. For these and other reasons, it is called "the three excellences."
"Excellent in meaning" means that the meaning of the Buddha-Dharma possesses deep benefit, yielding benefits in this present life, benefits in future lives, and the benefit of the supramundane path (lokottara-mārga). This is unlike non-Buddhist texts that aspire only to enhance the divine eye (divya-cakṣus).
"Excellent in expression" means that it can reveal the correct meaning by adapting to local vernacular languages. Therefore, it is called excellent in expression.

Why is this? The fruit of speech is what is called "meaning." Therefore, any speech that can elucidate meaning and principle is called excellent expression.

Furthermore, the Buddha-Dharma values practice in accordance with what is said, not mere speech. Therefore, adapting to local vernacular to enable the attainment of the path is called excellent expression. This is unlike non-Buddhist texts that prize only the language itself, where if the language or the sound is defective, the speaker commits an offense.

Furthermore, because it skillfully teaches the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it is called "excellent in meaning." Because it skillfully teaches the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is called "excellent in expression."
"A unique Dharma" means Buddha only teaches true Dharma. He does not engage in frivolous discourse (prapañca) by recounting ancient tales, nor does he mix the teaching of Dharma and non-Dharma.

Moreover, "a unique Dharma" means that it is taught solely for the sake of nirvāṇa without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa). Also, only a Buddha can teach it; therefore, it is called "a unique Dharma."

Question: There are sūtras in the śrāvaka section that were spoken only by śrāvakas, and there are other sūtras spoken by various gods (devas). Why then do you state that the Buddha alone speaks it?

Answer: The root of this Dharma comes entirely from Buddha. All these śrāvakas and gods are transmitting the Buddha's words. As it is said in the Vinaya: The Buddha-Dharma is defined as that which is spoken by the Buddha, spoken by his disciples, spoken by emanations, and spoken by gods. In essence, all wholesome speech that exists in the world is the speech of the Buddha; hence, it is called "a unique Dharma."
"Complete" means that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is not deficient in any way, as the characteristic of completeness is explained in the Udaka[rāmaputta] Sutta. Also, the Buddha-Dharma does not depend on other scriptures to be established. For example, a Vyākaraṇa text requires five types of texts for its grammar to be established. The Buddha-Dharma is not like that. Within a single verse (gāthā), its meaning is complete. For instance, the verse: "Do no evil, practice all good, and purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all the Buddhas." (Dhammapada 183). Therefore, it is called "complete."
"Pure and supple" refers to two kinds of purity. Because the expression is pure, it is called "pure." Because the meaning is pure, it is called "supple." Also, the Buddha permits using colloquial expressions (anvartha-vyañjana) within the correct meaning, and allows colloquial meanings (anvartha-artha) within correct expressions. This is unlike the non-Buddhists who rigidly adhere only to the scripture.

Moreover, in the Buddha-Dharma, one relies on the Dharma, not on the person. Within the Dharma, a distinction is also made: one relies on sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha) and not on sūtras of interpretable meaning (neyārtha). This is called a pure Dharma; it is not a mere adherence to scripture. Also, within the Buddha-Dharma, there are the three seals of the Dharma (dharma-mudrā): that all dharmas are without an ātman (sarva-dharmā anātmānaḥ); that all conditioned dharmas (saṃskṛta-dharma) are impermanent from moment to moment (kṣaṇika-anityāḥ); and that nirvāṇa is quiescent extinction (śānta-nirvāṇa). Any dialectician cannot refute these three seals of the Dharma. Because they are true, the Dharma is called "pure and supple."
"Conducive to the holy life" (brahmacarya) refers to the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgika-mārga). Brahman is a name for nirvāṇa. This path is able to lead to it; therefore, it is called the "path to brahman" or the holy life (brahmacarya).
The Dharma-Treasure is accomplished in such meritorious qualities; for this reason, it should be venerated.
content.pt:
Pergunta: Você afirma que se deve venerar o Dharma. Devido a quais qualidades meritórias ele deve ser venerado?

Resposta: O próprio Buda o louvou, dizendo: "O Dharma que ensinei é excelente no começo, excelente no meio, e excelente no fim, bom no significado e bom na expressão. É não adulterado e completo, puro e limpo, uma prática pura."

"Excelente no começo" (ādau kalyāṇa) significa que quando alguém o ouve, surge alegria.
"Excelente no meio" (madhye kalyāṇa) significa que quando alguém pratica os ensinamentos, isso cessa o sofrimento (duḥkha).
"Excelente no fim" (paryavasāne kalyāṇa) significa o nirvāṇa.

Além disso, a disciplina moral correta e pura (śīla) é excelente no começo; o samādhi é excelente no meio; e a sabedoria (prajñā) é excelente no fim.

Além disso, ouvir é excelente no começo; refletir é excelente no meio; e praticar é excelente no fim.

Ademais, ao primeiro entrar na via, diz-se que é excelente no começo; a não regressão é excelente no meio; e a obtenção do fruto imaculado (anāsrava-phala) é excelente no fim.

Além disso, o que o Buda ensinou com a voz sublime que corta as dúvidas das pessoas é chamado excelente no começo. O significado indubitável, como as verdades do sofrimento (duḥkha-satya) e sua origem (samudaya), é excelente no meio. Aquele que apreende o significado com sabedoria inabalável é chamado excelente no fim.

"Bom no significado" significa que ele elucida perfeitamente o significado. "Bom na expressão" significa que ele exprime perfeitamente e maravilhosamente. "Puro e limpo" significa que ele não mistura nenhuma visão corrompida. "Completo" significa que não há nada em falta. "Prática pura" (brahmacarya) designa as virtudes nobres imaculadas. Por causa destas razões, o Dharma deve ser venerado.

segments.label: 7 眾法品 (On Each Dharma | Sobre Cada Dharma)

content.zh:
復次佛自讚言：我法能滅、能到涅槃、能生正智、能善將導。能滅
者，滅貪恚等諸煩惱火，故曰能滅。如習不淨觀滅婬欲火，如習慈
心滅瞋恚等，不如外道斷食等法，故名能滅。能到涅槃者，佛法究
竟必至涅槃，不如外道住有分中著禪定等。又佛法中說一切有為皆
有過患，無稱讚處，不如婆羅門讚梵世等，故名佛法能到涅槃。能
生正智者，所有佛法皆為涅槃，是故能生正智。又佛法中有真智
果，如從聞慧生思慧、從思慧生修慧，故名佛法能生正智。能善將
導者，佛法先自善成，後令他人住正法中，故名善導。

復次佛法有
六：一曰善說、二曰現報、三曰無時、四曰能將、五曰來嘗、六曰
智者自知。善說者，佛說諸法如法實相，若不善法說不善相、善說
善相，故名善說。現報者，佛法能得現世果報，

如經中說：晨朝受
化令夕得道，夕為說法令朝得利。又現報者，如說現在，《沙門果
經》中說：現得恭敬名聞、禪定神通等利。

復次佛法皆有義理，故
能致得恭敬現報、後報及涅槃報；諸外道法無義理故，尚無現報及
後世報，何況涅槃，故曰現報。無時者，佛法不待某日月歲星宿吉
凶乃得修道、某日月歲不得修道，不如婆羅門法，初春婆羅門受
火、春末剎利受火等，復有或待日出或日未出而供養火，如見五穀
待時而種，或謂佛法亦當如是，故說無時。

如經中說：佛法易行，
行住坐臥無時不得。能將者，以正行故能將眾生至解脫處，故名能
將。來嘗者，佛法應當自身作證，不但隨他。如佛語比丘：汝等莫
但信我語也，當自思惟是法可行、是不可行。不如外道語弟子言：
捨是問答，如人淨洗不喜塵土，當如聾瘂但隨我語。故曰來嘗。智
者自知者，是佛法利，智慧人乃能信解；斷食等麁，愚者信樂，智
者不受，以正智慧能破煩惱，如是等法智者乃解。雖以甘饍充足其
身，一心精進貪恚不染，如是等事智者現知，如人病愈自知得離，
如水相冷飲者乃知。

復次或有過語法，如地堅相。堅何等相？不得
語答，觸乃可知，如生盲人不可語以青黃赤白。若人不得佛法味
者，不可語以佛法實義，以寂滅故。

復次佛法可自證知，不可以己
所證傳與他人，如財物等。如《婆羅延經》中佛言：我不能自斷汝
疑，能證我法汝疑自斷。

復次是法到他身時，不可得見如火傳等。
又凡夫愚人為無明山所障覆故不信是法，如因阿夷羅曰沙彌說大山
喻，故言智者自知。

復次佛法甚深、開示則淺，斷除虛偽，流布天
人。甚深者，佛法甚深，以不知因故。世間多見現果、不能知因，
故說自在天等邪因。十二因緣深故難解，世間智淺，於佛法中不生
深想，不能通達眾因緣法。乃至小草以眾因緣思惟觀察，其相轉
深。

如佛所說：眾因緣法，是事甚深。愛盡離滅及涅槃處，是亦難
見。
問曰：若因緣甚深，阿難何故生淺想耶？

答曰：有論師言，是語不
然。阿難是大弟子，通達法相，云何當言因緣法淺？又若以總相觀
因緣法，故生淺想。

所以者何？是人不能善分別觀煩惱業故。

復次
若人於本所學事得究竟，便生淺想，如得大智還觀初章。或復有人
智慧未成，於甚深法則生淺想。又佛善說法故，或有眾生便生淺
想。

復次佛法皆空，是空甚深，佛以種種因緣譬喻宣示，義則易
解，小兒亦知，如須陀耶沙彌等。

復次佛法堅固，諸言說中最為真
實，不如婆羅陀羅摩延經等但有語言、無有實義。如盧提梵志言：
世尊！諸比丘等於利益法真實法中精勤修學，所謂漏盡。

復次佛法
為利益一切世間故說，不如婆羅門言婆羅門法但自得道，餘人不
得。又佛法尊重，諸天王等五欲自恣亦來信受。以是因緣故應禮
法。
content.en:
Seventh Section: The Qualities of the Dharma

Furthermore, the Buddha himself praised it, saying: "My Dharma is able to extinguish, able to lead to nirvāṇa, able to give rise to correct wisdom, and able to guide well."
"Able to extinguish" means that it extinguishes the fires of the afflictions (kleśas) such as greed (rāga), aversion (dveṣa), and so forth; hence, it is called "able to extinguish." For example, the practice of contemplating impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) extinguishes the fire of sensual desire, and the practice of a mind of loving-kindness (maitrī-citta) extinguishes aversion and so forth. This is unlike the methods of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), such as fasting; hence, it is called "able to extinguish."
"Able to lead to nirvāṇa" means that the Buddha-Dharma ultimately and certainly arrives at nirvāṇa. This is unlike the non-Buddhists who abide in the realms of existence (bhava) and are attached to meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the like. Also, in the Buddha-Dharma, it is taught that all conditioned things (saṃskṛta) are fraught with peril, with nothing worthy of praise. This is unlike the brahmins who praise the world of Brahmā and so forth. Hence, the Buddha-Dharma is called "able to lead to nirvāṇa."
"Able to give rise to correct wisdom" means that since all of the Buddha-Dharma is for the sake of nirvāṇa, it is therefore able to give rise to correct wisdom (samyak-jñāna).

Moreover, within the Buddha-Dharma there is the fruit of true wisdom. For example, from the wisdom that arises from hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā) arises the wisdom that arises from reflection (cintāmayī-prajñā), and from the wisdom that arises from reflection arises the wisdom that arises from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā). Hence, the Buddha-Dharma is called "able to give rise to correct wisdom."
"Able to guide well" means that the Buddha-Dharma is first well-established in oneself, and afterwards enables others to abide in the true Dharma. Hence, it is called "good guidance."

Furthermore, the Buddha-Dharma has six qualities: first, it is well-expounded (svākhyāta); second, it is directly visible (sāṃdṛṣṭika); third, it is immediate (akālika); fourth, it is leading onward (aupanayika); fifth, it is inviting inspection (ehipaśyika); sixth, it is to be cognized by the wise for themselves (pratyātma-vedanīyo vijñaiḥ).
"Well-expounded" means that the Buddha teaches all dharmas according to their real characteristics. If a dharma is unwholesome, he explains its unwholesome characteristic; if it is wholesome, he explains its wholesome characteristic. Hence, it is called "well-expounded."
"Directly visible" means that the Buddha-Dharma can yield a result (vipāka) in the present life. As it is said in a sūtra: "If taught in the morning, one can attain the path by evening; if taught in the evening, one can attain the benefit by morning."

Moreover, "directly visible" refers to present benefits, as explained in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta (DN 2 or Dīrgha Āgama 27), where it states that one presently obtains the benefits of respect, fame, meditative absorption, and supernormal powers (abhijñā).

Furthermore, because the Buddha-Dharma is entirely endowed with meaning and principle, it can bring about the result of respect in the present, results in future lives, and the result of nirvāṇa. The teachings of the non-Buddhists, being devoid of meaning and principle, do not even yield present or future results, let alone nirvāṇa. Hence, it is called "directly visible."
"Immediate" means that with the Buddha-Dharma, one does not have to wait for a particular month, day, year, or auspicious or inauspicious astrological configuration to be able to cultivate the path; nor are there particular months, days, or years when one cannot cultivate the path. This is unlike the methods of the brahmins, where brahmins accept the ritual fire in early spring, kṣatriyas accept it in late spring, and so on. There are also those who wait for sunrise or before sunrise to make offerings to the fire. Just as one sees that grain must wait for the right season to be planted, one might think the Buddha-Dharma is also like this. Therefore, it is said to be "immediate." As it is stated in a sūtra: "The Buddha-Dharma is easy to practice; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is no time when it cannot be done."
"Leading onward" means that through correct practice, it can lead sentient beings to the state of liberation (vimokṣa). Hence, it is called "leading onward."
"Inviting inspection" means that one should personally bear witness to the Buddha-Dharma, not merely follow others. As the Buddha said to the monks: "You should not merely believe my words, but should reflect for yourselves whether this Dharma is to be practiced or not to be practiced." (cf. Kālāma Sutta, AN 3.65). This is unlike the non-Buddhists who tell their disciples: "Abandon this questioning and answering. Just as a person who has washed himself clean dislikes dust, so you should be like the deaf and mute and simply follow my words." Therefore, it is called "inviting inspection."
"To be cognized by the wise for themselves" means that only people of wisdom can believe in and understand the benefits of the Buddha-Dharma. Coarse practices like fasting are believed in and enjoyed by the foolish, but are not accepted by the wise. That correct wisdom can destroy the afflictions—such a dharma is understood only by the wise. Even while nourishing the body with fine food, to be single-mindedly diligent and undefiled by greed and aversion—such matters are directly cognized by the wise. It is like when a person recovers from an illness and cognizes for himself that he is free of it, or like the characteristic of water being cold, which is cognized only by the one who drinks it.

Furthermore, there are some dharmas that transcend language, such as the characteristic of hardness in the earth element. What is the characteristic of hardness? It cannot be answered in words; it can only be cognized through tactile contact. It is like being unable to describe blue, yellow, red, and white to a person born blind. If a person has not tasted the flavor of the Buddha-Dharma, one cannot describe its real meaning to them, because it is quiescent extinction (śānta).

Furthermore, the Buddha-Dharma can be personally verified and cognized, but what one has verified cannot be transmitted to another person like material goods. As the Buddha says in the Pārāyana-vagga (Sutta Nipāta V): "I cannot by myself cut off your doubt. When you are able to verify my Dharma, your doubt will be cut off by itself."

Furthermore, when this Dharma reaches another's person, it cannot be perceived, unlike the transmission of fire. Also, ordinary, foolish people are obstructed and covered over by the mountain of ignorance (avidyā) and so do not have faith in this Dharma, as explained in the parable of the great mountain for the novice Aciravata (Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.247). Therefore, it is said, "to be cognized by the wise for themselves."

Furthermore, the Buddha-Dharma is profound (gambhīra), but when explained, it is simple. It eliminates the false and is propagated among gods and humans. "Profound" means that the Buddha-Dharma is profound because the cause (hetu) is not cognized. The world mostly perceives the present effect (phala) but cannot cognize the cause; therefore, they posit erroneous causes (mithyā-hetu) like a creator god (Īśvara) and so forth. The twelve links of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) are profound and thus difficult to understand. The wisdom of the world is shallow; it does not generate a deep conception regarding the Buddha-Dharma and cannot penetrate the dharma of manifold causes and conditions. Even a tiny blade of grass, when reflected upon and examined through its manifold causes and conditions, has a characteristic that becomes ever more profound. As the Buddha said: "This dharma of manifold causes and conditions is a profound matter." The exhaustion of craving, dispassion, cessation, and the state of nirvāṇa are also difficult to perceive.

Question: If dependent origination is profound, why did Ānanda generate the thought that it was simple? (cf. Mahānidāna Sutta, DN 15).

Answer: Some masters of treatises say this account is not accurate. Ānanda was a great disciple who had penetrated the characteristics of dharmas. How could he have said that the dharma of dependent origination was simple? Alternatively, if one observes the dharma of dependent origination in a general way, one generates the thought that it is simple.

Why is this? Because such a person is unable to skillfully and analytically observe the afflictions and actions (kleśa-karman).

Furthermore, if a person attains the culmination of what they originally studied, they may generate the thought that it is simple, just as one who has attained great wisdom looks back at the first chapter. Or again, there are some whose wisdom is not yet mature, and they generate the thought that a profound dharma is simple. Also, because the Buddha teaches the Dharma skillfully, some sentient beings may generate the thought that it is simple.

Furthermore, all dharmas in the Buddha's teaching are empty (śūnya). This emptiness is profound. The Buddha proclaims and reveals it through various causes, conditions, and parables, and so its meaning becomes easy to understand, such that even a young child can cognize it, like the novice Sudāya and others.

Furthermore, the Buddha-Dharma is solid; among all doctrines, it is the most true. It is not like the Bhārata or Rāmāyaṇa scriptures, which consist only of language but have no real meaning. As the brahmin Lohicca said: "World-Honored One! The monks diligently train and study in the beneficial Dharma, the true Dharma, which is the exhaustion of the contaminants (āsrava-kṣaya)." (cf. Lohicca Sutta, DN 12).

Furthermore, the Buddha-Dharma is taught for the benefit of the entire world. This is unlike the brahmins who say that through the brahminical dharma, only they themselves can attain the path, while others cannot.
Also, the Buddha-Dharma is respected; kings of the gods and others who indulge freely in the five sensual pleasures also come to accept it with faith.
For these reasons, one should venerate the Dharma.
content.pt:
Sétima Seção: As Qualidades do Dharma

Além disso, o próprio Buda o elogiou, dizendo: "Meu Dharma é capaz de extinguir, capaz de conduzir ao nirvāṇa, capaz de dar origem à sabedoria correta, e capaz de levar ao bem, porque é exposto pelo Perfeitamente Desperto (Samyaksaṃbuddha)." O poder para cortar a ignorância (avidyā) etc. se chama capaz de extinguir; afastar-se dos cinco destinos (gati) para o supremo lugar incondicionado chama-se capaz de conduzir ao nirvāṇa (aupanayika). O conhecimento exaustivo sem resquício é dar origem à sabedoria correta; tornar-se um campo de mérito é chamado levar ao bem. Como ele destrói todas as aflições (kleśa) e assegura as qualidades sublimes, o Buda disse: "Eu atingi o despertar perfeito e conheço estes pormenores".

Ademais, o Dharma do Buda é livre dos defeitos da imoderação, por não louvar o extremo do prazer dos desejos nem o ascetismo extremo. O Dharma abandona ambos os extremos e trilha o caminho do meio (madhyamā-pratipad).

Além disso, o Dharma é bom (kalyāṇa) porque produz os frutos de entrada na correnteza (srotāpatti) e as demais santidades até o arhat, perfeitamente e sem desvios. Aquele que o ouve pode obter esses mesmos frutos, portanto não é ineficaz.

segments.label: 8 十二部經品 (On the Twelve-Fold Scripture | Os Doze Tipos de Escritura)

content.zh:
復次佛法分別有十二種：一修多羅、二祇夜、三和伽羅那、四伽
陀、五憂陀那、六尼陀那、七阿波陀那、八伊帝曰多伽、九闍陀
伽、十鞞佛略、十一阿浮多達磨、十二憂波提舍。修多羅者，直說
語言。祇夜者，以偈頌修多羅，或佛自說、或弟子說。
問曰：何故以偈頌修多羅？

答曰：欲令義理堅固，如以繩貫華次第
堅固。又欲嚴飾言辭令人喜樂，如以散華或持貫華以為莊嚴。又義
入偈中則要略易解。或有眾生樂直言者、有樂偈說。又先直說法，
後以偈頌，則義明了，令信堅固。又義入偈中，則次第相著，易可
讚說，是故說偈。或謂佛法不應造偈似如歌詠。此事不然，法應造
偈。

所以者何？佛自以偈說諸義故。又如經言：一切世間微妙言辭
皆出我法。是故偈頌有微妙語。
和伽羅那者，諸解義經名和伽羅耶。若有經無答無解，如四無礙等
經，名修多羅。有問答經，名和伽羅那。如說四種人，有從冥入
冥、從冥入明、從明入冥、從明入明。從冥入冥者，如貧賤人造三
惡業墮惡道等。如是等經名和伽羅那。
問曰：佛何故說無答無解經？

答曰：有經義理深重，是經義阿毘曇
中當別說，是故不解。或有人言：佛所說經皆有義解，但集法者撰
深義經置阿毘曇中。如因內結外結，人終夜解義，此義應在結使聚
中。
伽陀者，第二部說祇夜。祇夜名偈，偈有二種：一名伽陀、二名路
伽。路伽有二種：一順煩惱、二不順煩惱。不順煩惱者，祇夜中
說，是名伽陀。除二種偈，餘非偈經名憂陀那。尼陀那者，是經因
緣。

所以者何？諸佛賢聖所說經法要有因緣，此諸經緣或在修多羅
中或在餘處，是名尼陀那。阿波陀那者，本末次第說是也。如經中
說：智者言說則有次第，有義有解不令散亂，是名阿波陀那。伊帝
曰多伽者，是經因緣及經次第。若此二經在過去世，名伊帝曰多
伽，秦言此事過去如是。闍陀伽者，因現在事說過去事。如來雖說
未來世事，是事皆因過去現在故不別說。鞞佛略者，佛廣說經名鞞
佛略。有人不信，謂諸大聖樂寂滅故，不喜憒閙、厭世雜語，拔樂
眾根故不樂廣說，

如經中說：有得道人過二月已乃出一言。為斷此
故，說有廣經，饒益他故。如說如來二種說法：一廣、二略，廣勝
略故。阿浮陀達磨者，未曾有經。如說劫盡大變異事、諸天身量、
大地震動。有人不信如是等事，是故說此未曾有經，現業果報諸法
勢力不思議故。憂波提舍者，摩訶迦栴延等諸大智人廣解佛語，有
人不信謂非佛說，佛為是故說有論經。經有論故，義則易解。是十
二部經名為佛法。法寶具足如是功德，是故應禮。

僧寶論初
content.en:
Eighth Section: The Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras

Furthermore, the Buddha-Dharma is distinguished into twelve types: 1. Sūtra, 2. Geya, 3. Vyākaraṇa, 4. Gāthā, 5. Udāna, 6. Nidāna, 7. Avadāna, 8. Itivṛttaka, 9. Jātaka, 10. Vaipulya, 11. Adbhutadharma, and 12. Upadeśa.
Sūtra refers to prose teachings expressed directly.
Geya refers to versified repetitions of a sūtra, which may be spoken by the Buddha himself or by his disciples.

Question: Why is a sūtra repeated in verse?

Answer: To make the meaning and principle firm, just as flowers are held firmly in sequence when threaded on a string. Also, to adorn the words and bring joy to people, just as one uses scattered flowers or a garland of threaded flowers for adornment. Also, when the meaning is put into verse, it becomes concise and easy to understand. Some sentient beings prefer prose, while others prefer verse. Also, when the Dharma is first taught in prose and then repeated in verse, the meaning becomes clear and makes faith (śraddhā) firm. Also, when the meaning is put into verse, it is arranged in sequence and is easy to praise and recite. For these reasons, verses are spoken. Some might say that the Buddha-Dharma should not be composed in verse, as it resembles singing. This is not the case. The Dharma ought to be composed in verse.

Why is this? Because the Buddha himself used verses to explain various meanings. Also, as a sūtra says: "All the subtle and wondrous expressions in the world come from my Dharma." Therefore, verses contain subtle and wondrous language.
Vyākaraṇa refers to sūtras that explain meanings. If a sūtra has no answers or explanations, such as the sūtra on the four unhindered knowledges (catasṛ-pratisaṃvid), it is classified as a sūtra. A sūtra containing questions and answers is classified as a vyākaraṇa. For example, the teaching on the four kinds of persons: one who goes from darkness to darkness, one who goes from darkness to light, one who goes from light to darkness, and one who goes from light to light (cf. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.85). The one who goes from darkness to darkness is like a person of low and poor birth who performs the three kinds of evil actions and falls into a bad destiny (durgati), and so on. Sūtras like these are classified as vyākaraṇa.

Question: Why did the Buddha teach sūtras without answers or explanations?

Answer: Some sūtras have meanings and principles that are extremely profound. The meaning of such sūtras is to be explained separately in the Abhidharma; therefore, it is not explained in the sūtra itself. Alternatively, some say that all sūtras taught by the Buddha have explanations of their meaning, but the compilers of the Dharma selected the sūtras of profound meaning and placed them in the Abhidharma. For example, the teaching on the internal and external fetters, where a person spent the entire night explaining the meaning; this meaning belongs in the section on the fetters (saṃyojana).
Gāthā: The second division is called geya. Geya means "verse." There are two kinds of verse: one is called gāthā, the other is called loka [i.e., worldly poetry]. Loka is of two kinds: one that accords with the afflictions (kleśa) and one that does not accord with the afflictions. That which does not accord with the afflictions, spoken within a geya, is called gāthā.
Udāna refers to sūtras that are not in verse, excluding the two types of verse.
Nidāna refers to the causal circumstances of a sūtra.

Why is this? Because the sūtras and Dharma taught by the Buddhas and noble sages invariably have causal circumstances. These circumstances for the sūtras may be found within the sūtra itself or in another place. This is what is meant by nidāna.
Avadāna refers to a teaching that proceeds in sequence from beginning to end. As a sūtra says: "The speech of a wise person has a sequence; it has meaning and explanation and is not disordered." This is what avadāna means.
Itivṛttaka refers to the causal circumstances of a sūtra and the sequence of a sūtra. If these two aspects of a sūtra pertain to the past, it is called an itivṛttaka. In Chinese, this means, "this matter was thus in the past."
Jātaka refers to teachings that explain a past event based on a present event. Although the Tathāgata also speaks of future events, these events all depend on the past and present, so they are not separately classified.
Vaipulya refers to extensive sūtras taught by the Buddha. Some people do not believe this, thinking that because the great sages delight in quiescent extinction (śānta), they do not enjoy commotion, are averse to worldly conversation, and have uprooted the faculties that take pleasure in the manifold; therefore, they would not enjoy teaching at length. As a sūtra says: "There are people who have attained the path who, after more than two months, utter only a single word." To refute this, it is explained that there are extensive sūtras for the sake of benefiting others. As it is said, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma in two ways: one extensive, one concise. Extensive is better than concise.
Adbhutadharma refers to sūtras on wondrous events. For example, teachings on the great transformations at the end of an aeon (kalpa), the physical dimensions of the gods, and great earthquakes. Some people do not believe such things. Therefore, these sūtras on wondrous events are taught to show that the karmic results manifesting from actions and the power of dharmas are inconceivable (acintya).
Upadeśa refers to the extensive explanations of the Buddha's words by greatly wise individuals such as Mahākātyāyana. Some people do not believe these and say they are not the Buddha's speech. For their sake, the Buddha explained that there are sūtras of doctrinal discussion. Because the sūtras have these discussions, their meaning becomes easy to understand.
These twelve divisions of the sūtras are called the Buddha-Dharma. The Dharma-Treasure is complete in such meritorious qualities; for this reason, it should be venerated.

	•	On the Sangha Jewel (僧寶論)
content.pt:
Oitava Seção: As Doze Divisões dos Sūtras

Além disso, o Buddha-Dharma se distingue em doze tipos: 1. Sūtra, 2. Geya, 3. Vyākaraṇa, 4. Gāthā, 5. Udāna, 6. Nidāna, 7. Avadāna, 8. Itivṛttaka, 9. Jātaka, 10. Vaipulya, 11. Adbhutadharma, 12. Upadeśa.

Sūtra refere-se a ensinamentos onde o Buda fala diretamente os quatro dharmas de moralidade (śīla), generosidade (dāna) etc. Algumas vezes ele nomeia certas práticas. Tudo isto é chamado Sūtra.
Geya refere-se a versos. Existem dois tipos: gāthā (verso do Dharma) e loka (verso mundano que acompanha as aflições). O gāthā é o que não acompanha as aflições (kleśa).
Vyākaraṇa é a explicação profética das vidas futuras dos discípulos.
Gāthā são estrofes poéticas sem prosa.
Udāna são sūtras ensinados pelo Buda por sua própria iniciativa, sem ninguém ter perguntado, expressando a exultação pela sabedoria profunda.
Nidāna são os relatos das origens e circunstâncias que levaram o Buda a dar um certo ensinamento ou estabelecer um preceito.
Avadāna refere-se a ensinamentos com explicações lógicas em sequência de causa e efeito e analogias.
Itivṛttaka denota "Assim foi dito no passado".
Jātaka são histórias dos nascimentos passados do Buda nas suas vidas de Bodhisattva.
Vaipulya são os sūtras extensos com ensinamentos amplos e profundos visando o benefício vasto dos seres.
Adbhutadharma aborda os eventos miraculosos e maravilhosos (como os tremores de terra e dimensões divinas).
Upadeśa consiste em debates e explicações detalhadas da doutrina, frequentemente por discípulos sábios como Mahākātyāyana, esclarecendo e categorizando o significado das falas do Buda.

Essas doze divisões perfazem o Dharma sagrado. A Joia do Dharma é completa e perfeita nestas qualidades; por essa razão, deve ser venerada.

segments.label: 9 清淨品 (On Purity | Sobre a Pureza)

content.zh:
問曰：汝先言應禮僧，何故應禮？

答曰：佛於處處自讚歎僧，是僧
寶戒品清淨，定品、慧品、解脫品、解脫知見品清淨，應請、應
禮、合掌、供養，無上福田、能益施者。戒品清淨者，佛弟子眾持
戒無瑕，乃至小罪深懷畏懼。又佛弟子不為福報生人天等，亦不怖
畏墮地獄等，而勤持戒但樂善法，故名清淨。又持淨戒不限時節，
不如婆羅門六月持戒，長夜受持乃至究竟，故名清淨。又持淨戒離
於二邊，離五欲樂亦離苦身，故名聖所愛戒，是戒名為智者所愛。
又心淨故戒亦清淨。又深心止惡，不但守戒怖畏後世，故名僧寶戒
品清淨。定品清淨者，若定能生真智，故名清淨。慧品清淨者，若
慧能盡煩惱，故名清淨。解脫清淨者，若得盡諸煩惱非但能遮，故
名解脫清淨。解脫知見清淨者，於諸煩惱盡中得智，謂我生盡，非
未盡煩惱中言我生盡，是名解脫知見清淨。應請應禮應供養者，以
能具足如是功德故，應求請禮敬供養。福田者，於中殖福獲報無
量，乃至涅槃猶不可盡。能益施者，能令施者功德增益。如八功德
田滋茂五穀不令敗壞，僧田亦爾，成就八功德故，能令施種功德增
長，是故應禮。

19
content.en:
Treatise on the Saṅgha-Treasure, First Part: Ninth Section on Purity

Question: You stated previously that one should venerate the Saṅgha. For what reason should it be venerated?

Answer: The Buddha himself praised the Saṅgha in various places. This Saṅgha-treasure is pure in the aggregate of moral discipline (śīla-skandha), pure in the aggregate of concentration (samādhi-skandha), pure in the aggregate of wisdom (prajñā-skandha), pure in the aggregate of liberation (vimukti-skandha), and pure in the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha). It is worthy of invitation, worthy of veneration, worthy of palms joined in respect, worthy of offerings, an unsurpassed field of merit (puṇya-kṣetra), and able to benefit the donor.
"Pure in the aggregate of moral discipline" means that the community of the Buddha's disciples maintains the moral precepts without flaw, holding a deep sense of fear even regarding minor offenses.

Moreover, the Buddha's disciples do not diligently maintain the moral precepts for the sake of meritorious rewards such as birth among humans or gods (devas), nor out of fear of falling into the hells and the like. Rather, they do so simply out of delight in wholesome dharmas. Therefore, it is called "pure." Also, they maintain the pure moral precepts without being limited by time or season, unlike the brahmins who maintain precepts for six months. They undertake and maintain them for a long time, until the very end. Therefore, it is called "pure." Also, in maintaining the pure moral precepts, they are free from the two extremes: they are free from the pleasure of the five sensual desires and also free from self-mortification. Therefore, it is called the moral discipline cherished by the noble ones (ārya), and this moral discipline is called that which is cherished by the wise.

Furthermore, because the mind (citta) is pure, the moral discipline is also pure. Also, with a profound mind, they cease evil, not merely observing the precepts out of fear of a future life. Therefore, the Saṅgha-treasure is called "pure in the aggregate of moral discipline."
"Pure in the aggregate of concentration" means that if a state of concentration (samādhi) is able to give rise to true wisdom, it is therefore called "pure."
"Pure in the aggregate of wisdom" means that if a state of wisdom (prajñā) is able to exhaust the afflictions (kleśa), it is therefore called "pure."
"Pure in liberation" means that if one attains the exhaustion of all afflictions, not merely their suppression, it is therefore called "pure in liberation" (vimukti).
"Pure in the knowledge and vision of liberation" means that one obtains the cognition (jñāna) that "my births are exhausted" upon the exhaustion of all afflictions. It does not mean saying "my births are exhausted" while the afflictions are not yet exhausted. This is what is meant by "pure in the knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimukti-jñāna-darśana).
"Worthy of invitation, worthy of veneration, worthy of offerings" means that because they are complete in such meritorious qualities, one should request their presence, venerate them, and make offerings.
"A field of merit" (puṇya-kṣetra) means that by planting merit therein, one obtains immeasurable rewards, which are not exhausted even up to the attainment of nirvāṇa.
"Able to benefit the donor" means that it can cause the donor's merit to increase. Just as a field with eight excellent qualities nourishes the five grains and does not let them spoil, so too is the field of the Saṅgha. Because it possesses the eight excellent qualities, it can cause the seeds of giving (dāna) to grow in merit. For this reason, it should be venerated.
content.pt:
Nona Seção sobre a Pureza

Pergunta: Você declarou anteriormente que se deve venerar o Saṅgha. Por qual razão deve ser venerado?

Resposta: O próprio Buda elogiou o Saṅgha em vários lugares. Este Saṅgha é puro no agregado da disciplina moral (śīla-skandha), puro no agregado da concentração (samādhi-skandha), puro no agregado da sabedoria (prajñā-skandha), puro no agregado da libertação (vimukti-skandha) e puro no agregado do conhecimento e visão da libertação (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha). É digno de convite, digno de veneração, digno de mãos juntas em respeito, digno de oferendas, um insuperável campo de mérito (puṇya-kṣetra), e capaz de beneficiar o doador.

"Puro no agregado da disciplina moral" significa que a comunidade de discípulos do Buda mantém os preceitos morais sem falha, guardando um profundo temor mesmo em relação a pequenas ofensas. Não mantêm os preceitos pelo desejo de recompensas celestiais nem pelo medo do inferno, mas sim pelo deleite nos dharmas salutares.

"Puro no agregado da concentração" significa que um estado de samādhi é capaz de originar a verdadeira sabedoria, sendo assim "puro".

"Puro no agregado da sabedoria" quer dizer que a sabedoria (prajñā) pode exaurir as aflições (kleśa), e portanto é pura.

"Puro na libertação" (vimukti) significa atingir a total exaustão das aflições, e não apenas sua supressão.

"Puro no conhecimento e visão da libertação" (vimukti-jñāna-darśana) designa o conhecimento (jñāna) irrefutável de que "meus nascimentos estão exauridos".

"Digno de convite, veneração e oferendas" mostra que a comunidade detém tais qualidades e por isso merece as devidas homenagens e provisões, sendo um verdadeiro campo de mérito (puṇya-kṣetra) onde as sementes da doação (dāna) frutificam incomensuravelmente, tal como a terra fértil nutre e guarda as boas sementes, não as deixando perecer e beneficiando o doador.

segments.label: 10 分別賢聖品 (On Distinguishing the Sages and Noble Ones | Sábios e Nobres)

content.zh:
問曰：以何法故名之為僧？

答曰：四行四得戒定慧等功德清淨，故
名為僧。四行者，行須陀洹、行斯陀含、行阿那含、行阿羅漢。四
得者，須陀洹、斯陀含、阿那含、阿羅漢。行須陀洹有三種人：一
隨信行、二隨法行、三隨無相行。信行者，若人未得空無我智，信
佛法故隨佛語行，故名信行。

如經中說：我於是事以信故行。若得
真智則不但隨信行，

如經中說：知不作者、不信者等，是名上人。
是故當知未得真智名隨信行，

如經中說：若人於法能以少慧觀忍樂
者，是名信行。過凡夫地、未得須陀洹果，於其中間不得命終，是
名信行。是人在聞思慧中正觀諸法，心忍欲樂，雖未得空無我智，
能生世間似忍法心，自此以來名過凡夫地。

所以者何？後當廣說。
若無信等五根，是人則住外凡夫中。是人漸習得煖法等修慧，仍本
名故，亦名信行，以終不及法行人故。是經應言要必當得須陀洹
果，不應言不得命終。

所以者何？是信行者以尚遠故。如郁伽長者
供養眾僧，天神示言：某是阿羅漢、某是行阿羅漢者，乃至某是須
陀洹、某是行須陀洹者。若在十五心中，不可得示，當知行須陀洹
者有近有遠，是名信行。法行者，是人得空無我智，在煖頂忍第一
法中隨順法行。謂空無我等是名法行，是二行人。入見諦道，見滅
諦故名無相行。是三種人，名行須陀洹果者，世俗道中無斷結故，
不得名為行三果者。此事後當說。須陀洹者，

如佛經說：若人斷三
結，身見、疑、戒取，名須陀洹，不墮惡道，必得正智，極至七
有。
問曰：若須陀洹見諦所斷煩惱都盡，滅無量苦，如《池喻經》說，
何故但言斷三結耶？

答曰：此事後當廣說，謂身見盡故餘等亦盡。
不墮惡道者，後業聚中亦當廣說。必至菩提者，是人入法流中必至
涅槃。如木在恒河，離八因緣必到大海。極七有者，是人於七世中
無漏智熟，如歌羅羅等七日變成；又如服酥等，極至七日堅病則
消；又如親族限至七世；又如七步蛇螫人身時，以四大力故得至七
步，以毒力故不得至八；又欺誑法極至七世；又如七日出時則劫燒
盡。如是七世集無漏慧燒煩惱盡。又法應七有，有須陀洹今世入涅
槃，有第二第三極至第七，是名須陀洹。行斯陀含者，思惟所斷結
有九品，若斷一二至三四五，是名行斯陀含者。有人言：以一無礙
道斷。是事不然，佛經中說以無量心斷，如《斧柯喻經》中說。又
行斯陀含者，亦名家家，是人或二或三往來，或於現身得入涅槃，
是名行斯陀含者。斯陀含者，一來此間便入涅槃。是人思惟所斷結
薄，住是薄中，名斯陀含。是斯陀含，或今世入涅槃。行阿那含
者，若斷第七第八品結，是人皆名行阿那含，斷第八品是名一種。
行阿那含者，或有今世即入涅槃。盡離欲界九品結故，名阿那含。
是阿那含差別八種，所謂中陰滅者、有生有滅者、有不行滅者、有
行滅者、有上行至阿迦尼吒滅者、有至無色處者、有轉世者、有現
滅者，隨上中下根故有差別。中陰滅者亦有三種，上、中、下根。
有阿那含深厭世間，有少障礙不得現滅，是人則於中陰中滅。生亦
三種，謂生滅者、行滅者、不行滅者。生滅者，生時深厭離有即入
涅槃，是名生滅，以根利故。或有生已諸無漏道自然在前，不加勤
行而入涅槃，是不行滅，以根中故。或有生已深畏受身，勤修行道
乃入涅槃，是名行滅，以根鈍故。上行滅者亦有三種，若從一處終
至一處生，便入涅槃，是名利根；二三處生，是名中根；一切處終
一切處生，是名鈍根。從初禪至廣果天是名決定。到廣果已若生淨
居，是人不復到無色處，以樂慧故。若入無色處者，是人終不生淨
居天，以樂定故。轉世者，若先世得須陀洹果、斯陀含果，後轉身
得阿那含果，是人不入色無色界。現滅者，第一利根，即於現身得
入涅槃。復有二人，一名信解脫、二名見得，是二人者根差別故。
若鈍根學人在思惟道名信解脫，利名見得。若阿那含具八解脫，是
名身證。是等皆名行阿羅漢者，以斷結同故。若盡斷滅一切煩惱，
名阿羅漢。阿羅漢有九種，退相、守相、死相、可進相、住相、不
壞相、慧解脫相、俱解脫相、不退相。是諸阿羅漢，以得信等根故
有差別。最鈍根者是名退相，退失三昧，退三昧故無漏智慧不能現
前。守相者，根小勝故，若護三昧則不退失、不護則退。前退相
者，雖護亦退。死相者，根又小勝，深厭諸有，是人不能得三昧
故，無漏智慧難得現前，設得喜失，故求死也。住相者，若得三昧
不進不退是名住相。前三種在退分三昧，住相者在住分三昧。可進
相者，若得三昧轉深增益，是人住在增分三昧。不壞相者，得三昧
已，種種因緣不能敗壞，是人住在達分三昧，慧最利故，善取三昧
入住起相，故不可壞，因滅盡定故。有二人，不得此定名慧解脫，
得此定者名俱解脫。不退相者，所得功德盡無退失。如經中說，佛
語比丘：若我弟子以床輿我，我先所得盡無退失。如是九種名無學
人。先十八學人及九無學，是二十七人名為一切世間福田，僧中具
足，是故應禮也。

Tenth Section: Distinguishing the Noble Sages

Question: Due to what dharmas is one called a member of the Saṅgha?

Answer: One is called a member of the Saṅgha because of purity in the meritorious qualities of moral discipline (śīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (prajñā), and so forth, which characterize the four [types of individuals] practicing the path and the four [types of individuals] who have attained the fruit.
The four practicing the path are: the one practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpatti-pratipannaka), the one practicing for the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka), the one practicing for the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmi-pratipannaka), and the one practicing for the fruit of an arhat (arhat-pratipannaka). The four who have attained the fruit are: the stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the non-returner (anāgāmin), and the arhat.
Among those practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer, there are three types of person: 1. the faith-follower (śraddhānusārin), 2. the dharma-follower (dharmānusārin), and 3. the formless-follower (anākāra-cārin).
The faith-follower is a person who has not yet attained the wisdom (jñāna) of emptiness and no-ātman but who, due to faith (śraddhā) in the Buddha's teaching, practices in accordance with the Buddha's words. Hence, they are called a faith-follower. As it says in a sūtra: "Regarding this matter, I proceed on account of faith." If one has attained true wisdom, one does not proceed merely by following faith. As a sūtra says: "One who cognizes, who is not a 'doer,' not a 'believer'..." this is called a superior person. Therefore, it should be cognized that one who has not yet attained true wisdom is called a faith-follower. As a sūtra says: "A person who is able to contemplate, accept, and delight in the Dharma with a little wisdom is called a faith-follower." This person has passed beyond the stage of an ordinary being (pṛthagjana) but has not yet attained the fruit of a stream-enterer. In this interim state, they cannot pass away. This is the faith-follower. This person, while in the stages of the wisdom arising from hearing and reflection, correctly contemplates all dharmas. Their mind (citta) accepts and delights in this. Although they have not yet attained the wisdom of emptiness and no-ātman, they are able to generate a worldly mind (citta) that has a quality resembling acceptance (kṣānti). From this point on, they are said to have passed beyond the stage of an ordinary being. The reason will be explained later. If a person does not have the five faculties (pañca-indriya) of faith, etc., they remain among the 'external' ordinary beings. As this person gradually practices and attains the wisdom arising from cultivation, such as the dharma of 'warmth' (uṣmagata), they are still called a faith-follower based on their original designation, because they are ultimately not equal to a dharma-follower. The sūtra should say, "they will certainly attain the fruit of a stream-enterer," not that "they cannot pass away," because the faith-follower is still far from the fruit. For example, when the householder Ugra was making offerings to the Saṅgha, a god pointed out to him: "This one is an arhat, this one is practicing for the fruit of an arhat... this one is a stream-enterer, this one is practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer." If one were in the fifteen moments of the mind of the path of vision, one could not be pointed out in this way. It should be cognized that among those practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer, some are near and some are far. This is the faith-follower.
The dharma-follower is a person who has attained the wisdom of emptiness and no-ātman and who, while in the stages of 'warmth' (uṣmagata), 'summits' (mūrdhan), 'acceptance' (kṣānti), and 'supreme worldly dharma' (laukikāgradharma), practices in accordance with the Dharma—that is, emptiness, no-ātman, and so forth. This is the dharma-follower.
When these two types of practitioner enter the path of vision (darśana-mārga) and perceive the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya), they are called formless-followers. These three types of person are called those practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer. Because no fetters (saṃyojana) are cut off on the worldly path (laukika-mārga), they cannot be called those practicing for the other three fruits. This matter will be explained later.
A stream-enterer (srotāpanna), as the Buddha's sūtras say, is a person who has cut off the three fetters: identity view (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and adherence to rules and observances (śīlavrata-parāmarśa). They are called a stream-enterer, are not subject to falling into bad destinies, will certainly attain correct wisdom, and will be reborn at most seven more times.

Question: If a stream-enterer has completely exhausted all the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of vision and has extinguished immeasurable suffering (duḥkha), as stated in the Parable of the Pond Sūtra, why is it said that they have cut off only three fetters?

Answer: This question will be explained later. In brief, because identity view is exhausted, the others are also exhausted.
That they are "not subject to falling into bad destinies" will also be explained at length later in the section on action (karman). That they "will certainly arrive at awakening (bodhi)" means that this person has entered the stream of the Dharma and will certainly arrive at nirvāṇa, just as a piece of wood in the Ganges river, if free from eight conditions, will certainly reach the great ocean. "At most seven more times" means that in seven lifetimes, this person's undefiled wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) matures, just as the kalala embryo develops in seven days. Or, it is like taking clarified butter, where after at most seven days a chronic illness is eliminated. Or, it is like kinship being limited to seven generations. Or, like a seven-step snake, when it bites a person, they can take up to seven steps due to the force of the four great elements (mahābhūta), but due to the force of the venom, they cannot reach the eighth. Or, a deceitful method lasts at most for seven generations. Or, like when the seven suns appear, the aeon is consumed by fire. In the same way, over seven lifetimes, one accumulates undefiled wisdom and burns up the afflictions.

Furthermore, the dharma dictates seven existences. There are stream-enterers who enter nirvāṇa in this very life, some in the second, some in the third, up to a maximum of the seventh. This is the stream-enterer.
One practicing for the fruit of a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka) is one who, with respect to the nine grades of fetters to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), has cut off from one or two up to three, four, or five. This is a practitioner for the fruit of a once-returner. Some say these are cut off with a single path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga). This is not correct. The Buddha's sūtras state that they are cut off with an immeasurable mind (citta), as stated in the Parable of the Saw Sūtra (Majjhima Nikāya 21 or Madhyama Āgama 193). Also, one practicing for the fruit of a once-returner is also called a 'clan-to-clan' (kolaṃkola). This person may pass from birth to birth two or three times, or may enter nirvāṇa in the present life. This is one practicing for the fruit of a once-returner.
A once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) returns to this world once and then enters nirvāṇa. This person's fetters to be abandoned by the path of cultivation are attenuated, and they abide in this state of attenuation. This is a once-returner. This once-returner may also enter nirvāṇa in the present life.
One practicing for the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmi-pratipannaka) is a person who has cut off the seventh or eighth grade of fetters. One who has cut off the eighth grade is a specific type. A practitioner for the fruit of a non-returner may also enter nirvāṇa in this present life.
One who has completely cut off the nine grades of fetters of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is called a non-returner (anāgāmin). There are eight distinct types of non-returner: 1. one who attains extinction in the intermediate state (antarā-parinirvāyin), 2. one who attains extinction upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin), 3. one who attains extinction without exertion (asaṃskāra-parinirvāyin), 4. one who attains extinction with exertion (sasaṃskāra-parinirvāyin), 5. one who proceeds upstream to Akaniṣṭha (ūrdhvasrotas-akaniṣṭha-ga), 6. one who proceeds to the formless realm, 7. one who transmigrates, and 8. one who attains extinction in the present. These distinctions exist due to their superior, middling, or inferior faculties.
The one who attains extinction in the intermediate state also has three types, based on superior, middling, and inferior faculties. There is a non-returner who is deeply weary of the world but, due to some minor impediment, does not attain extinction in the present. This person then attains extinction in the intermediate state.
Those who attain extinction upon rebirth are also of three types: one who attains extinction upon rebirth, one who attains extinction with exertion, and one who attains extinction without exertion. The one who attains extinction upon rebirth is one who, at the time of rebirth, is deeply weary and detached from existence and immediately enters nirvāṇa. This is extinction upon rebirth, and it is due to sharp faculties. There is another who, after being reborn, finds that the undefiled paths naturally arise before them, and without applying diligent effort, they enter nirvāṇa. This is extinction without exertion, and it is due to middling faculties. There is another who, after being reborn, is deeply fearful of embodiment and, by diligently cultivating the path, enters nirvāṇa. This is extinction with exertion, and it is due to dull faculties.
Whoever goes upstream also has three types. If one passes away from one place and is reborn in one other place before entering nirvāṇa, this is one with sharp faculties. If reborn in two or three places, this is one with middling faculties. If one passes away from every place and is reborn in every place [up to Akaniṣṭha], this is one with dull faculties. Proceeding from the first dhyāna up to the Bṛhatphala heaven is definite. Having reached Bṛhatphala, if one is reborn in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), this person does not again proceed to the formless realm, because they delight in wisdom. If one enters the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu), this person is never reborn in the Pure Abodes, because they delight in concentration.
The one who transmigrates is a person who in a previous life attained the fruit of a stream-enterer or once-returner and in a later embodiment attains the fruit of a non-returner. This person does not enter the form or formless realms.
The one who attains extinction in the present is of the foremost sharp faculties and enters nirvāṇa in the present body.

Furthermore, there are two other types: one called liberated by faith (śraddhā-vimukta) and one called attained by view (dṛṣṭi-prāpta). These two are distinguished by their faculties. A practitioner with dull faculties on the path of cultivation is called liberated by faith; one with sharp faculties is called attained by view. If a non-returner has fully accomplished the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa), they are called a body-witness (kāya-sākṣin).
All of these types are called those practicing for the fruit of an arhat, because they share in the abandonment of fetters.
One who has completely cut off and extinguished all afflictions is called an arhat. There are nine kinds of arhat: 1. the one liable to fall back (parihāṇa-dharman), 2. the one who is on guard (anurakṣaṇā-dharman), 3. who thinks of death (cetana-dharman), 4. the one capable of advancing (prativedhanā-dharman), 5. the one who is stationary (sthita-dharman), 6. the one who is imperturbable (akopya-dharman), 7. the one liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta), 8. the one liberated in both ways (ubhayato-bhāga-vimukta), and 9. the one who is not liable to fall back (aparihāṇa-dharman).
These various arhats are distinguished by the faculties of faith, etc., that they have attained. The one with the dullest faculties is the one liable to fall back. They fall back from their concentration (samādhi), and because they fall back from concentration, their undefiled wisdom cannot manifest. The one who is on guard has slightly superior faculties. If they protect their concentration, they do not fall back. If they do not protect it, they fall back. The first type, the one liable to fall back, falls back even if they protect it. The one who thinks of death has faculties that are again slightly superior. They are deeply weary of all forms of existence. Because this person is unable to [easily] attain concentration, their undefiled wisdom is difficult to manifest. Even if it is attained, they are apt to lose it, and therefore they seek death. The one who is stationary is one who, having attained concentration, neither advances nor regresses. This is the stationary one. The first three types abide in a concentration that is in the category of regression. The stationary one abides in a concentration that is in the category of stability. The one capable of advancing is one who, having attained concentration, deepens and increases it. This person abides in a concentration that is in the category of progress. The one who is imperturbable is one who, having attained concentration, cannot be caused to lose it by any variety of conditions. This person abides in a concentration that is in the category of penetration, because their wisdom is extremely sharp and they are skilled at grasping the characteristics of entering, abiding in, and emerging from concentration. Therefore, they are imperturbable. This is due to the concentration of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). There are two types: one who does not attain this concentration is called liberated by wisdom; one who does attain this concentration is called liberated in both ways. The one who is not liable to fall back is one whose attained meritorious qualities are never lost. As it is said in a sūtra, the Buddha told a monk: "If my disciples were to carry me on a bier, what I have previously attained would never be lost."
These nine types are called those who are no-longer-trainees (aśaikṣa). The preceding eighteen trainees (śaikṣa) and the nine no-longer-trainees—these twenty-seven types of person—are called the field of merit for the entire world. They are fully present in the Saṅgha. For this reason, it should be venerated.
content.pt:
Décima Seção: Distinguindo os Nobres Sábios

Pergunta: Devido a quais dharmas alguém é chamado um membro da Saṅgha?

Resposta: Alguém é chamado membro da Saṅgha pela sua pureza nas qualidades meritórias expostas acima, tais como o agregado de sabedoria, moralidade e emancipação (vimukti). Existem 27 tipos de seres que cultivam o Caminho e recebem os frutos (phala): desde aqueles que estão ingressando na correnteza (srotāpanna), até o Arhat que completou o caminho sem resíduos (aśaikṣa). Esta coletividade sublime que alcança a imortalidade, que rompeu os laços dos desejos (kāma) e eliminou as tendências latentes da ignorância (avidyā-anuśaya), compõe a suprema Saṅgha que purifica o mundo. Por ser um corpo perfeitamente unido na pureza de corpo, fala e mente, o conjunto dos nobres discípulos constitui o campo do mérito primordial.

segments.label: 11 福田品 (On the Field of Merit | Campo de Mérito)

content.zh:
問曰：以何等故此諸賢聖名為福田？

答曰：斷貪恚等諸煩惱盡故名
福田，如說稊稗不去害善穀苗，是故施無欲人得報利大。又是人心
空故名福田。

所以者何？以空相故諸貪恚等煩惱不起、不生惡業。
又諸賢聖得不作法故名福田。又是人等所得禪定皆悉清淨，永離大
小諸煩惱故。又棄捨憂樂故名福田。又能斷除五種心縛，心得清淨
故名福田。又成就八種功德田故。又以七定具善護心故。又能盡滅
七種漏故，無諸漏失。又具足戒等七淨法故，又能成就少欲知足等
八功德故，又能度彼岸及勤求度故名福田。

又經中說：但能發心欲
行善法尚多利益，況修行耶。是諸賢聖常行善法，故名福田。又經
中說：誰施主家有持戒比丘，受供養已入無量定，是施主家得無量
福。眾中有入無量三昧、無相三昧、無動三昧，能令施主得無量
報，故名福田。

又經中說：三事和合故得大福，一曰有信、二曰施
物、三曰福田。於眾僧中多功德人，功德人中信心易生。又施眾僧
具九因緣故獲大果。又施眾僧，以受者淨故施必清淨。又施有八
種，有清淨心少、施物亦少、施破戒人，有清淨心少、所施物多、
施破戒人，有清淨心少、施物亦少、施持戒人，有清淨心少、所施
物多、施持戒人，有清淨心多、施四種物亦爾。於僧中施、必當成
就若二若三。一切善人皆因眾僧增益功德，然後隨意回向菩提。又
所施僧，此物皆當得解脫果，於生死中終不能盡。又所施眾僧皆為
嚴心。又若於一人生信淨心或時可壞，於眾僧中信心清淨終不壞
敗。又於一人生愛敬心或不能廣，於眾僧中生信敬心，緣無量故心
則廣大。又施為一切入僧數人，以心大故果報亦大。以是等緣諸賢
聖人名為福田，是故應禮。◎

◎
