segments.label: 131 邊見品 (On Extremist Views | Visão)

content.zh:
若說諸法或斷或常，是名邊見。有論師言，若人說我若斷若常，是
名邊見，非一切法。

所以者何？現見外物有斷滅故。經中說：有見
名常，無見名斷。又身即是神，名為斷見。身異神異，是名常見。
又死後不作名曰斷見，死後還作名為常見。死後亦作亦不作，是中
所有作者名常，所不作者名斷。非作非不作亦如是。
問曰：是第四不應名見。

答曰：是人於世諦中亦無人法，故名為
見。常無常邊無邊等四句亦如是。

又經中說：六觸入盡滅，有異餘
即為常，無異餘即名斷。又若見我先作，後當更作，是名常見；我
先不作，後不更作，是為斷見。又《邪見經》說：人身七分，地、
水、火、風、苦、樂、壽命。若其死時，四大歸本，根歸虛空。又
說：以刀輪害眾生，積為肉聚無殺生罪，是名斷見。及《梵網經》
中說斷見相，若言有後世，作者即是受者，是名常見。
問曰：斷常見云何生？

答曰：隨以何因緣說，死後還作是因緣，故
生常邊見。隨以何因緣說，死後不作是因緣，故生斷滅見。
問曰：此見云何斷？

答曰：正修習空則無我見，我見無故則無二
邊。如《炎摩伽經》中說：若一一陰非人，和合陰亦非人，離陰亦
非人。現在如是不可得，云何當說阿羅漢死後不作？故知人不可
得。人不可得故，我見及斷常見亦無。又見諸法從眾緣生，則無二
邊。又如說：見世間集則滅無見，見世間滅則滅有見。又行中道故
則滅二邊。

所以者何？見諸法相續生則滅斷見，見念念滅則滅常
見。

又說：五陰非即是人，亦不離陰是人，故知非常非斷。能得異
身故不得為一，俱是眾生故不得為異。又五陰相續故，有眾生生
死，是中不得言即，以是相續異故，亦不得言異，以相續中可說一
故。又從此陰彼陰異故不得言常，從自相續因緣力生故不得言斷。
content.en:
To say that the various dharmas are either annihilated or permanent is called the view of extremes (antagrāha-dṛṣṭi).

A master of treatises has said: If a person says that the ātman is either annihilated or permanent, this is called the view of extremes; it does not apply to all dharmas. Why is that? Because external objects are directly apprehended as being annihilated. In a sūtra it is said: "The view of existence (bhava-dṛṣṭi) is eternalism; the view of non-existence (vibhava-dṛṣṭi) is annihilationism." Also, [the view that] "the body is the same as the soul" is called the view of annihilationism. [The view that] "the body is different from the soul" is the view of eternalism. Also, [the view that] after death nothing further is created is called the view of annihilationism. [The view that] after death something is created again is called the view of eternalism. [The view that] after death something is both created and not created—in this, that which is the agent is called permanent, and that which is not the agent is called annihilated. The same applies to [the view that it is] neither created nor not created.

Question: This fourth [view] ought not to be called a view.

Answer: This person holds that in the conventional truth there is neither a person nor dharmas; therefore, it is called a view. The four propositions concerning permanent and impermanent, finite and infinite, and so on, are also like this.

Furthermore, in a sūtra it is said: "Upon the complete cessation of the six bases of contact, if there is something other that remains, this is eternalism. If there is nothing other that remains, this is annihilationism." Also, if one holds the view that the ātman acted previously and will act again in the future, this is the view of eternalism. [If one holds the view that] the ātman did not act previously and will not act again in the future, this is the view of annihilationism. Also, in the Sūtra on Wrong Views, it says that the human body has seven components: earth, water, fire, wind, pleasure, pain, and the life-force. At the time of death, the four great elements return to their source, and the faculties return to space. It also says: "By harming sentient beings with a wheel of blades, piling them up into a mound of flesh, there is no sin of taking life." This is called the view of annihilationism. And in the Brahmajāla Sutta (DN 1), the characteristics of the view of annihilationism are spoken of. If one says that there is a future life and that the agent is the same as the experiencer, this is the view of eternalism.

Question: How do the views of annihilationism and eternalism arise?

Answer: By whatever reason one asserts that after death something is created again, on account of this reason, the view of the extreme of eternalism arises. By whatever reason one asserts that after death nothing is created, on account of this reason, the view of annihilationism arises.

Question: How are these views to be severed?

Answer: By rightly cultivating emptiness, the view of an ātman becomes non-existent. Because the view of an ātman is non-existent, the two extremes are then non-existent. As it is said in the Yamaka Sutta (cf. SN 22.85): "If each of the aggregates is not the person, the combination of the aggregates is also not the person, and apart from the aggregates there is also no person. If in the present it is thus unattainable, how can one assert that after an Arhat dies, they are not created again?" Therefore, it is known that a person is unattainable. Because a person is unattainable, the view of an ātman and the views of annihilationism and eternalism are also non-existent.

Furthermore, by apprehending that all dharmas arise from a collection of conditions, the two extremes are then non-existent. Also, as it is said: "By seeing the origin of the world, one eliminates the view of non-existence. By seeing the cessation of the world, one eliminates the view of existence." (cf. Kaccānagotta Sutta, SN 12.15). Also, by practicing the middle path, the two extremes are then extinguished. Why is that? By apprehending the arising of the various dharmas in continuous succession, one extinguishes the view of annihilationism. By apprehending their ceasing from moment to moment, one extinguishes the view of eternalism. It is also said: "The five aggregates are not the person, nor is the person separate from the aggregates." Therefore, it is known that it is neither permanent nor annihilated. Because one can attain a different body, it cannot be one. Because they are both [within the continuity of] a sentient being, they cannot be different. Also, because of the continuity of the five aggregates, there is the birth and death of a sentient being. In this, one cannot say it is the "same," because the continuity is different. Nor can one say it is "different," because within a continuity one can speak of a unity. Also, because the later aggregates are different from these aggregates, one cannot say it is permanent. Because they arise from the causal power of their own continuity, one cannot say it is annihilated.

The same applies to [the view that it is] neither created nor not created.

Pergunta: This fourth [view] ought not to be called a view.

Resposta: This person holds that in the conventional truth there is neither a person nor dharmas; therefore, it is called a view. The four propositions concerning permanent and impermanent, finite and infinite, and so on, are also like this.

Furthermore, in a sūtra it is said: "Upon the complete cessation of the six bases of contact, if there is something other that remains, this is eternalism. If there is nothing other that remains, this is annihilationism." Also, if one holds the view that the ātman acted previously and will act again in the future, this is the view of eternalism. [If one holds the view that] the ātman did not act previously and will not act again in the future, this is the view of annihilationism. Also, in the Sūtra on Wrong Views, it says that the human body has seven components: earth, water, fire, wind, pleasure, pain, and the life-force. At the time of death, the four great elements return to their source, and the faculties return to space. It also says: "By harming sentient beings with a wheel of blades, piling them up into a mound of flesh, there is no sin of taking life." This is called the view of annihilationism. And in the Brahmajāla Sutta (DN 1), the characteristics of the view of annihilationism are spoken of. If one says that there is a future life and that the agent is the same as the experiencer, this is the view of eternalism.

Pergunta: How do the views of annihilationism and eternalism arise?

Resposta: By whatever reason one asserts that after death something is created again, on account of this reason, the view of the extreme of eternalism arises. By whatever reason one asserts that after death nothing is created, on account of this reason, the view of annihilationism arises.

Pergunta: How are these views to be severed?

Resposta: By rightly cultivating emptiness, the view of an ātman becomes non-existent. Because the view of an ātman is non-existent, the two extremes are then non-existent. As it is said in the Yamaka Sutta (cf. SN 22.85): "If each of the aggregates is not the person, the combination of the aggregates is also not the person, and apart from the aggregates there is also no person. If in the present it is thus unattainable, how can one assert that after an Arhat dies, they are not created again?" Therefore, it is known that a person is unattainable. Because a person is unattainable, the view of an ātman and the views of annihilationism and eternalism are also non-existent.

Furthermore, by apprehending that all dharmas arise from a collection of conditions, the two extremes are then non-existent. Also, as it is said: "By seeing the origin of the world, one eliminates the view of non-existence. By seeing the cessation of the world, one eliminates the view of existence." (cf. Kaccānagotta Sutta, SN 12.15). Also, by practicing the middle path, the two extremes are then extinguished. Why is that? By apprehending the arising of the various dharmas in continuous succession, one extinguishes the view of annihilationism. By apprehending their ceasing from moment to moment, one extinguishes the view of eternalism. It is also said: "The five aggregates are not the person, nor is the person separate from the aggregates." Therefore, it is known that it is neither permanent nor annihilated. Because one can attain a different body, it cannot be one. Because they are both [within the continuity of] a sentient being, they cannot be different. Also, because of the continuity of the five aggregates, there is the birth and death of a sentient being. In this, one cannot say it is the "same," because the continuity is different. Nor can one say it is "different," because within a continuity one can speak of a unity. Also, because the later aggregates are different from these aggregates, one cannot say it is permanent. Because they arise from the causal power of their own continuity, one cannot say it is annihilated.

content.zh:
若實有法而生無心，是名邪見，如言無四諦、三寶等。經中說邪
見，謂無施無祠無燒、無善無惡無善惡業報、無今世無後世、無父
母無眾生受生，世間無阿羅漢正行正至自明了證此世後世，知我生
盡、梵行已成、所作已辦，從此身已更無餘身者。施，名為利他故
與。祠，名以韋陀語言因天故祠。燒，名於天祠中燒蘇等物。善，
名能得愛果三種善業。惡，名得不愛果三種惡業。善惡業報，名今
世善惡名等，及天身等後世報。今世名現在，後世名未來。父母名
能生。眾生受生，名從今世至後世。阿羅漢，名盡煩惱者，謂無此
事，故名邪見。又眾生垢淨、有知見無知見皆無因緣，又無力無勇
及此果等，名為邪見。取要言之，所有倒心皆名邪見。如無常常
想、苦為樂想、不淨淨想、無我我想，非勝勝想、勝非勝想，淨道
非淨想、非淨道淨想，無中有想、有中無想。如是等諸顛倒心，謂
阿毘曇中五見，《梵網經》中六十二見，皆名邪見。
問曰：是邪見云何生？

答曰：以癡故生。染著非因以因，故邪見
生。又以染著樂因故說無苦，又失空道故說無苦。以無受苦者故，
若說世間萬物無因無緣，或說因自在等不因於愛，是名無集。隨以
何因緣說無泥洹，或異說泥洹是名無滅，若無泥洹道何所至耶？或
說更有異解脫道，謂斷食等，是名無道。無佛者，是人言：諸法無
量，云何一人能盡知耶？或生是念：佛為人中之尊，以無人故，當
知無佛；無煩惱盡，故名無法；無有正行得此法者，故曰無僧。以
布施現果不可得故，謂無布施。又有經書說無布施，比知亦不決
定，世間有好布施者而更貧窮、有慳貪者而得富貴，以是等因故說
無施。無祠、無燒亦如是。若火燒物為灰，是中有何等果？無善惡
無善惡業報者言：若神是常則無善惡，若神無常則無後世，無後世
故則無善惡、無善惡業報、無今世者，分析諸法終歸都無。無後世
者，隨以死後不作因緣故，謂無後世。無父母者，亦以分分析之令
盡。又說，如因糞生虫，糞非虫父母。又頭等身分，非即父母身
分。又諸法念念滅故，以何為父母耶？無眾生受生者，眾生法無
故，今世尚無，況能受身。又思惟言：是眾生為是身耶、為非身
耶？若是身者，眼見此身埋則為土、燒則成灰、虫食為糞，故無受
生。非身則有二種，若心、若離心。若是心者，心法生滅念念不
住，況至後身。若離心則不計我，於他心中尚不計我，況無心處，
是故無受生者。無阿羅漢者，是人見一切人，飢則求食、寒則求
溫、熱則求涼、毀害則瞋、敬養則喜，故無有能盡煩惱者。又經書
或說無阿羅漢，隨逐此經故生是見。垢淨等無因緣者，是人見此垢
法自然而生。又有垢者即體是垢，故說無因。知見無知見亦如是。
無力無勇者，見一切眾生皆假因緣。或有言：由自在天能有所作。
又見眾生屬業因緣不自在故，說無力無勇及此果。無常常想者，隨
以何因緣破念念滅，以是因緣故生常見，又說諸法滅時還為微塵，
或言還歸本性。又諸法雖滅，以憶想故能受苦樂，則生常想。又說
神是常、音聲亦常，以是等緣故生常想。苦謂樂者，隨以何因緣說
言有樂，如先三受品中說，以是因緣故生樂想。不淨淨想者，以染
著身故，眼見不淨而生淨想。或作是念，我得人根，見此人身不
淨，更有眾生以之為淨，如是等緣故生淨想。無我我想者，見陰相
續生，而取一相以之為我。又如先生身見因緣，以是因緣故生我
想。非勝勝想者，是人於富蘭那等外道師中而生勝想。又梵王自
說：我是大梵天王、造萬物者如是等。有人言：若人具足受五欲
樂，是名勝法。又言：若人離欲入初禪乃至四禪，是最勝法。又
說：世間現見眾生中，婆羅門為尊，非現見眾生中天為最尊，是非
勝勝想。勝非勝想者，一切眾生中佛為最勝，有人於中不生勝想，
作如是言：是剎利種，又學道日淺，又謂佛法言不巧妙，文辭煩重
不如韋陀，此不名勝。眾僧中有四品人，是故不勝。如是等勝中生
非勝想。非淨道中淨道想者，若人言以灰水等洗令人清淨，又說生
死盡訖名清淨道。又但貪著持戒梵行供養天等，亦說由自在天故得
清淨。或說苦行本業盡故名清淨道。又斷葷辛及蘇酪等故得清淨。
又淨洗浴，以韋陀語呪然後飲食，名清淨道。以如是等種種邪道而
得解脫，不以八直為清淨道。有中生無想者，若法世諦中有，亦說
為無。無中生有想者，若說有陀羅驃、有有分者，亦說有數量等求
那，亦說總相別相及集，亦說世性等無物為有。如是等因緣生顛倒
心，皆名邪見。於此邪見中別四種見，餘殘重者皆名邪見。
問曰：是邪見云何斷？

答曰：經中佛說，正見能消邪見。
問曰：正見云何生？

答曰：若見聞比知正決定故，則正見生。又善
修正定則正見生，

如經說：攝心能如實知，非散心也。
問曰：是邪見有何等過？

答曰：一切過咎及諸衰惱皆由邪見。此人
謂無罪福及善惡業報，故現在無諸好事，況未來世。如是破善惡
人，名斷善根，決定當墮阿鼻地獄。如阿毘曇六足中說，殺是人
罪，輕殺虫蟻。又此邪見人污染世間，為多減損眾生故生，如毒樹
生為惱害故。又此人所起身口意業皆為惡報，

如經中說：邪見人所
起身口意業欲瞋思念皆為惡報，如種苦瓠、拘賒毒枝必害蔓陀樹
種，是中所有地種水火風種皆為苦味，以種苦故。如是邪見人諸餘
心心數法，以邪見故皆得惡報，是故此人雖有施等終無好果，以先
為邪見心所壞故。是人所作不善皆是增上，以久集惡心故。又以戒
法故能制非法，是人無善惡故無所禁忌，深為放逸行不善法，定破
慚愧二種白法，與畜生無異。又若人言無善惡，是人心中常懷不
善。又是人無有能受善法因緣。

所以者何？是人不能親近善人、不
聞善法，惡心易起、善心難生，以易起惡故無善因緣，如是漸積則
斷善根。又此邪見人名在難處，如地獄眾生不任得道。如此人雖生
中國，具足六根能別好醜，亦不任得道。又此邪見人無惡不造，不
忌輕重。又少作不善亦墮地獄，以重罪心起是業故。如業品中解地
獄業，以是因緣此人所作皆為地獄。又此人不能盡罪惡業，以不善
法常在心故。又此人展轉地獄難得解脫。

所以者何？斷善根人，若
善根未相續間，終不脫地獄，是人邪見在心中故，善根云何得相續
耶？又邪見人名不可治，猶如病人死相已現，雖有良醫不能復治。
是人亦爾，無餘善故，乃至諸佛亦不能治，是故必墮阿鼻地獄。
content.en:
If, in relation to an ultimately real dharma, one gives rise to the thought that it is non-existent, this is called a wrong view, as when one says there are no Four Truths, no Three Jewels, and so on. In a sūtra, wrong view (mithyā-dṛṣṭi) is described as [the view that]: "There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice. There is no wholesome and no unwholesome; there is no result of wholesome and unwholesome actions. There is no this world, no other world. There are no parents. There are no sentient beings who are spontaneously born. In the world, there are no Arhats, who, through right practice and right entry, having clearly and directly realized this world and the next, know for themselves, 'For me, birth is exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, and after this body there will be no other.'" (cf. Sāmaññaphala Sutta, DN 2).

"Giving" (dāna) is to give for the sake of benefiting another. "Offering" (yajña) is to make offerings on account of the gods, using the words of the Vedas. "Sacrifice" (huta) is to burn ghee and other things in the offerings to the gods. "Wholesome" refers to the three kinds of wholesome actions that are able to bring about a desirable result. "Unwholesome" refers to the three kinds of unwholesome actions that bring about an undesirable result. "The result of wholesome and unwholesome actions" refers to a good or bad reputation and so on in this life, and the retribution of a celestial body and so on in a future life. "This world" refers to the present. "The other world" refers to the future. "Parents" refers to those who give birth. "Sentient beings who are spontaneously born" refers to those who pass from this world to the next. "Arhat" refers to one who has exhausted the afflictions. To say that these matters do not exist is called wrong view.

Furthermore, [the view that] the defilement and purity of sentient beings, their knowledge and vision or lack of knowledge and vision, are all without cause and condition; and also that there is no power, no heroic effort, and no fruit of these—is called wrong view. In short, all inverted states of mind are called wrong view. For example: the perception of permanence in the impermanent; the perception of bliss in suffering; the perception of purity in the impure; the thought of an ātman in what is non-ātman; the thought that what is not supreme is supreme; the thought that what is supreme is not supreme; the thought that a pure path is not pure; the thought that an impure path is pure; the thought of existence in what is non-existent; and the thought of non-existence in what is existent. These and other such inverted states of mind—such as the five views in the Abhidharma and the sixty-two views in the Brahmajāla Sutta (DN 1)—are all called wrong view.

---

Question: How does this wrong view arise?

---

Answer: It arises because of delusion (moha). By being attached to a non-cause as a cause, wrong view arises. Also, by being attached to the cause of pleasure, one says there is no suffering. Also, by having lost the path of emptiness, one says there is no suffering, because there is no one who experiences the suffering. If one says that the ten thousand things of the world are without cause and without condition, or says they are caused by a sovereign god (Īśvara) and so on and not by craving (tṛṣṇā), this is [the view of] no origin. By whatever reason one says there is no nirvāṇa, or gives a different explanation of nirvāṇa, this is [the view of] no cessation. If there is no path to nirvāṇa, where does one arrive? Or if one says there is another, different path to liberation, such as fasting and so on, this is [the view of] no path. As for "no Buddha," this person says: "The dharmas are limitless; how can one person know them all completely?" Or one gives rise to this thought: "The Buddha is the most honored among humans, but since there is no person, one should know there is no Buddha." "No dharma" is because the afflictions are not exhausted. "No Sangha" is because there is no one who, through right practice, attains this dharma.

Because the present fruit of giving is unattainable, one thinks there is no giving. Also, there are scriptures that say there is no giving. Inference is also not definitive. In the world, there are those who are very generous and yet become poor. There are those who are stingy and yet become wealthy. For these and other such reasons, one says there is no giving. The case of "no offering" and "no sacrifice" is also like this. If fire burns a thing to ashes, what kind of fruit is there in that?

One who says "no wholesome and unwholesome, and no result of wholesome and unwholesome actions" argues: "If the soul (ātman) is permanent, then there is no wholesome and unwholesome. If the soul is impermanent, then there is no future life. Because there is no future life, there is no wholesome and unwholesome, and no result of wholesome and unwholesome actions." As for "no this world," one analyzes the various dharmas until they are reduced to nothingness. As for "no other world," by whatever reason one asserts that nothing is created after death, on account of this one thinks there is no other world. As for "no parents," one also analyzes them into parts until they are exhausted. Also, one says: "Just as a worm is born from dung, the dung is not the worm's parents." Also, the parts of the body, such as the head, are not the same as the parts of the parents' bodies. Also, because the dharmas cease moment by moment, what could be the parents? As for "no sentient beings who are spontaneously born," because the dharma "sentient being" is non-existent, it does not even exist in this life, let alone being able to take on a body. Also, one reflects: "Is this sentient being the body, or is it not the body? If it is the body, the eye apprehends this body being buried and becoming earth, burned and becoming ash, or eaten by worms and becoming dung. Therefore, there is no one who is reborn. If it is not the body, it is of two kinds: either it is the mind, or it is separate from the mind. If it is the mind, the dharmas of the mind arise and cease and do not abide from moment to moment, let alone reaching a future body. If it is separate from the mind, one does not posit an ātman. One does not even posit an ātman in the mind of another, let alone in a place without a mind. For this reason, there is no one who is reborn." As for "no Arhats," this person observes all people: when hungry, they seek food; when cold, they seek warmth; when hot, they seek coolness; when harmed, they become angry; when revered and supported, they become pleased. Therefore, there is no one who can exhaust the afflictions. Also, some scriptures say there are no Arhats. By following these scriptures, one gives rise to this view. As for "defilement, purity, and so on are without cause and condition," this person apprehends this defiled dharma as arising spontaneously. Also, one who is defiled is defiled in their very essence; therefore, one says it is without a cause. "Knowledge and vision or lack of knowledge and vision" is also like this. As for "no power, no heroic effort," one apprehends that all sentient beings depend on causes and conditions. Or some say: "It is due to the sovereign god (Īśvara) that things can be done." Also, apprehending that sentient beings are subject to the causes and conditions of karma and are not in control, one says there is no power, no heroic effort, and no fruit of these.

As for "the perception of permanence in the impermanent," by whatever reason one refutes momentariness, for this reason one gives rise to the view of permanence. Also, one says that when the various dharmas cease, they revert to the finest particles, or one says they return to a primordial nature. Also, although the various dharmas cease, because of memory and perception one can experience pleasure and pain; thus one gives rise to the perception of permanence. Also, one says the soul is permanent, and sound is also permanent. For these and other such reasons, one gives rise to the perception of permanence. As for "[perceiving] what is suffering as bliss," by whatever reason one says there is bliss, as was said previously in the chapter on the three feelings, for this reason one gives rise to the perception of bliss. As for "the perception of purity in the impure," because of attachment to the body, the eye apprehends impurity but gives rise to a perception of purity. Or one has this thought: "I have obtained human faculties. I apprehend this human body as impure, but there are other sentient beings who take it to be pure." For these and other such reasons, one gives rise to a perception of purity. As for "the thought of an ātman in what is non-ātman," one apprehends the aggregates arising in continuous succession and apprehends a single mark, taking it to be an ātman. Also, as was explained before regarding the conditions for the arising of identity view, for these reasons one gives rise to the thought of an ātman.

As for "the thought that what is not supreme is supreme," this person gives rise to the thought of supremacy in relation to the external teachers such as Pūraṇa. Also, Brahmā himself says: "I am the Great Brahmā, the king, the creator of the ten thousand things," and so on. Some people say: "If a person fully receives the pleasures of the five desires, this is the supreme dharma." Others say: "If a person is detached from desire and enters the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, this is the most supreme dharma." It is also said: "Among the sentient beings directly apprehended in the world, the Brahmins are the most honored. Among the sentient beings not directly apprehended, the gods are the most honored." This is the thought that what is not supreme is supreme. As for "the thought that what is supreme is not supreme," among all sentient beings, the Buddha is the most supreme. Some people do not give rise to a thought of his supremacy, saying: "He is of the Kṣatriya caste." Also, "the time since he began to study the path is short." Also, they think the Buddha's Dharma is not skillful in its wording, and that its prose is cumbersome and heavy, unlike the Vedas. "This is not supreme." "In the Sangha there are four classes of people; therefore, it is not supreme." In these and other such supreme things, one gives rise to the thought that they are not supreme.

As for "the thought that what is not a pure path is a pure path," if a person says that washing with ash, water, and so on makes people pure, or says that the final exhaustion of birth and death is the pure path, or merely is attached to observing precepts, the holy life, and making offerings to the gods, it is also said that one attains purity on account of the sovereign god. Or it is said that by means of asceticism, when one's original karma is exhausted, this is the pure path. Also, by abstaining from pungent herbs and from ghee, cheese, and so on, one attains purity. Also, by purifying oneself with bathing and reciting the words of the Vedas as a spell before eating and drinking, this is the pure path. By these and other such various wrong paths one is liberated, and one does not take the eight straight [factors] to be the pure path.

As for "the thought of non-existence in what is existent," if a dharma exists in the conventional truth, one also says it is non-existent. As for "the thought of existence in what is non-existent," if one says there is a substance (dravya), there is a whole-which-has-parts; also says there are qualities (guṇa) such as quantity; also says there are general and particular characteristics, and combination; also says there are the nature of the world and other such non-things as existent. Because of these and other such conditions, an inverted mind arises. All are called wrong view. Among these wrong views, four views are distinguished, and the remaining serious ones are all called wrong view.

---

Question: How is this wrong view to be severed?

---

Answer: In a sūtra the Buddha said that right view is able to eliminate wrong view.

---

Question: How does right view arise?

---

Answer: If one's apprehension, hearing, and inference become rightly determined, then right view arises. Also, by skillfully cultivating right concentration, right view arises. As a sūtra says: "A concentrated mind is able to know in accordance with reality; a scattered mind is not."

---

Question: What are the faults of this wrong view?

---

Answer: All faults and all ills and afflictions are due to wrong view. This person holds that there is no sin and merit and no result of wholesome and unwholesome actions; therefore, in the present there are no good things, to say nothing of a future life. Such a person who refutes the wholesome and unwholesome is said to have severed the wholesome roots and will certainly fall into the Avīci hell. As it is said in the six books of the Abhidharma, the sin of killing this person is lighter than killing an insect or an ant. Also, this person with wrong view pollutes the world; they are born for the sake of causing great loss and harm to sentient beings, just as a poisonous tree is born for the sake of causing affliction and harm. Also, the bodily, verbal, and mental actions that this person performs all have a bad result. As it is said in a sūtra: "For a person with wrong view, the bodily, verbal, and mental actions, desires, aversions, and thoughts they perform all have a bad result. It is like planting a bitter gourd or a poisonous branch of the Kuśa plant; it will certainly harm the seed of the Mandāra tree. In this, the earth-seed, the water-, fire-, and wind-seeds will all become a bitter flavor, because the seed is bitter." In the same way, for a person with wrong view, the various other mind and mental factors, because of the wrong view, all receive a bad result. For this reason, although this person may perform giving and so on, there will never be a good fruit, because it has first been destroyed by the mind of wrong view. All the unwholesome deeds that this person performs are of the highest degree, because they have for long accumulated an evil mind. Also, it is because of the dharma of the precepts that one is able to restrain what is not the dharma. This person, believing there is no wholesome and unwholesome, has no prohibitions or taboos. Deeply engaged in heedlessness, they perform unwholesome dharmas and definitively destroy the two white dharmas of shame and disregard for others, being no different from an animal. Also, if a person says there is no wholesome and unwholesome, this person's mind constantly harbors the unwholesome. Also, this person has no condition by which they can receive wholesome dharmas. Why is that? This person cannot draw near to good people and does not hear the good Dharma. An evil mind is easy to arouse; a wholesome mind is difficult to produce. Because it is easy to arouse evil, there is no wholesome condition. In this way, by gradual accumulation, one severs the wholesome roots. Also, this person with wrong view is said to be in a state of calamity, like a sentient being in hell who is not fit to attain the path. Although this person may be born in the central country, have complete sense faculties, and be able to distinguish good from bad, they are also not fit to attain the path. Also, this person with wrong view creates no evil they do not do, having no scruples about light or heavy [sins]. Also, by performing a small unwholesome act, they also fall into hell, because the action is performed with a mind of grave sin. As is explained in the chapter on karma regarding the karma for hell, for this reason, all that this person does is for the sake of hell. Also, this person is unable to exhaust their sinful and evil karma, because the unwholesome dharmas are constantly in their mind. Also, for this person, passing from one hell to another, it is difficult to attain liberation. Why is that? For a person who has severed the wholesome roots, as long as the wholesome roots have not become continuous again, they will never be freed from hell. For this person, because the wrong view is in their mind, how can the wholesome roots become continuous? Also, a person with wrong view is said to be incurable. It is like a sick person for whom the signs of death have already appeared. Although there may be a good physician, they can no longer be cured. This person is also like this; because they have no other wholesome [qualities], even the Buddhas cannot cure them. For this reason, they will certainly fall into the Avīci hell.
content.pt:
If, in relation to an ultimately real dharma, one gives rise to the thought that it is non-existent, this is called a wrong view, as when one says there are no Four Truths, no Three Jewels, and so on. In a sūtra, wrong view (mithyā-dṛṣṭi) is described as [the view that]: "There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice. There is no wholesome and no unwholesome; there is no result of wholesome and unwholesome actions. There is no this world, no other world. There are no parents. There are no sentient beings who are spontaneously born. In the world, there are no Arhats, who, through right practice and right entry, having clearly and directly realized this world and the next, know for themselves, 'For me, birth is exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done is done, and after this body there will be no other.'" (cf. Sāmaññaphala Sutta, DN 2).

"Giving" (dāna) is to give for the sake of benefiting another. "Offering" (yajña) is to make offerings on account of the gods, using the words of the Vedas. "Sacrifice" (huta) is to burn ghee and other things in the offerings to the gods. "Wholesome" refers to the three kinds of wholesome actions that are able to bring about a desirable result. "Unwholesome" refers to the three kinds of unwholesome actions that bring about an undesirable result. "The result of wholesome and unwholesome actions" refers to a good or bad reputation and so on in this life, and the retribution of a celestial body and so on in a future life. "This world" refers to the present. "The other world" refers to the future. "Parents" refers to those who give birth. "Sentient beings who are spontaneously born" refers to those who pass from this world to the next. "Arhat" refers to one who has exhausted the afflictions. To say that these matters do not exist is called wrong view.

Furthermore, [the view that] the defilement and purity of sentient beings, their knowledge and vision or lack of knowledge and vision, are all without cause and condition; and also that there is no power, no heroic effort, and no fruit of these—is called wrong view. In short, all inverted states of mind are called wrong view. For example: the perception of permanence in the impermanent; the perception of bliss in suffering; the perception of purity in the impure; the thought of an ātman in what is non-ātman; the thought that what is not supreme is supreme; the thought that what is supreme is not supreme; the thought that a pure path is not pure; the thought that an impure path is pure; the thought of existence in what is non-existent; and the thought of non-existence in what is existent. These and other such inverted states of mind—such as the five views in the Abhidharma and the sixty-two views in the Brahmajāla Sutta (DN 1)—are all called wrong view.

---

Pergunta: How does this wrong view arise?

---

Resposta: It arises because of delusion (moha). By being attached to a non-cause as a cause, wrong view arises. Also, by being attached to the cause of pleasure, one says there is no suffering. Also, by having lost the path of emptiness, one says there is no suffering, because there is no one who experiences the suffering. If one says that the ten thousand things of the world are without cause and without condition, or says they are caused by a sovereign god (Īśvara) and so on and not by craving (tṛṣṇā), this is [the view of] no origin. By whatever reason one says there is no nirvāṇa, or gives a different explanation of nirvāṇa, this is [the view of] no cessation. If there is no path to nirvāṇa, where does one arrive? Or if one says there is another, different path to liberation, such as fasting and so on, this is [the view of] no path. As for "no Buddha," this person says: "The dharmas are limitless; how can one person know them all completely?" Or one gives rise to this thought: "The Buddha is the most honored among humans, but since there is no person, one should know there is no Buddha." "No dharma" is because the afflictions are not exhausted. "No Sangha" is because there is no one who, through right practice, attains this dharma.

Because the present fruit of giving is unattainable, one thinks there is no giving. Also, there are scriptures that say there is no giving. Inference is also not definitive. In the world, there are those who are very generous and yet become poor. There are those who are stingy and yet become wealthy. For these and other such reasons, one says there is no giving. The case of "no offering" and "no sacrifice" is also like this. If fire burns a thing to ashes, what kind of fruit is there in that?

One who says "no wholesome and unwholesome, and no result of wholesome and unwholesome actions" argues: "If the soul (ātman) is permanent, then there is no wholesome and unwholesome. If the soul is impermanent, then there is no future life. Because there is no future life, there is no wholesome and unwholesome, and no result of wholesome and unwholesome actions." As for "no this world," one analyzes the various dharmas until they are reduced to nothingness. As for "no other world," by whatever reason one asserts that nothing is created after death, on account of this one thinks there is no other world. As for "no parents," one also analyzes them into parts until they are exhausted. Also, one says: "Just as a worm is born from dung, the dung is not the worm's parents." Also, the parts of the body, such as the head, are not the same as the parts of the parents' bodies. Also, because the dharmas cease moment by moment, what could be the parents? As for "no sentient beings who are spontaneously born," because the dharma "sentient being" is non-existent, it does not even exist in this life, let alone being able to take on a body. Also, one reflects: "Is this sentient being the body, or is it not the body? If it is the body, the eye apprehends this body being buried and becoming earth, burned and becoming ash, or eaten by worms and becoming dung. Therefore, there is no one who is reborn. If it is not the body, it is of two kinds: either it is the mind, or it is separate from the mind. If it is the mind, the dharmas of the mind arise and cease and do not abide from moment to moment, let alone reaching a future body. If it is separate from the mind, one does not posit an ātman. One does not even posit an ātman in the mind of another, let alone in a place without a mind. For this reason, there is no one who is reborn." As for "no Arhats," this person observes all people: when hungry, they seek food; when cold, they seek warmth; when hot, they seek coolness; when harmed, they become angry; when revered and supported, they become pleased. Therefore, there is no one who can exhaust the afflictions. Also, some scriptures say there are no Arhats. By following these scriptures, one gives rise to this view. As for "defilement, purity, and so on are without cause and condition," this person apprehends this defiled dharma as arising spontaneously. Also, one who is defiled is defiled in their very essence; therefore, one says it is without a cause. "Knowledge and vision or lack of knowledge and vision" is also like this. As for "no power, no heroic effort," one apprehends that all sentient beings depend on causes and conditions. Or some say: "It is due to the sovereign god (Īśvara) that things can be done." Also, apprehending that sentient beings are subject to the causes and conditions of karma and are not in control, one says there is no power, no heroic effort, and no fruit of these.

As for "the perception of permanence in the impermanent," by whatever reason one refutes momentariness, for this reason one gives rise to the view of permanence. Also, one says that when the various dharmas cease, they revert to the finest particles, or one says they return to a primordial nature. Also, although the various dharmas cease, because of memory and perception one can experience pleasure and pain; thus one gives rise to the perception of permanence. Also, one says the soul is permanent, and sound is also permanent. For these and other such reasons, one gives rise to the perception of permanence. As for "[perceiving] what is suffering as bliss," by whatever reason one says there is bliss, as was said previously in the chapter on the three feelings, for this reason one gives rise to the perception of bliss. As for "the perception of purity in the impure," because of attachment to the body, the eye apprehends impurity but gives rise to a perception of purity. Or one has this thought: "I have obtained human faculties. I apprehend this human body as impure, but there are other sentient beings who take it to be pure." For these and other such reasons, one gives rise to a perception of purity. As for "the thought of an ātman in what is non-ātman," one apprehends the aggregates arising in continuous succession and apprehends a single mark, taking it to be an ātman. Also, as was explained before regarding the conditions for the arising of identity view, for these reasons one gives rise to the thought of an ātman.

As for "the thought that what is not supreme is supreme," this person gives rise to the thought of supremacy in relation to the external teachers such as Pūraṇa. Also, Brahmā himself says: "I am the Great Brahmā, the king, the creator of the ten thousand things," and so on. Some people say: "If a person fully receives the pleasures of the five desires, this is the supreme dharma." Others say: "If a person is detached from desire and enters the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, this is the most supreme dharma." It is also said: "Among the sentient beings directly apprehended in the world, the Brahmins are the most honored. Among the sentient beings not directly apprehended, the gods are the most honored." This is the thought that what is not supreme is supreme. As for "the thought that what is supreme is not supreme," among all sentient beings, the Buddha is the most supreme. Some people do not give rise to a thought of his supremacy, saying: "He is of the Kṣatriya caste." Also, "the time since he began to study the path is short." Also, they think the Buddha's Dharma is not skillful in its wording, and that its prose is cumbersome and heavy, unlike the Vedas. "This is not supreme." "In the Sangha there are four classes of people; therefore, it is not supreme." In these and other such supreme things, one gives rise to the thought that they are not supreme.

As for "the thought that what is not a pure path is a pure path," if a person says that washing with ash, water, and so on makes people pure, or says that the final exhaustion of birth and death is the pure path, or merely is attached to observing precepts, the holy life, and making offerings to the gods, it is also said that one attains purity on account of the sovereign god. Or it is said that by means of asceticism, when one's original karma is exhausted, this is the pure path. Also, by abstaining from pungent herbs and from ghee, cheese, and so on, one attains purity. Also, by purifying oneself with bathing and reciting the words of the Vedas as a spell before eating and drinking, this is the pure path. By these and other such various wrong paths one is liberated, and one does not take the eight straight [factors] to be the pure path.

As for "the thought of non-existence in what is existent," if a dharma exists in the conventional truth, one also says it is non-existent. As for "the thought of existence in what is non-existent," if one says there is a substance (dravya), there is a whole-which-has-parts; also says there are qualities (guṇa) such as quantity; also says there are general and particular characteristics, and combination; also says there are the nature of the world and other such non-things as existent. Because of these and other such conditions, an inverted mind arises. All are called wrong view. Among these wrong views, four views are distinguished, and the remaining serious ones are all called wrong view.

---

Pergunta: How is this wrong view to be severed?

---

Resposta: In a sūtra the Buddha said that right view is able to eliminate wrong view.

---

Pergunta: How does right view arise?

---

Resposta: If one's apprehension, hearing, and inference become rightly determined, then right view arises. Also, by skillfully cultivating right concentration, right view arises. As a sūtra says: "A concentrated mind is able to know in accordance with reality; a scattered mind is not."

---

Pergunta: What are the faults of this wrong view?

---

Resposta: All faults and all ills and afflictions are due to wrong view. This person holds that there is no sin and merit and no result of wholesome and unwholesome actions; therefore, in the present there are no good things, to say nothing of a future life. Such a person who refutes the wholesome and unwholesome is said to have severed the wholesome roots and will certainly fall into the Avīci hell. As it is said in the six books of the Abhidharma, the sin of killing this person is lighter than killing an insect or an ant. Also, this person with wrong view pollutes the world; they are born for the sake of causing great loss and harm to sentient beings, just as a poisonous tree is born for the sake of causing affliction and harm. Also, the bodily, verbal, and mental actions that this person performs all have a bad result. As it is said in a sūtra: "For a person with wrong view, the bodily, verbal, and mental actions, desires, aversions, and thoughts they perform all have a bad result. It is like planting a bitter gourd or a poisonous branch of the Kuśa plant; it will certainly harm the seed of the Mandāra tree. In this, the earth-seed, the water-, fire-, and wind-seeds will all become a bitter flavor, because the seed is bitter." In the same way, for a person with wrong view, the various other mind and mental factors, because of the wrong view, all receive a bad result. For this reason, although this person may perform giving and so on, there will never be a good fruit, because it has first been destroyed by the mind of wrong view. All the unwholesome deeds that this person performs are of the highest degree, because they have for long accumulated an evil mind. Also, it is because of the dharma of the precepts that one is able to restrain what is not the dharma. This person, believing there is no wholesome and unwholesome, has no prohibitions or taboos. Deeply engaged in heedlessness, they perform unwholesome dharmas and definitively destroy the two white dharmas of shame and disregard for others, being no different from an animal. Also, if a person says there is no wholesome and unwholesome, this person's mind constantly harbors the unwholesome. Also, this person has no condition by which they can receive wholesome dharmas. Why is that? This person cannot draw near to good people and does not hear the good Dharma. An evil mind is easy to arouse; a wholesome mind is difficult to produce. Because it is easy to arouse evil, there is no wholesome condition. In this way, by gradual accumulation, one severs the wholesome roots. Also, this person with wrong view is said to be in a state of calamity, like a sentient being in hell who is not fit to attain the path. Although this person may be born in the central country, have complete sense faculties, and be able to distinguish good from bad, they are also not fit to attain the path. Also, this person with wrong view creates no evil they do not do, having no scruples about light or heavy [sins]. Also, by performing a small unwholesome act, they also fall into hell, because the action is performed with a mind of grave sin. As is explained in the chapter on karma regarding the karma for hell, for this reason, all that this person does is for the sake of hell. Also, this person is unable to exhaust their sinful and evil karma, because the unwholesome dharmas are constantly in their mind. Also, for this person, passing from one hell to another, it is difficult to attain liberation. Why is that? For a person who has severed the wholesome roots, as long as the wholesome roots have not become continuous again, they will never be freed from hell. For this person, because the wrong view is in their mind, how can the wholesome roots become continuous? Also, a person with wrong view is said to be incurable. It is like a sick person for whom the signs of death have already appeared. Although there may be a good physician, they can no longer be cured. This person is also like this; because they have no other wholesome [qualities], even the Buddhas cannot cure them. For this reason, they will certainly fall into the Avīci hell.

content.zh:
於非實事中生決定心，但是事實，餘皆妄語，是名見取。及先說非
勝法中定生勝想，亦名見取。
問曰：見取有何過？

答曰：是人得少功德自以為足。又是人唐勞其
功。

所以者何？是人於非善事中生妙善想，勤加精進，以是因緣後
則心悔。又是人為智者所笑，以非勝中生勝想故。又若人非勝謂勝
是愚癡相，猶如盲人於瓦礫中生金銀想，為有目者之所輕笑。見取
有如是等過。若人捨智，以洗浴等戒望得清淨，名為戒取。

問曰：
不以戒故得清淨耶？

答曰：以智慧得清淨戒，為智慧根本。
問曰：戒取有何過？

答曰：所說見取之過，以下事為足等，皆是此
過。又戒取因緣唐受諸苦，謂受寒熱、臥灰土木刺棘等上、投淵赴
火自墜高等，後世亦受劇苦果報。

如經中說：持牛戒若成則還為
牛，若不能成則墮地獄。又此人從冥入冥，以受此法現世得苦、後
亦苦故。又此人得深重罪。

所以者何？以非法為法，毀壞真法，亦
謗行正法者，令多眾生背真淨法、墮罪中故，積集大罪，故受阿鼻
地獄果報。寧止不行勿行邪道。

所以者何？若本不行，易令行道，
邪行敗心故難入道。又雖是怨賊，不能令人衰惱，如生邪見。所以
者何？怨賊不能污人，如隨逐邪見，受外道所行種種邪戒，裸形無
恥、灰土塗身、拔髮等故。又此邪見人，皆失世間一切利樂，現在
失五欲樂，後失生善處樂及泥洹樂。若人求樂得苦、求解得縛，不
名狂耶？

所以者何？以施一飡因緣可得生天，此人行邪行故，雖施
身命無所利益。
content.en:
To give rise to a definitive thought concerning an unreal matter, thinking, "This alone is the truth; all else is false," is called the view of grasping at views (dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa). Also, as was said before, to definitively give rise to the thought that an inferior dharma is supreme is also called the view of grasping at views.

Question: What are the faults of the view of grasping at views?

Answer: This person, having obtained a small merit, considers themself to be sufficient.

Furthermore, this person's efforts are in vain. Why is that? This person, giving rise to the thought that a non-wholesome matter is sublime and wholesome, diligently applies themself. For this reason, they will later have remorse.

Furthermore, this person is ridiculed by the wise, because they give rise to the thought of supremacy in what is not supreme. Also, if a person holds that what is not supreme is supreme, this is a mark of delusion. It is like a blind person who gives rise to the thought of gold and silver in what is a potsherd, and is scorned and ridiculed by one who has sight. The view of grasping at views has these and other such faults.

If a person abandons wisdom and, by means of precepts and practices such as ritual bathing, hopes to attain purity, this is called the view of grasping at precepts and practices (śīla-vrata-parāmarśa).

Question: Is it not through precepts (śīla) that one attains purity?

Answer: It is with wisdom that one attains purity. The precepts are the foundation for wisdom.

Question: What are the faults of the view of grasping at precepts and practices?

Answer: The faults spoken of for the view of grasping at views—such as considering a lower matter to be sufficient—are all faults of this as well.

Furthermore, on account of the view of grasping at precepts, one uselessly undergoes various sufferings, such as enduring cold and heat, lying on ash, earth, wood, thorns, and spikes, plunging into deep water, entering a fire, and throwing oneself from a height. In a future life, one also receives the result of intense suffering. As it is said in a sūtra: "One who undertakes the cow-vow, if it is perfected, is reborn as a cow. If it is not perfected, they fall into hell." (cf. Kukkuravatika Sutta, MN 57). Also, this person goes from darkness into darkness, because by undertaking this practice they receive suffering in the present life and also suffering in the future. Also, this person acquires a deep and heavy fault. Why is that? By taking a non-dharma to be the Dharma, they destroy the true Dharma. They also slander those who practice the true Dharma, causing many sentient beings to turn their backs on the true and pure Dharma and fall into wrongdoing. Thus they accumulate great demerit and receive the result of the Avīci hell. It is better to stop and not practice than to practice a wrong path. Why is that? If one had not originally practiced, it would be easy to cause them to practice the path. Because wrong practice ruins the mind, it is difficult to enter the path. Also, even an enemy or a thief cannot cause a person the decay and affliction that the arising of a wrong view can. Why is that? An enemy or a thief cannot pollute a person in the way that following a wrong view can. By receiving the various wrong precepts and practices of the outsiders—such as nakedness without shame, smearing the body with ash, and pulling out the hair—[the mind is polluted]. Also, this person with a wrong view loses all the benefit and happiness of the world. In the present, they lose the pleasure of the five desires. In the future, they lose the bliss of birth in a good destiny and the bliss of nirvāṇa. If a person seeks pleasure but obtains suffering, and seeks liberation but obtains bondage, are they not to be called mad? Why is that? On account of the cause of giving a single meal, one could be born in heaven. This person, because they follow a wrong practice, gains no benefit even if they sacrifice their own body and life.
content.pt:
Dar origem a um pensamento definitivo a respeito de um assunto irreal, pensar: "Só isso é a verdade; todo o resto é falso", é chamado de visão de apego a pontos de vista (dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa).

Além disso, como foi dito antes, dar origem definitivamente ao pensamento de que um dharma inferior é supremo também é chamado de visão de apego a pontos de vista.

Pergunta: Quais são as falhas da visão de apego às visões?

Resposta: Esta pessoa, tendo obtido um pequeno mérito, considera-se suficiente.

Além disso, os esforços desta pessoa são em vão. Por que é que? Essa pessoa, dando origem ao pensamento de que um assunto não saudável é sublime e benéfico, aplica-se diligentemente. Por esta razão, mais tarde sentirão remorso.

Além disso, essa pessoa é ridicularizada pelos sábios, pois estes dão origem ao pensamento de supremacia naquilo que não é supremo.

Além disso, se uma pessoa sustenta que o que não é supremo é supremo, isso é uma marca de ilusão. É como uma pessoa cega que dá origem ao pensamento de ouro e prata no que é um caco de cerâmica, e é desprezada e ridicularizada por alguém que tem visão. A visão de apego a pontos de vista tem essas e outras falhas.

Se uma pessoa abandona a sabedoria e, por meio de preceitos e práticas como o banho ritual, espera alcançar a pureza, isso é chamado de visão do apego a preceitos e práticas (śīla-vrata-parāmarśa).

Pergunta: Não é através dos preceitos (śīla) que se alcança a pureza?

Resposta: É com sabedoria que se alcança a pureza. Os preceitos são a base da sabedoria.

Pergunta: Quais são as falhas da visão de apego a preceitos e práticas?

Resposta: As falhas mencionadas para a visão de apego a pontos de vista – como considerar um assunto inferior como suficiente – são todas falhas disso também.

Além disso, devido à visão de apego aos preceitos, a pessoa passa inutilmente por vários sofrimentos, tais como suportar o frio e o calor, deitar-se sobre cinzas, terra, madeira, espinhos e estacas, mergulhar em águas profundas, entrar no fogo e atirar-se de uma altura. Numa vida futura, também se recebe o resultado de um sofrimento intenso. Como é dito em um sutra: "Aquele que faz o voto de vaca, se for aperfeiçoado, renasce como uma vaca. Se não for aperfeiçoado, ele cai no inferno." (cf. Kukkuravatika Sutta, MN 57).

Além disso, essa pessoa passa de escuridão em escuridão, porque ao realizar esta prática ela recebe sofrimento na vida presente e também sofrimento no futuro.

Além disso, essa pessoa adquire uma falha profunda e pesada. Por que é que? Ao considerarem um não-dharma como sendo o Dharma, eles destroem o verdadeiro Dharma. Eles também caluniam aqueles que praticam o verdadeiro Dharma, fazendo com que muitos seres sencientes virem as costas ao verdadeiro e puro Dharma e cometam erros. Assim eles acumulam grande demérito e recebem o resultado do inferno Avīci. É melhor parar e não praticar do que praticar um caminho errado. Por que é que? Se alguém não tivesse praticado originalmente, seria fácil fazer com que praticasse o caminho. Como a prática errada arruína a mente, é difícil entrar no caminho.

Além disso, mesmo um inimigo ou um ladrão não pode causar a uma pessoa a decadência e a aflição que o surgimento de uma visão errada pode causar. Por que é que? Um inimigo ou um ladrão não pode poluir uma pessoa da mesma forma que seguir um ponto de vista errado. Ao receber os vários preceitos e práticas erradas dos estranhos – como a nudez sem vergonha, untar o corpo com cinzas e arrancar os cabelos – [a mente fica poluída].

Além disso, essa pessoa com uma visão errada perde todos os benefícios e felicidade do mundo. No presente, perdem o prazer dos cinco desejos. No futuro, eles perderão a bem-aventurança do nascimento em um bom destino e a bem-aventurança do nirvāṇa. Se uma pessoa busca o prazer, mas obtém sofrimento, e busca a libertação, mas obtém a escravidão, ela não deve ser chamada de louca? Por que é que? Pela causa de dar uma única refeição, alguém poderia nascer no céu. Essa pessoa, por seguir uma prática errada, não obtém nenhum benefício, mesmo que sacrifique seu próprio corpo e sua vida.

segments.label: 134 隨煩惱品 (On Secondary Afflictions | Aflições)

content.zh:
心重欲眠名睡。心攝離覺名眠。心散諸塵名掉。心懷憂結名悔，所
謂不應作而作、應作而不作。曲心詐善名諂。諂心事成名誑。自作
惡不羞名無慚。眾中為惡不羞不戁名無愧。心隨不善名放逸。實無
功德，示相令人謂有，名詐現奇特。為利養故，口悅人意，名羅波
那。欲得他物，表欲得相，如言此物好等，名為現相。若為呰毀此
人，故稱讚餘人，如言汝父精進汝不及也，名為憿切。若以施求
施，言是施物從某邊得，如是等名以利求利。若人有喜睡病，名單
致利。若得好處，行道因緣具足，而常愁憂，名為不喜。若人頻申
身不調適，為睡眠因緣，名為頻申。若人不知調適飲食多少，名初
不調。若不堪精進，名為退心。若諸尊長有所言說，不敬不畏，名
不敬肅。喜樂惡人，名樂惡友。如是等名隨煩惱，從煩惱生故。
content.en:
When the mind is heavy and wants to sleep, it is called drowsiness (styāna). When the mind is withdrawn and separate from awareness, it is called torpor (middha). When the mind is scattered among the various sense objects, it is called agitation (auddhatya). When the mind harbors sorrow and fetters, it is called regret (kaukṛtya), namely, having done what should not be done, and not having done what should be done.
A crooked mind feigning goodness is called concealment (mrakṣa). When the matter of the mind of concealment is accomplished, it is called deceit (śāṭhya). Doing evil oneself and feeling no shame is called shamelessness (āhrīkya). Doing evil in a crowd without shame or fear of reproach is called disregard for others (anapatrāpya). When the mind follows what is unwholesome, it is called heedlessness (pramāda).
When one is in reality without merit but displays a sign causing others to think one has it, this is called falsely displaying special qualities. For the sake of gain and support, to please another's mind with one's speech is called flattery (lapanā). To desire another's possession and show a sign of one's desire, such as saying, "This object is good," and so on, is called hinting (naimittikatā). If, for the sake of denigrating this person, one praises another person, as in saying, "Your father was diligent, but you do not measure up," this is called insinuation (naiṣpeṣikatā). If one uses a gift to seek a gift, saying, "This gift was obtained from so-and-so," and other such things, this is called seeking gain with gain (lābhena lābha-niścikīrṣatā).
If a person has a sickness of joy and sleep, this is called dhandhālita. If one has obtained a good place and the conditions for practicing the path are complete, but one is constantly sorrowful, this is called discontent. If a person is yawning and their body is ill-at-ease, this being a condition for sleep, it is called yawning. If a person does not know how to regulate the amount of their food and drink, this is called lack of regulation in eating. If one is unable to bear exertion, this is called a discouraged mind. If, when a venerable elder says something, one is not respectful and not afraid, this is called lack of reverence. Delighting in evil people is called delighting in bad friends.
These and others like them are called secondary afflictions (upakleśa), because they arise from the [primary] afflictions.
content.pt:
Quando a mente está pesada e quer dormir, isso se chama sonolência (styāna). Quando a mente está retraída e separada da consciência, isso é chamado de torpor (middha). Quando a mente está dispersa entre os vários objetos dos sentidos, isso é chamado de agitação (auddhatya). Quando a mente abriga tristeza e grilhões, isso é chamado de arrependimento (kaukṛtya), ou seja, ter feito o que não deveria ser feito e não ter feito o que deveria ser feito.
Uma mente distorcida fingindo bondade é chamada de ocultação (mrakṣa). Quando a questão da ocultação da mente é cumprida, isso é chamado de engano (śāṭhya). Fazer o mal e não sentir vergonha é chamado de falta de vergonha (āhrīkya). Fazer o mal no meio de uma multidão sem vergonha ou medo de reprovação é chamado de desrespeito pelos outros (anapatrāpya). Quando a mente segue o que é prejudicial, isso é chamado de negligência (pramāda).
Quando alguém, na realidade, não tem mérito, mas exibe um sinal que faz com que os outros pensem que o possui, isso é chamado de falsa exibição de qualidades especiais. Por uma questão de ganho e apoio, agradar a mente de outra pessoa com o seu discurso é chamado de bajulação (lapanā). Desejar a posse de outra pessoa e mostrar um sinal de seu desejo, como dizer: “Este objeto é bom”, e assim por diante, é chamado de insinuação (naimittikatā). Se, para denegrir essa pessoa, alguém elogia outra, como dizendo: “Seu pai foi diligente, mas você não está à altura”, isso é chamado de insinuação (naiṣpeṣikatā). Se alguém usa uma dádiva para buscar uma dádiva, dizendo: “Esta dádiva foi obtida de fulano de tal”, e outras coisas semelhantes, isso é chamado de buscar ganho com ganho (lābhena labha-niścikīrṣatā).
Se uma pessoa tem uma doença da alegria e do sono, isso é chamado de dhandhālita. Se alguém obteve um bom lugar e as condições para praticar o caminho estão completas, mas está constantemente triste, isso é chamado de descontentamento. Se uma pessoa está bocejando e seu corpo está desconfortável, sendo esta uma condição para dormir, isso é chamado de bocejo. Se uma pessoa não sabe regular a quantidade de comida e bebida, isso se chama falta de regulação na alimentação. Se alguém é incapaz de suportar o esforço, isso é chamado de mente desanimada. Se, quando um venerável ancião diz algo, alguém não é respeitoso e não tem medo, isso é chamado de falta de reverência. Deleitar-se com pessoas más é chamado de deleitar-se com maus amigos.
Estas e outras semelhantes são chamadas de aflições secundárias (upakleśa), porque surgem das aflições [primárias].

segments.label: 135 不善根品 (On Unwholesome Roots | Virtuoso)

content.zh:
三不善根，謂貪、恚、癡。
問曰：憍慢等亦應是不善根，何故但說三耶？

答曰：一切煩惱皆是
三種煩惱分，慢等是癡分，故不別說。又三種煩惱多在眾生心中，
慢等不爾。又一切未離欲者乃至蚊蟻，是三煩惱皆在心中，憍慢等
不如是。又貪是瞋不善根，違失所貪則隨生瞋。癡為二本。所以者
何？若人無癡，則不貪瞋。

又經中說：十不善業有三種，從貪瞋癡
生。不說從慢等生。又有三種受，更無第四。是三受中三煩惱使，
若別有慢等，於何受中使？是事實不可說，當知此三是諸煩惱本。
問曰：何故樂受中貪使？對曰：現見此中生故。

如經中說：人得樂
觸生喜、苦觸則不喜，是人於諸受中集滅味過出不如實知故。不苦
不樂受中無明使使。

所以者何？是人於無色界繫諸陰相續不如實知
故，則於是中生寂滅想、若解脫想、若不苦不樂想、若我想，是故
說不苦不樂中癡生。
問曰：是諸使為法中使、眾生中使耶？

答曰：因法生眾生心，隨眾
生心則受諸受，隨諸受貪等煩惱使，故知因法生使而使眾生。何以
知之？若眾生未斷此使則此使使，若斷則不復使。若法中使，法常
有故，使應常使，常不應斷。又非眾生數亦應有使，若然者，若以
人使故壁等有使，以人識故，壁等亦應有識，是事實無。然則無阿
羅漢，餘人使故有使。
問曰：是使未斷則使，斷則不使。

答曰：二種使使，一緣使、二相
應使。是使若斷若不斷，即是緣及相應，何故說斷則不使？若爾，
更應說第三使相，以不可說故當知無也。又使能緣異地而不使，故
知但眾生中使，非法中也。
問曰：二種使使，一緣使、二相應使。是眾生諸使非緣非相應，云
何當使？

答曰：是事先答，諸使因法生而使眾生，如阿毘曇身中說
欲界眾生幾使使等。若不使眾生，云何有如是問？
問曰：若使使眾生，經中說樂受中貪使，此則相違。

答曰：是不盡
語，應言樂受中生貪而使眾生。
問曰：是貪亦因色等生，此中何故但說因樂受生？

答曰：以憶想分
別歡喜等故貪生，非但從色等生。
問曰：因苦受亦生貪，如說樂者不求、苦者多求。何故但說從樂受
生？

答曰：不以苦受故貪生，是人為苦所惱，故於樂受中生貪。
問曰：不苦不樂受中亦貪使使，何故但說樂受中耶？

答曰：是人以
不苦不樂受為樂故貪生，故說樂受中貪使。以此三受中三煩惱使，
故但說三。◎

◎
content.en:
The three unwholesome roots (trīṇy-akuśala-mūlāni) are: greed, ill-will, and delusion.

Question: Conceit (māna) and so on ought also to be unwholesome roots. Why are only three spoken of?

Answer: All the afflictions (kleśa) are divisions of these three kinds of affliction. Conceit and so on are a division of delusion (moha); therefore, they are not spoken of separately.

Furthermore, these three kinds of affliction are frequently present in the minds of sentient beings; conceit and so on are not. Also, for all those not yet detached from desire, down to mosquitos and ants, these three afflictions are all present in their minds; conceit and so on are not like this. Also, greed is the unwholesome root of ill-will; if one is frustrated in what one craves, ill-will then arises. Delusion is the root of both. Why is that? If a person were without delusion, they would not have greed or ill-will. It is also said in a sūtra that the ten unwholesome actions are of three kinds, arising from greed (rāga), ill-will (dveṣa), and delusion (moha); it is not said that they arise from conceit and so on.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of feeling (vedanā), and there is no fourth. In these three feelings, the three afflictions lie latent. If there were a separate conceit and so on, in which feeling would they lie latent? This matter truly cannot be explained. One should know that these three are the root of all the afflictions.

Question: Why does the latent tendency of greed lie latent in pleasant feeling?

Answer: Because it is directly apprehended as arising in this case. As it is said in a sūtra: "A person, upon experiencing a pleasant contact, gives rise to delight; upon experiencing a painful contact, they are not delighted." It is because this person, in relation to the various feelings, does not know in accordance with reality their origin, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them. The latent tendency of ignorance lies latent in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Why is that? Because this person does not know in accordance with reality the continuity of the aggregates connected with the formless realm, they then give rise in that state to a perception of tranquility, or a perception of liberation, or a perception of neither-painful-nor-pleasant, or a thought of an ātman. For this reason, it is said that in what is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, delusion arises.

Question: Do these latent tendencies (anuśaya) lie latent in the dharma or in the sentient being?

Answer: On account of a dharma, a sentient being's mind arises. In accordance with the sentient being's mind, they experience the various feelings. In accordance with the various feelings, the afflictions of greed and so on lie latent. Therefore, it is known that the latent tendency arises on account of a dharma but obsesses the sentient being. How is this known? If a sentient being has not yet severed this latent tendency, then this latent tendency obsesses them. If they have severed it, it no longer obsesses them. If it were to lie latent in the dharma, since the dharma is always present, the latent tendency ought to always be obsessing, and it ought to never be severed. Also, it ought also to exist in what is not counted as a sentient being. If that were so, then just as a wall has a latent tendency because a person's latent tendency obsesses it, so too, because a person has consciousness, a wall ought also to have consciousness. This is in reality not so. In that case, there would be no Arhats, because they would have latent tendencies on account of the latent tendencies of other people.

Question: This latent tendency obsesses when it is not yet severed, and does not obsess when it is severed.

Answer: The obsession of a latent tendency is of two kinds: one is obsession by way of the object, and the other is obsession by way of association. This latent tendency, whether it is severed or not yet severed, is precisely the object and the association. Why then say that it does not obsess when it is severed? If so, a third characteristic of the latent tendency ought to be explained, but because it cannot be explained, one should know that it does not exist.

Furthermore, a latent tendency can have a different level as its object but does not obsess it. Therefore, it is known that it only obsesses in a sentient being, not in a dharma.

Question: The obsession of a latent tendency is of two kinds: one is obsession by way of the object, and the other is obsession by way of association. The various latent tendencies of this sentient being are neither the object nor the association. How then do they obsess?

Answer: This matter was answered previously. The various latent tendencies arise on account of a dharma but obsess the sentient being. As it is said in the section on the body in the Abhidharma: "How many latent tendencies obsess a sentient being of the desire realm?" and so on. If they did not obsess the sentient being, how could there be such a question?

Question: If the latent tendency obsesses the sentient being, a sūtra says, "the latent tendency of greed lies latent in pleasant feeling." This is then a contradiction.

Answer: This is an incomplete statement. It ought to say, "Greed arises in relation to pleasant feeling and obsesses the sentient being."

Question: This greed also arises on account of form (rūpa) and so on. In this context, why is it only said to arise on account of pleasant feeling?

Answer: Greed arises because of recollection, discrimination, and delight, not merely from form and so on.

Question: Greed also arises on account of painful feeling, as it is said, "One who is happy does not seek; one who is in pain seeks much." Why is it only said to arise from pleasant feeling?

Answer: Greed does not arise on account of painful feeling. This person, being afflicted by pain, therefore gives rise to a craving for pleasant feeling.

Question: The latent tendency of greed also lies latent in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Why is it only said to be in pleasant feeling?

Answer: This person takes the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling to be a pleasure, and for this reason greed arises. Therefore, it is said that the latent tendency of greed lies latent in pleasant feeling. Because in these three feelings the three afflictions lie latent, for this reason only three are spoken of.
