content.zh:
真慧名智。真者謂空無我，是中智慧名為真智。假名中慧，名想非
智。

所以者何？經中說：如刀能割，聖弟子以智慧刀能斷結縛使纏
一切煩惱，不說餘法。不以不實能斷煩惱，故知智慧為實。
問曰：汝但說慧能斷煩惱。是事不然。

所以者何？以想亦能斷諸煩
惱，

如經中說：善修無常想故，能破一切欲染色染及無色染、一切
戲調憍慢無明。

答曰：不然。慧斷煩惱，以想名說。佛二種語，一
實語、二名字語。如經中說慈斷瞋恚，而是慈法實不斷結，但智能
斷，如說智刀斷諸煩惱。故知慈能斷結，是名字語。又《慧義經》
中說：解知故名慧。解知何事？謂色無常如實知無常，受想行識無
常如實知無常。是名智慧。又說，聖弟子定攝心者如實知見。是故
知第一義緣名為智慧。又智慧喻中說智刀慧箭等，是喻皆示斷除煩
惱；但真智慧能斷煩惱，故知智慧為實。

又偈中說：行者見世間，
一切諸天人，退失真智故，貪著於名色。世間多見虛妄常樂淨等，
名失真智。若見真實空無我等，名得真智。故知智慧為實。又經中
佛說：若人失財名失少利，若失智慧名失大利。又說，於諸利中財
是少利，慧為最利。又說，於諸明中日月明小，慧明第一。若慧非
實，佛以何故作如是說？

又經中說：慧根是聖諦攝。

又說：苦集智
等當知真實，緣第一諦是名智慧。

又說：於諸法中智慧為上。又
說：無上正遍知亦說慧眼。故知其實。又佛十力皆是智性，故知智
慧為實，緣第一義。
問曰：若爾，則無世間智慧。

答曰：實無世間智慧。何以知之？世
間心緣假名，出世間心緣空無我。

所以者何？世間即是假名，出於
假名名出世間。
問曰：汝說不然。

所以者何？經中說：識何所識？謂識色聲香味觸
法。如是陰界入等皆以識識，今是識皆應名出世間。是故汝言世間
心但緣假名不能緣實，是事不然。又意識亦能實緣，以能緣受想行
等故。又佛說二種正見，世間、出世間。見有福罪等名為世間，若
聖弟子緣苦習滅道無漏念相應慧名出世間。

又偈中說：得世上正
見，雖往來生死，乃至百千世，常不墮惡道。

又經中說：邪行者得
生善處，是人罪業未成、善緣先熟，或臨死時正見相應、善心現
前，故生善處。又十善道中亦說正見。汝云何言無世間智？又佛自
說有三種慧，聞慧、思慧、修慧。聞慧、思慧皆是世間，修慧二
種。

又佛生念：羅睺羅比丘未能成就得解脫慧。又說：五法能令未
熟解脫心熟。此皆是世間智慧。

又經中說：有人能出而不能觀，有
人能觀而不能渡。得世間智故名能出，未見四諦故不能觀。若見四
諦而未得漏盡，故名不渡。

又佛自說：法智、比智、他心智、世
智。

又說：宿命智、生死智皆是有漏。

又說：法住智、泥洹智。如
是等經中說，故當知有有漏智。

答曰：若有有漏智慧，今應當說有
漏、無漏智差別相。
問曰：若法墮有是名有漏，異則無漏。

答曰：何法名墮有？何法名
不墮有？是事應答。若不能答，則非有漏無漏相。汝言有世間心緣
非假名，謂識諸塵等，是事不然。

所以者何？佛說凡夫常隨假名，
是義以一切凡夫心不破假名故，常隨我相終不得離，雖見色亦不離
瓶等相，故凡夫心不緣實義。雖緣受想等法，亦見是我我所，故知
一切世間心皆緣假名。汝言有諸世間智慧，謂二種正見等。今當
答，心有二種，癡心、智心。緣假名法是名癡心，若但緣法謂空無
我是名智心。如《解無明經》中說：無明者不知先、不知後、不知
先後，不知業、不知報、不知先後業報。如是等處處如實不知、不
見、不解，癡妄黑闇，故名為無明。如實不知者，謂不知空無我。
是凡夫心常在假名，緣假名故名為無明，緣空名智。今若一切世間
心皆緣假名，緣假名心名為無明，何得言有世間智慧？
問曰：如汝說智慧相緣假名名無明者，今阿羅漢應有無明，亦有緣
瓶等心故。

答曰：阿羅漢無緣瓶等心。

所以者何？初得道時已壞一
切假名相，故但為事用故說瓶等，不著見慢。有三種語，一從見
生、二從慢生、三從事用生。凡夫若說瓶若說人，是語皆從見生。
學人雖無我見，以失正念故，於五陰中以我慢相說是人是瓶，如
《差摩伽經》中說。事用生者，謂阿羅漢如大迦葉見僧伽梨言是我
物，天神生疑，佛釋之言：此人永拔慢根、燒盡因緣，云何有慢？
但以世間名字故說。故知阿羅漢無瓶等心。
問曰：若無世間智慧，說二種正見等經當云何通？

答曰：此皆是
想，以智名說。佛能通達諸法實相，隨可度眾生立種種名，如智慧
以受等名說，所謂受者於諸法得解脫，亦說善修無常等想能破一切
煩惱，亦說第四不黑不白業能盡諸業，所謂學思。又說以意斷諸貪
著。又說信能度河一心度海，精進除苦慧能清淨。又說眼欲見色。
眼實無欲，但心欲見以眼名說。
問曰：若世間智實是想者，何故名智？若無因緣說名為智，則一切
想皆應名智。亦可說有二種想，一緣世諦、二緣第一義諦。

答曰：
不然。想有種種差別，有想極癡乃至不識世間善惡，有想次癡能別
善惡，有想小癡能緣骨相等，不離假名則不能壞諸陰相。此想能順
壞陰相智，故佛說智。又此想能與實智作因，故名為智。世間有因
中說果，如說食金、施人五事、女為戒垢、好岸渠樂法伏人樂。又
《七漏經》中說：用斷等漏因名漏。又說以食為命，草為牛羊，亦
說衣食等物皆是外命，若奪人財即是奪命。此皆說因為果，如是智
因說智，故無咎也。
問曰：諸念處及煖等中，心能緣實法，是無漏耶？

答曰：無漏心能
破假名，是故隨心能破假名，從此以來名為無漏。
問曰：齊何處心能破假名？

答曰：隨能具足見五陰生滅相，爾時得
無常想，無常想能令行者具無我想。如說聖弟子以無常想修心則能
住無我想，以無我想修心能速得解脫貪恚癡等。

所以者何？若無我
想修心則能住苦想，以我想故雖苦不覺。是故若法無常無我亦苦，
智者則能深生惡厭，故無我想能具苦想。
問曰：汝何故壞次第說？經中說：若無常即是苦，苦即是無我。故
無常想能具苦想，苦想能具無我想。

答曰：經中說：無常想修聖弟
子，心能住無我想。故無常想能具足無我想。又如是說亦有道理。
所以者何？說我者為成後世，故說我是常；是故若見五陰無常，即
知無我。

如經中說：若人說眼是我，則無道理。

所以者何？眼有生
滅。若眼是我，我即生滅。有如是過。
問曰：此二經當云何通？

答曰：苦想二種，一從無常想生，名壞苦
想；一從無我想生，名行苦想。是故二經亦不相違。
問曰：若爾者，念處、煖等法中有無常想，此法皆應是無漏。答
曰：念處等中若是無漏，有何咎耶？
問曰：凡夫心不應是無漏，亦凡夫心有妄念等，云何當是無漏？答
曰：此人非直是凡夫，是人名行須陀洹果。
問曰：行須陀洹果在見諦道中，念處等法不名見諦。

答曰：行須陀
洹果有近有遠，住念處等中名遠行者，見諦名近。何以知之？佛於
《斧柯喻經》中說：若知若見故得漏盡。知見何法？謂此色等此色
等生、此色等滅。若不修道則不得漏盡，修之則得，如抱卵喻。又
行者常修道品，煩惱微塵雖不數覺，盡已乃知，如斧柯喻。又行者
常修三十七品，欲縛結纏易可散壞，如海舡喻。故知從念處來修習
道品，皆名初果者。又若一念若十五念中不得修習。當知此是遠行
須陀洹者。
問曰：初說知此色等此色等生、此色等滅，是初果道，後三喻是三
果道，是故不名行初果者。

答曰：若卵不抱則壞，抱則成就。如是
從念處來初發修習，若不能成不名為行，能成則是學人，名不爛壞
能堪受者。是故若於念處等中爛壞則名凡夫，若修習成則名行初果
者猶在㲉中，若得出㲉名須陀洹。故知在念處等中名遠行者。又郁
伽長者供養眾僧，天神示言：此是阿羅漢乃至此是行初果者。若在
見諦道，云何可示？當知是遠行者。

又經中佛說：若無信等五根，
是人名住外凡夫中。是義說有內外凡夫，若不得達分善根名外凡
夫，得名為內。是內凡夫亦名聖人亦名凡夫，因外凡夫故名聖人，
因見諦道故名凡夫。如阿難語車匿言：凡夫不能念色空無我，受想
行識空無我，一切諸行無常，一切法無我寂滅泥洹。爾時車匿來入
法位，亦說凡夫不能念此。
問曰：若近若遠俱名行者，有何差別？

答曰：若見滅諦名真行者，
若在遠分善根，見五陰無常苦空無我而未見滅，是名名字行者。所
以者何？如經中說，比丘問佛：何名見法？佛言：因眼緣色生眼
識，即共生受想思等，是一切法皆無常敗壞不可保信。若法無常即
是苦，是苦生亦苦、住亦苦、數數起相亦苦，乃至意法亦如是。若
此苦滅餘苦不生，更無相續，行者心念是處寂滅微妙，謂捨一切虛
妄，貪愛盡、滅、離，寂、泥洹。若於此法中心入信解，不動不
轉、不憂不怖，從此已來名為見法。故知行者，若以無常等行觀見
五陰名遠行者，若見滅諦名近行者。如車匿答諸上座：我亦能念色
等無常，而於一切行滅愛盡泥洹。心不能入通達信解，若如是知，
不名見法。

又說：行者若於此法，以軟慧信忍，名信行者。過凡夫
地入正法位，不得初果終不中夭。若以利慧信忍，是名法行。見此
法已能斷三結名須陀洹，明了無餘名阿羅漢。故知見滅名近行者。
問曰：行者何故不盡見滅？

答曰：經中說，諸法無性，從眾緣生，
是法甚深。一切愛盡寂滅泥洹，是處難見。佛觀十二因緣滅故成無
上道。又法印中說：行者若觀五陰無常敗壞虛妄不堅固，亦名為
空，而名知見未淨。此經後說，行者作如是念：我所見所聞所嗅所
嘗所觸所念，以此因緣生識，是識因緣為常無常？即知無常。若從
無常因緣生識，云何當常？是故見一切五陰無常，從眾緣生，盡相
壞相離相滅相。爾時行者知見清淨。以說滅盡名知見淨，故知見滅
名見聖諦。又先法住智、後泥洹智，故見滅諦名得聖道。
content.en:
Answer: True wisdom (bhūta-prajñā) is called knowledge (jñāna). "True" refers to emptiness (śūnyatā) and non-ātman (anātman); the wisdom therein is called true knowledge. Wisdom concerning provisional designations (prajñapti) is called perception (saṃjñā), not knowledge. Why is that? It is said in a sūtra: "Just as a knife can cut, so the noble disciple with the knife of wisdom can sever the fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, and all afflictions." It does not mention any other dharma. Afflictions cannot be severed by what is not real. Therefore, it is known that wisdom is real.

Question: You only say that wisdom can sever the afflictions. This is not so. Why is that? Because perception can also sever the afflictions. As it is said in a sūtra: "By skillfully cultivating the perception of impermanence (anitya-saṃjñā), one can destroy all lust for the desire realm, lust for the form realm, and lust for the formless realm, as well as all frivolity, conceit, and ignorance."

Answer: It is not so. Wisdom severs the afflictions, but it is spoken of using the name of perception. The Buddha has two kinds of speech. One is speech about the real, and the other is speech using names. For instance, it is said in a sūtra that loving-kindness (maitrī) severs ill-will. However, the dharma of loving-kindness does not in reality sever the fetters; only knowledge can sever them, as it is said that the knife of knowledge severs the afflictions. Therefore, to say that loving-kindness can sever the fetters is speech using names.

Furthermore, in the Sūtra on the Meaning of Wisdom it is said: "Because it understands and knows, it is called wisdom." What does it understand and know? It is to know with certainty that form (rūpa) is impermanent (anitya), just as it is. It is to know with certainty that feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are impermanent, just as they are. This is called wisdom. It is also said that a noble disciple whose mind is collected in concentration (samādhi) knows and sees in accordance with reality. Therefore, it is known that apprehending the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is called wisdom.

Furthermore, in the similes for wisdom, such things as the knife of knowledge and the arrow of wisdom are mentioned. These similes all indicate the elimination of the afflictions. Only true wisdom can sever the afflictions. Therefore, it is known that wisdom is real. It is also said in a verse: "The practitioner sees that in the world, all gods and humans have lost true knowledge, and for this reason they grasp with craving at name-and-form (nāma-rūpa)." The world mostly sees the false views of permanence, bliss, purity, and so on; this is called losing true knowledge. If one sees the reality of emptiness, non-ātman, and so on, this is called attaining true knowledge. Therefore, it is known that wisdom is real.

Furthermore, in a sūtra the Buddha said: "If a person loses wealth, it is called a small loss. If one loses wisdom, it is called a great loss." It is also said that among all gains, wealth is a small gain, while wisdom is the greatest gain. It is also said that among all lights, the light of the sun and moon is small; the light of wisdom is supreme. If wisdom were not real, why would the Buddha speak in this way?

Moreover, it is said in a sūtra: "The faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is included in the Noble Truths." It is also said that the knowledge of suffering and its origin, and so on, should be known as real. Apprehending the ultimate truth is called wisdom. It is also said: "Among all dharmas, wisdom is supreme." Also, supreme, perfect, complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) is also referred to as the eye of wisdom. Therefore, it is known that it is real.

Furthermore, the ten powers (daśa-bala) of the Buddha are all of the nature of knowledge. Thus, it is known that wisdom is real and apprehends the ultimate truth.

Question: If so, then there is no worldly wisdom.

Answer: In reality, there is no worldly wisdom. How is this known? The worldly mind apprehends provisional designations (prajñapti). The supramundane mind apprehends emptiness and non-ātman. Why is that? The "world" is just provisional designation. To go beyond provisional designation is called "supramundane."

Question: What you say is not so. Why is that? In a sūtra it is said: "What does consciousness cognize? It cognizes forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas." In this way, the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana) are all cognized by consciousness. Now, all this consciousness should be called supramundane. Therefore, your statement that the worldly mind only apprehends provisional designations and cannot apprehend reality is not so.

Moreover, mind-consciousness (mano-vijñāna) can also apprehend reality, as it is able to apprehend feeling, perception, formations, and so on. Also, the Buddha spoke of two kinds of right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi): worldly and supramundane. The view that there is merit and demerit is worldly. The wisdom associated with the untainted (anāsrava) thought of a noble disciple who apprehends suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is supramundane. It is also said in a verse: "Having attained the supreme worldly right view, although one may come and go in birth and death for even a hundred thousand eons, one will never fall into an evil destiny." It is also said in a sūtra: "One who acts wrongly may be born in a good destiny. This is because this person's sinful karma has not yet matured and the wholesome conditions ripen first, or because at the time of death they are endowed with right view and a wholesome mind arises, and thus they are born in a good destiny."

Furthermore, right view is also mentioned in the ten wholesome paths (daśa-kuśala-mārga). How can you say there is no worldly knowledge? Also, the Buddha himself spoke of three kinds of wisdom: wisdom from hearing, wisdom from contemplating, and wisdom from cultivating (śrutamayī, cintāmayī, bhāvanāmayī prajñā). The wisdom from hearing and contemplating are both worldly. The wisdom from cultivating is of two kinds. Also, the Buddha had the thought: "The bhikṣu Rāhula has not yet perfected the wisdom that brings liberation." He also said: "Five dharmas can cause the immature mind of liberation to mature." These all refer to worldly wisdom. It is also said in a sūtra: "There is one who can go forth but cannot contemplate. There is one who can contemplate but cannot cross over." One who attains worldly knowledge is called 'one who can go forth'; because they have not yet seen the Four Truths, they 'cannot contemplate'. If one has seen the Four Truths but has not yet exhausted the taints (āsrava), one is called one who 'does not cross over'.

Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke of: knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna), analogical knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna), and worldly knowledge (laukika-jñāna). He also said that knowledge of past lives (pūrva-nivāsa-jñāna) and knowledge of death and rebirth (cyuty-upapāda-jñāna) are both tainted (sāsrava). He also spoke of knowledge of the stability of the dharma (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) and knowledge of nirvāṇa. Because it is stated in these and other sūtras, one should know that there is tainted knowledge

Answer: If there is tainted wisdom, then the differentiating characteristics of tainted and untainted knowledge should now be explained.

Question: If a dharma falls within existence (bhava), it is tainted (sāsrava). If it is otherwise, it is untainted (anāsrava).

Answer: What dharma is called "falling within existence"? What dharma is called "not falling within existence"? This matter should be answered. If you cannot answer, then these are not the characteristics of tainted and untainted. You said that there are worldly minds that apprehend what is not a provisional designation, for instance, in cognizing the sense objects. This is not so. Why is that? The Buddha said that the ordinary person (puthujjana, pṛthagjana) always follows provisional designations. The meaning of this is that the minds of all ordinary persons do not break through provisional designations; they always follow the mark of an ātman and can never get free of it. Although they see form, they do not get free of the marks of a jar and so on. Therefore, the mind of an ordinary person does not apprehend the real meaning. Although they apprehend dharmas like feeling and perception, they also see them as 'this is an ātman' or 'what belongs to an ātman'. Therefore, it is known that all worldly minds apprehend provisional designations. You said that there are various kinds of worldly wisdom, such as the two kinds of right view. I will now answer this. There are two kinds of mind: a mind of ignorance and a mind of knowledge. To apprehend the dharma of provisional designation is a mind of ignorance. To apprehend only the dharma, that is, emptiness and non-ātman, is a mind of knowledge. As it is said in the Sūtra that Explains Ignorance: "Ignorance (avidyā) is not knowing the past, not knowing the future, not knowing the past and future; not knowing karma, not knowing its result, not knowing past and future karma and its result." In these and other places, not knowing, not seeing, and not understanding in accordance with reality, being deluded, confused, and in darkness, is called ignorance (cf. Majjhima Nikāya 9). "Not knowing in accordance with reality" means not knowing emptiness and non-ātman. The mind of this ordinary person is always in provisional designation. Because it apprehends provisional designation, it is called ignorance. Apprehending emptiness is called knowledge. Now, if all worldly minds apprehend provisional designation, and the mind that apprehends provisional designation is called ignorance, how can it be said that there is worldly wisdom?

Question: According to your explanation of the characteristic of wisdom, if apprehending a provisional designation is called ignorance, then an Arhat should have ignorance, because they also have a mind that apprehends jars and so on.

Answer: An Arhat does not have a mind that apprehends jars and so on. Why is that? At the moment of first attaining the path, they have already destroyed all marks of provisional designation. They speak of jars and so on only for the sake of practical activity, without being attached to views or conceit. There are three kinds of speech: one born from views, one born from conceit, and one born from practical activity. When an ordinary person speaks of a jar or a person, this speech is born from views. A learner (śaikṣa), although they are without the view of an ātman, because they have lost right mindfulness, through the mark of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna), speaks of 'this person' or 'this jar' in relation to the five aggregates, as is said in the Chemaka Sūtra (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.89). Speech born from practical activity refers to an Arhat, such as when the great Kāśyapa saw a saṃghāṭī robe and said, "This is my thing." A celestial being gave rise to a doubt, and the Buddha explained it, saying: "This person has eternally uprooted the root of conceit and burned up its conditions. How could he have conceit? He speaks thus only because of worldly convention." Therefore, it is known that an Arhat does not have a mind that apprehends jars and so on.

Question: If there is no worldly wisdom, how should the sūtras that speak of the two kinds of right view and so on be explained?

Answer: These are all perceptions (saṃjñā), spoken of with the name of knowledge. The Buddha, who is able to penetrate the true nature of all dharmas, establishes various names according to the beings who can be saved. For example, wisdom is spoken of with names like feeling, as in "one who has feeling gains liberation from the dharmas." It is also said that by skillfully cultivating the perception of impermanence, one can destroy all afflictions. It is also said that the fourth kind of karma, which is neither dark nor bright, can exhaust all other karma, and this refers to the volition of a learner. It is also said that greed and attachment are severed by the mind. It is also said that faith crosses the river, a unified mind crosses the ocean, diligence removes suffering, and wisdom brings purity. It is also said that the eye desires to see form. The eye in reality has no desire, but the mind desires to see, and this is spoken of using the name of the eye.

Question: If worldly knowledge is in reality perception, why is it called knowledge? If it is called knowledge without any reason, then all perceptions should be called knowledge. It could also be said that there are two kinds of perception: one that apprehends conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and one that apprehends ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

Answer: It is not so. There are various different kinds of perception. There is a perception that is extremely foolish, to the point of not recognizing good and evil in the world. There is a perception that is secondarily foolish, which can distinguish good and evil. There is a perception that is slightly foolish, which can apprehend the marks of a skeleton and so on, but without getting free of provisional designation, it cannot destroy the marks of the aggregates. This perception is able to accord with the knowledge that destroys the marks of the aggregates, so the Buddha calls it knowledge. Also, this perception can act as a cause for real knowledge, so it is called knowledge. In the world, the effect is sometimes spoken of in the cause. For example, one speaks of "eating gold," "giving a person the five things," "a woman is a blemish on the precepts," "a good shore," "a ditch," "the joy of the dharma," and "the joy of subduing people." Also, in the Sūtra on the Seven Taints (cf. Majjhima Nikāya 2), the causes for abandoning the taints (āsrava) are called taints. It is also said that food is life, grass is for cattle and sheep. It is also said that clothes, food, and other things are all external life. If one robs a person of their wealth, one is robbing them of their life. In all these cases, the cause is spoken of as the effect. In the same way, the cause of knowledge is spoken of as knowledge, so there is no fault.

Question: In the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and in the stages of heat (uṣmagata) and so on, the mind is able to apprehend real dharmas. Is this untainted (anāsrava)?

Answer: An untainted mind is able to break through provisional designations. Therefore, from the point at which the mind is able to break through provisional designations, it is called untainted.

Question: At what point is the mind able to break through provisional designations?

Answer: When it is able to fully see the arising and ceasing marks of the five aggregates (skandha). At that time, one attains the perception of impermanence, and the perception of impermanence enables the practitioner to perfect the perception of non-ātman. As it is said: "When a noble disciple cultivates the mind with the perception of impermanence, they are able to abide in the perception of non-ātman. By cultivating the mind with the perception of non-ātman, they can quickly gain liberation from greed, hatred, delusion, and so on." Why is that? If one cultivates the mind with the perception of non-ātman, one is then able to abide in the perception of suffering. Because of the thought of an ātman, one does not feel suffering even when it is present. Therefore, if a dharma is impermanent and without an ātman, it is also suffering. The wise person is then able to generate a deep sense of revulsion. Thus, the perception of non-ātman perfects the perception of suffering.

Question: Why are you subverting the sequence? In the sūtra it is said: "What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-ātman." Therefore, the perception of impermanence perfects the perception of suffering, and the perception of suffering perfects the perception of non-ātman.

Answer: It is said in a sūtra: "When a noble disciple cultivates the mind with the perception of impermanence, they are able to abide in the perception of non-ātman." Therefore, the perception of impermanence perfects the perception of non-ātman.

Moreover, there is a principle for stating it this way. Why is that? One speaks of an ātman in order to establish a future life; thus, one says the ātman is permanent. Therefore, if one sees that the five aggregates are impermanent, one immediately knows there is no ātman. As it is said in a sūtra: "If a person says the eye is an ātman, there is no principle in that. Why is that? The eye is subject to arising and ceasing. If the eye were an ātman, then the ātman would arise and cease." There is this fault.

Question: How are these two sūtras to be reconciled?

Answer: There are two kinds of perception of suffering. One arises from the perception of impermanence and is called the perception of the suffering of collapse. One arises from the perception of non-ātman and is called the perception of the suffering of formations. Therefore, the two sūtras do not contradict each other.

Question: If so, then in the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the stages of heat (uṣmagata), and so on, there is the perception of impermanence. All these stages should be untainted.

Answer: If the foundations of mindfulness and so on are untainted, what is the fault in that?

Question: The mind of an ordinary person should not be untainted. Also, the mind of an ordinary person has deluded thoughts and so on. How can it be untainted?

Answer: This person is not just an ordinary person; this person is called one who is practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotaāpatti).

Question: One who is practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer is on the path of seeing (darśana-mārga). The stages of the foundations of mindfulness and so on are not called the path of seeing.

Answer: Practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer can be near or far. Abiding in the foundations of mindfulness and so on is called a distant practitioner. The path of seeing is called a near practitioner. How is this known? The Buddha said in the Sūtra with the Simile of the Ax Handle (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.95): "It is through knowing and seeing that the exhaustion of the taints is attained." Knowing and seeing what dharma? It is this form, the arising of this form, the cessation of this form, and so on. If one does not cultivate the path, one will not attain the exhaustion of the taints. If one cultivates it, one will attain it, as in the simile of hatching an egg. Also, the practitioner constantly cultivates the factors of enlightenment; although the fine dust of the afflictions is not frequently noticed, one knows it only when it is exhausted, as in the simile of the ax handle. Also, the practitioner constantly cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The bonds, fetters, and wrappings of desire are easily dispersed and destroyed, as in the simile of the sea-going vessel. Therefore, it is known that cultivating the factors of enlightenment starting from the foundations of mindfulness is all called being on the path to the first fruit. Also, if one cannot cultivate in one moment or in fifteen moments, one should know that this is a distant practitioner for stream-entry.

Question: The first part says that knowing "this form, the arising of this form, the cessation of this form" is the path to the first fruit. The latter three similes refer to the path to the third fruit. Therefore, it is not called practicing for the first fruit.

Answer: If an egg is not hatched, it will spoil; if it is hatched, it will succeed. In the same way, beginning the cultivation from the foundations of mindfulness, if one cannot succeed, it is not called practice. If one can succeed, one is a learner, called one who does not spoil and is able to endure. Therefore, if one spoils in the stages of the foundations of mindfulness and so on, one is called an ordinary person. If the cultivation succeeds, one is called one practicing for the first fruit who is still in the shell. If one comes out of the shell, one is called a stream-enterer (srotaāpanna). Therefore, it is known that being in the stages of the foundations of mindfulness and so on is called a distant practitioner. Also, the householder Ugga was making offerings to the community of monks, and a celestial being pointed out: "This is an Arhat... this is one practicing for the first fruit." (cf. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.21). If this person were on the path of seeing, how could they be pointed out? One should know that this is a distant practitioner. Also, in a sūtra the Buddha said: "If a person is without the five faculties of faith and so on, this person is said to abide among the external ordinary persons." The meaning is that there are internal and external ordinary persons. If one has not attained the wholesome roots that are conducive to penetration, one is an external ordinary person. If one has attained them, one is internal. This internal ordinary person is also called a noble one and also an ordinary person. In relation to the external ordinary person, they are called a noble one. In relation to the path of seeing, they are called an ordinary person. As Ānanda said to Channa: "An ordinary person cannot contemplate that form is empty and without an ātman, that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are empty and without an ātman, that all formations are impermanent, that all dharmas are without an ātman, and that nirvāṇa is quiescent." (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.90). At that time, when Channa was about to enter the stage of the dharma, it was also said that an ordinary person cannot contemplate this.

Question: If both the near and the far are called practitioners, what is the difference?

Answer: If one sees the truth of cessation, one is called a true practitioner. If one is in the distant stage of the wholesome roots and sees that the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without an ātman, but has not yet seen cessation, one is called a practitioner in name only. Why is that? As it is said in a sūtra, a bhikṣu asked the Buddha: "What is called seeing the dharma?" The Buddha said: "Conditioned by the eye and form, eye-consciousness arises. Together with it arise feeling, perception, volition, and so on. All these dharmas are impermanent, subject to decay, and cannot be relied upon. Whatever dharma is impermanent is suffering. The arising of this suffering is suffering, its duration is suffering, and the mark of its repeated occurrence is suffering. It is the same up to the mind and its objects. If this suffering ceases and other suffering does not arise, and there is no more continuation, the practitioner's mind thinks: 'This state is quiescent, subtle,' that is, the abandoning of all falsehood, the exhaustion of craving, cessation, detachment, tranquility, nirvāṇa. If with regard to this dharma the mind enters into faith and understanding, is unshakable, unmoving, without sorrow, without fear, from this point on, it is called seeing the dharma." Therefore, it is known that if a practitioner contemplates and sees the five aggregates with the characteristics of impermanence and so on, they are a distant practitioner. If they see the truth of cessation, they are a near practitioner. As Channa replied to the elders: "I too can contemplate that form and so on are impermanent, but with regard to the cessation of all formations, the exhaustion of craving, nirvāṇa, my mind cannot enter, penetrate, and have faith and understanding." If one knows in this way, it is not called seeing the dharma. It is also said: "If a practitioner has gentle wisdom, faith, and forbearance with regard to this dharma, they are called a faith-follower (śraddhānusārin). Having passed beyond the stage of an ordinary person, they enter the stage of the true dharma. They will not die before attaining the first fruit. If they have sharp wisdom, faith, and forbearance, they are called a dharma-follower (dharmānusārin). Having seen this dharma, they are able to sever the three fetters and are called a stream-enterer. When all is clarified without remainder, one is called an Arhat." Therefore, it is known that seeing cessation makes one a near practitioner.

Question: Why does the practitioner not yet see cessation completely?

Answer: It is said in a sūtra: "The fact that dharmas are without a self-nature and arise from a collection of conditions—this dharma is extremely profound. The exhaustion of all craving, quiescent nirvāṇa—this state is difficult to see." The Buddha, by contemplating the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination, attained the unsurpassed path. Also, in the Sūtra of the Seal of the Dharma it is said: "If a practitioner contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent, subject to decay, false, and not solid, this is also called emptiness, but their knowledge and vision are said to be not yet pure." Later in this sūtra it says, the practitioner has this thought: "That which I have seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched, and thought about, with these as conditions consciousness arises. Is the consciousness that arises from these impermanent conditions permanent or impermanent?" They immediately know it is impermanent. If consciousness arises from impermanent conditions, how could it be permanent? Therefore, they see that all five aggregates are impermanent, arise from a collection of conditions, and have the marks of exhaustion, destruction, separation, and cessation. At that time, the practitioner's knowledge and vision are pure. Because it says that purity of knowledge and vision is the exhaustion of cessation, it is known that seeing cessation is seeing the Noble Truths. Also, first comes the knowledge of the stability of the dharma (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), and afterwards the knowledge of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-jñāna). Therefore, seeing the truth of cessation is attaining the noble path.
content.pt:
Answer: True wisdom (bhūta-prajñā) is called knowledge (jñāna). "True" refers to emptiness (śūnyatā) and non-ātman (anātman); the wisdom therein is called true knowledge. Wisdom concerning provisional designations (prajñapti) is called perception (saṃjñā), not knowledge. Why is that? It is said in a sūtra: "Just as a knife can cut, so the noble disciple with the knife of wisdom can sever the fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, and all afflictions." It does not mention any other dharma. Afflictions cannot be severed by what is not real. Therefore, it is known that wisdom is real.

Question: You only say that wisdom can sever the afflictions. This is not so. Why is that? Because perception can also sever the afflictions. As it is said in a sūtra: "By skillfully cultivating the perception of impermanence (anitya-saṃjñā), one can destroy all lust for the desire realm, lust for the form realm, and lust for the formless realm, as well as all frivolity, conceit, and ignorance."

Answer: It is not so. Wisdom severs the afflictions, but it is spoken of using the name of perception. The Buddha has two kinds of speech. One is speech about the real, and the other is speech using names. For instance, it is said in a sūtra that loving-kindness (maitrī) severs ill-will. However, the dharma of loving-kindness does not in reality sever the fetters; only knowledge can sever them, as it is said that the knife of knowledge severs the afflictions. Therefore, to say that loving-kindness can sever the fetters is speech using names.

Furthermore, in the Sūtra on the Meaning of Wisdom it is said: "Because it understands and knows, it is called wisdom." What does it understand and know? It is to know with certainty that form (rūpa) is impermanent (anitya), just as it is. It is to know with certainty that feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are impermanent, just as they are. This is called wisdom. It is also said that a noble disciple whose mind is collected in concentration (samādhi) knows and sees in accordance with reality. Therefore, it is known that apprehending the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is called wisdom.

Furthermore, in the similes for wisdom, such things as the knife of knowledge and the arrow of wisdom are mentioned. These similes all indicate the elimination of the afflictions. Only true wisdom can sever the afflictions. Therefore, it is known that wisdom is real. It is also said in a verse: "The practitioner sees that in the world, all gods and humans have lost true knowledge, and for this reason they grasp with craving at name-and-form (nāma-rūpa)." The world mostly sees the false views of permanence, bliss, purity, and so on; this is called losing true knowledge. If one sees the reality of emptiness, non-ātman, and so on, this is called attaining true knowledge. Therefore, it is known that wisdom is real.

Furthermore, in a sūtra the Buddha said: "If a person loses wealth, it is called a small loss. If one loses wisdom, it is called a great loss." It is also said that among all gains, wealth is a small gain, while wisdom is the greatest gain. It is also said that among all lights, the light of the sun and moon is small; the light of wisdom is supreme. If wisdom were not real, why would the Buddha speak in this way?

Moreover, it is said in a sūtra: "The faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya) is included in the Noble Truths." It is also said that the knowledge of suffering and its origin, and so on, should be known as real. Apprehending the ultimate truth is called wisdom. It is also said: "Among all dharmas, wisdom is supreme." Also, supreme, perfect, complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) is also referred to as the eye of wisdom. Therefore, it is known that it is real.

Furthermore, the ten powers (daśa-bala) of the Buddha are all of the nature of knowledge. Thus, it is known that wisdom is real and apprehends the ultimate truth.

Question: If so, then there is no worldly wisdom.

Answer: In reality, there is no worldly wisdom. How is this known? The worldly mind apprehends provisional designations (prajñapti). The supramundane mind apprehends emptiness and non-ātman. Why is that? The "world" is just provisional designation. To go beyond provisional designation is called "supramundane."

Question: What you say is not so. Why is that? In a sūtra it is said: "What does consciousness cognize? It cognizes forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and dharmas." In this way, the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana) are all cognized by consciousness. Now, all this consciousness should be called supramundane. Therefore, your statement that the worldly mind only apprehends provisional designations and cannot apprehend reality is not so.

Moreover, mind-consciousness (mano-vijñāna) can also apprehend reality, as it is able to apprehend feeling, perception, formations, and so on. Also, the Buddha spoke of two kinds of right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi): worldly and supramundane. The view that there is merit and demerit is worldly. The wisdom associated with the untainted (anāsrava) thought of a noble disciple who apprehends suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is supramundane. It is also said in a verse: "Having attained the supreme worldly right view, although one may come and go in birth and death for even a hundred thousand eons, one will never fall into an evil destiny." It is also said in a sūtra: "One who acts wrongly may be born in a good destiny. This is because this person's sinful karma has not yet matured and the wholesome conditions ripen first, or because at the time of death they are endowed with right view and a wholesome mind arises, and thus they are born in a good destiny."

Furthermore, right view is also mentioned in the ten wholesome paths (daśa-kuśala-mārga). How can you say there is no worldly knowledge? Also, the Buddha himself spoke of three kinds of wisdom: wisdom from hearing, wisdom from contemplating, and wisdom from cultivating (śrutamayī, cintāmayī, bhāvanāmayī prajñā). The wisdom from hearing and contemplating are both worldly. The wisdom from cultivating is of two kinds. Also, the Buddha had the thought: "The bhikṣu Rāhula has not yet perfected the wisdom that brings liberation." He also said: "Five dharmas can cause the immature mind of liberation to mature." These all refer to worldly wisdom. It is also said in a sūtra: "There is one who can go forth but cannot contemplate. There is one who can contemplate but cannot cross over." One who attains worldly knowledge is called 'one who can go forth'; because they have not yet seen the Four Truths, they 'cannot contemplate'. If one has seen the Four Truths but has not yet exhausted the taints (āsrava), one is called one who 'does not cross over'.

Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke of: knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna), analogical knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna), and worldly knowledge (laukika-jñāna). He also said that knowledge of past lives (pūrva-nivāsa-jñāna) and knowledge of death and rebirth (cyuty-upapāda-jñāna) are both tainted (sāsrava). He also spoke of knowledge of the stability of the dharma (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) and knowledge of nirvāṇa. Because it is stated in these and other sūtras, one should know that there is tainted knowledge

Answer: If there is tainted wisdom, then the differentiating characteristics of tainted and untainted knowledge should now be explained.

Question: If a dharma falls within existence (bhava), it is tainted (sāsrava). If it is otherwise, it is untainted (anāsrava).

Answer: What dharma is called "falling within existence"? What dharma is called "not falling within existence"? This matter should be answered. If you cannot answer, then these are not the characteristics of tainted and untainted. You said that there are worldly minds that apprehend what is not a provisional designation, for instance, in cognizing the sense objects. This is not so. Why is that? The Buddha said that the ordinary person (puthujjana, pṛthagjana) always follows provisional designations. The meaning of this is that the minds of all ordinary persons do not break through provisional designations; they always follow the mark of an ātman and can never get free of it. Although they see form, they do not get free of the marks of a jar and so on. Therefore, the mind of an ordinary person does not apprehend the real meaning. Although they apprehend dharmas like feeling and perception, they also see them as 'this is an ātman' or 'what belongs to an ātman'. Therefore, it is known that all worldly minds apprehend provisional designations. You said that there are various kinds of worldly wisdom, such as the two kinds of right view. I will now answer this. There are two kinds of mind: a mind of ignorance and a mind of knowledge. To apprehend the dharma of provisional designation is a mind of ignorance. To apprehend only the dharma, that is, emptiness and non-ātman, is a mind of knowledge. As it is said in the Sūtra that Explains Ignorance: "Ignorance (avidyā) is not knowing the past, not knowing the future, not knowing the past and future; not knowing karma, not knowing its result, not knowing past and future karma and its result." In these and other places, not knowing, not seeing, and not understanding in accordance with reality, being deluded, confused, and in darkness, is called ignorance (cf. Majjhima Nikāya 9). "Not knowing in accordance with reality" means not knowing emptiness and non-ātman. The mind of this ordinary person is always in provisional designation. Because it apprehends provisional designation, it is called ignorance. Apprehending emptiness is called knowledge. Now, if all worldly minds apprehend provisional designation, and the mind that apprehends provisional designation is called ignorance, how can it be said that there is worldly wisdom?

Question: According to your explanation of the characteristic of wisdom, if apprehending a provisional designation is called ignorance, then an Arhat should have ignorance, because they also have a mind that apprehends jars and so on.

Answer: An Arhat does not have a mind that apprehends jars and so on. Why is that? At the moment of first attaining the path, they have already destroyed all marks of provisional designation. They speak of jars and so on only for the sake of practical activity, without being attached to views or conceit. There are three kinds of speech: one born from views, one born from conceit, and one born from practical activity. When an ordinary person speaks of a jar or a person, this speech is born from views. A learner (śaikṣa), although they are without the view of an ātman, because they have lost right mindfulness, through the mark of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna), speaks of 'this person' or 'this jar' in relation to the five aggregates, as is said in the Chemaka Sūtra (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.89). Speech born from practical activity refers to an Arhat, such as when the great Kāśyapa saw a saṃghāṭī robe and said, "This is my thing." A celestial being gave rise to a doubt, and the Buddha explained it, saying: "This person has eternally uprooted the root of conceit and burned up its conditions. How could he have conceit? He speaks thus only because of worldly convention." Therefore, it is known that an Arhat does not have a mind that apprehends jars and so on.

Question: If there is no worldly wisdom, how should the sūtras that speak of the two kinds of right view and so on be explained?

Answer: These are all perceptions (saṃjñā), spoken of with the name of knowledge. The Buddha, who is able to penetrate the true nature of all dharmas, establishes various names according to the beings who can be saved. For example, wisdom is spoken of with names like feeling, as in "one who has feeling gains liberation from the dharmas." It is also said that by skillfully cultivating the perception of impermanence, one can destroy all afflictions. It is also said that the fourth kind of karma, which is neither dark nor bright, can exhaust all other karma, and this refers to the volition of a learner. It is also said that greed and attachment are severed by the mind. It is also said that faith crosses the river, a unified mind crosses the ocean, diligence removes suffering, and wisdom brings purity. It is also said that the eye desires to see form. The eye in reality has no desire, but the mind desires to see, and this is spoken of using the name of the eye.

Question: If worldly knowledge is in reality perception, why is it called knowledge? If it is called knowledge without any reason, then all perceptions should be called knowledge. It could also be said that there are two kinds of perception: one that apprehends conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and one that apprehends ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

Answer: It is not so. There are various different kinds of perception. There is a perception that is extremely foolish, to the point of not recognizing good and evil in the world. There is a perception that is secondarily foolish, which can distinguish good and evil. There is a perception that is slightly foolish, which can apprehend the marks of a skeleton and so on, but without getting free of provisional designation, it cannot destroy the marks of the aggregates. This perception is able to accord with the knowledge that destroys the marks of the aggregates, so the Buddha calls it knowledge. Also, this perception can act as a cause for real knowledge, so it is called knowledge. In the world, the effect is sometimes spoken of in the cause. For example, one speaks of "eating gold," "giving a person the five things," "a woman is a blemish on the precepts," "a good shore," "a ditch," "the joy of the dharma," and "the joy of subduing people." Also, in the Sūtra on the Seven Taints (cf. Majjhima Nikāya 2), the causes for abandoning the taints (āsrava) are called taints. It is also said that food is life, grass is for cattle and sheep. It is also said that clothes, food, and other things are all external life. If one robs a person of their wealth, one is robbing them of their life. In all these cases, the cause is spoken of as the effect. In the same way, the cause of knowledge is spoken of as knowledge, so there is no fault.

Question: In the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and in the stages of heat (uṣmagata) and so on, the mind is able to apprehend real dharmas. Is this untainted (anāsrava)?

Answer: An untainted mind is able to break through provisional designations. Therefore, from the point at which the mind is able to break through provisional designations, it is called untainted.

Question: At what point is the mind able to break through provisional designations?

Answer: When it is able to fully see the arising and ceasing marks of the five aggregates (skandha). At that time, one attains the perception of impermanence, and the perception of impermanence enables the practitioner to perfect the perception of non-ātman. As it is said: "When a noble disciple cultivates the mind with the perception of impermanence, they are able to abide in the perception of non-ātman. By cultivating the mind with the perception of non-ātman, they can quickly gain liberation from greed, hatred, delusion, and so on." Why is that? If one cultivates the mind with the perception of non-ātman, one is then able to abide in the perception of suffering. Because of the thought of an ātman, one does not feel suffering even when it is present. Therefore, if a dharma is impermanent and without an ātman, it is also suffering. The wise person is then able to generate a deep sense of revulsion. Thus, the perception of non-ātman perfects the perception of suffering.

Question: Why are you subverting the sequence? In the sūtra it is said: "What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-ātman." Therefore, the perception of impermanence perfects the perception of suffering, and the perception of suffering perfects the perception of non-ātman.

Answer: It is said in a sūtra: "When a noble disciple cultivates the mind with the perception of impermanence, they are able to abide in the perception of non-ātman." Therefore, the perception of impermanence perfects the perception of non-ātman.

Moreover, there is a principle for stating it this way. Why is that? One speaks of an ātman in order to establish a future life; thus, one says the ātman is permanent. Therefore, if one sees that the five aggregates are impermanent, one immediately knows there is no ātman. As it is said in a sūtra: "If a person says the eye is an ātman, there is no principle in that. Why is that? The eye is subject to arising and ceasing. If the eye were an ātman, then the ātman would arise and cease." There is this fault.

Question: How are these two sūtras to be reconciled?

Answer: There are two kinds of perception of suffering. One arises from the perception of impermanence and is called the perception of the suffering of collapse. One arises from the perception of non-ātman and is called the perception of the suffering of formations. Therefore, the two sūtras do not contradict each other.

Question: If so, then in the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the stages of heat (uṣmagata), and so on, there is the perception of impermanence. All these stages should be untainted.

Answer: If the foundations of mindfulness and so on are untainted, what is the fault in that?

Question: The mind of an ordinary person should not be untainted. Also, the mind of an ordinary person has deluded thoughts and so on. How can it be untainted?

Answer: This person is not just an ordinary person; this person is called one who is practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotaāpatti).

Question: One who is practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer is on the path of seeing (darśana-mārga). The stages of the foundations of mindfulness and so on are not called the path of seeing.

Answer: Practicing for the fruit of a stream-enterer can be near or far. Abiding in the foundations of mindfulness and so on is called a distant practitioner. The path of seeing is called a near practitioner. How is this known? The Buddha said in the Sūtra with the Simile of the Ax Handle (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.95): "It is through knowing and seeing that the exhaustion of the taints is attained." Knowing and seeing what dharma? It is this form, the arising of this form, the cessation of this form, and so on. If one does not cultivate the path, one will not attain the exhaustion of the taints. If one cultivates it, one will attain it, as in the simile of hatching an egg. Also, the practitioner constantly cultivates the factors of enlightenment; although the fine dust of the afflictions is not frequently noticed, one knows it only when it is exhausted, as in the simile of the ax handle. Also, the practitioner constantly cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The bonds, fetters, and wrappings of desire are easily dispersed and destroyed, as in the simile of the sea-going vessel. Therefore, it is known that cultivating the factors of enlightenment starting from the foundations of mindfulness is all called being on the path to the first fruit. Also, if one cannot cultivate in one moment or in fifteen moments, one should know that this is a distant practitioner for stream-entry.

Question: The first part says that knowing "this form, the arising of this form, the cessation of this form" is the path to the first fruit. The latter three similes refer to the path to the third fruit. Therefore, it is not called practicing for the first fruit.

Answer: If an egg is not hatched, it will spoil; if it is hatched, it will succeed. In the same way, beginning the cultivation from the foundations of mindfulness, if one cannot succeed, it is not called practice. If one can succeed, one is a learner, called one who does not spoil and is able to endure. Therefore, if one spoils in the stages of the foundations of mindfulness and so on, one is called an ordinary person. If the cultivation succeeds, one is called one practicing for the first fruit who is still in the shell. If one comes out of the shell, one is called a stream-enterer (srotaāpanna). Therefore, it is known that being in the stages of the foundations of mindfulness and so on is called a distant practitioner. Also, the householder Ugga was making offerings to the community of monks, and a celestial being pointed out: "This is an Arhat... this is one practicing for the first fruit." (cf. Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.21). If this person were on the path of seeing, how could they be pointed out? One should know that this is a distant practitioner. Also, in a sūtra the Buddha said: "If a person is without the five faculties of faith and so on, this person is said to abide among the external ordinary persons." The meaning is that there are internal and external ordinary persons. If one has not attained the wholesome roots that are conducive to penetration, one is an external ordinary person. If one has attained them, one is internal. This internal ordinary person is also called a noble one and also an ordinary person. In relation to the external ordinary person, they are called a noble one. In relation to the path of seeing, they are called an ordinary person. As Ānanda said to Channa: "An ordinary person cannot contemplate that form is empty and without an ātman, that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are empty and without an ātman, that all formations are impermanent, that all dharmas are without an ātman, and that nirvāṇa is quiescent." (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.90). At that time, when Channa was about to enter the stage of the dharma, it was also said that an ordinary person cannot contemplate this.

Question: If both the near and the far are called practitioners, what is the difference?

Answer: If one sees the truth of cessation, one is called a true practitioner. If one is in the distant stage of the wholesome roots and sees that the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without an ātman, but has not yet seen cessation, one is called a practitioner in name only. Why is that? As it is said in a sūtra, a bhikṣu asked the Buddha: "What is called seeing the dharma?" The Buddha said: "Conditioned by the eye and form, eye-consciousness arises. Together with it arise feeling, perception, volition, and so on. All these dharmas are impermanent, subject to decay, and cannot be relied upon. Whatever dharma is impermanent is suffering. The arising of this suffering is suffering, its duration is suffering, and the mark of its repeated occurrence is suffering. It is the same up to the mind and its objects. If this suffering ceases and other suffering does not arise, and there is no more continuation, the practitioner's mind thinks: 'This state is quiescent, subtle,' that is, the abandoning of all falsehood, the exhaustion of craving, cessation, detachment, tranquility, nirvāṇa. If with regard to this dharma the mind enters into faith and understanding, is unshakable, unmoving, without sorrow, without fear, from this point on, it is called seeing the dharma." Therefore, it is known that if a practitioner contemplates and sees the five aggregates with the characteristics of impermanence and so on, they are a distant practitioner. If they see the truth of cessation, they are a near practitioner. As Channa replied to the elders: "I too can contemplate that form and so on are impermanent, but with regard to the cessation of all formations, the exhaustion of craving, nirvāṇa, my mind cannot enter, penetrate, and have faith and understanding." If one knows in this way, it is not called seeing the dharma. It is also said: "If a practitioner has gentle wisdom, faith, and forbearance with regard to this dharma, they are called a faith-follower (śraddhānusārin). Having passed beyond the stage of an ordinary person, they enter the stage of the true dharma. They will not die before attaining the first fruit. If they have sharp wisdom, faith, and forbearance, they are called a dharma-follower (dharmānusārin). Having seen this dharma, they are able to sever the three fetters and are called a stream-enterer. When all is clarified without remainder, one is called an Arhat." Therefore, it is known that seeing cessation makes one a near practitioner.

Question: Why does the practitioner not yet see cessation completely?

Answer: It is said in a sūtra: "The fact that dharmas are without a self-nature and arise from a collection of conditions—this dharma is extremely profound. The exhaustion of all craving, quiescent nirvāṇa—this state is difficult to see." The Buddha, by contemplating the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination, attained the unsurpassed path. Also, in the Sūtra of the Seal of the Dharma it is said: "If a practitioner contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent, subject to decay, false, and not solid, this is also called emptiness, but their knowledge and vision are said to be not yet pure." Later in this sūtra it says, the practitioner has this thought: "That which I have seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched, and thought about, with these as conditions consciousness arises. Is the consciousness that arises from these impermanent conditions permanent or impermanent?" They immediately know it is impermanent. If consciousness arises from impermanent conditions, how could it be permanent? Therefore, they see that all five aggregates are impermanent, arise from a collection of conditions, and have the marks of exhaustion, destruction, separation, and cessation. At that time, the practitioner's knowledge and vision are pure. Because it says that purity of knowledge and vision is the exhaustion of cessation, it is known that seeing cessation is seeing the Noble Truths. Also, first comes the knowledge of the stability of the dharma (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), and afterwards the knowledge of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-jñāna). Therefore, seeing the truth of cessation is attaining the noble path.

content.zh:
問曰：汝說但見滅諦名行果者。是事不然。

所以者何？經中佛說：
我及汝等不能如實見四諦，故久處生死。今見是四諦，身因緣斷、
生死根盡，更不受有。當知見四諦故名行果者，非但見滅。又佛
說：上法所謂四諦，是故行者應悉知見。

又說：若人法服毀形正信
出家，皆為見四諦故。若人欲得須陀洹、斯陀含、阿那含道，皆為
見四諦故。若得阿羅漢、辟支佛、佛道，皆已見四諦故。故知非但
見滅諦也。

又佛自說四諦以次第得。又《轉法輪經》中說：我觀此
苦、此苦因、此苦滅、此苦滅道，於是中生眼智明覺。如是三轉皆
說四諦。

又經中說：鮮淨白疊投之池中即時受色，此人如是，即於
一坐見四真諦。

又說：行者淨心正觀苦諦乃至道諦，如是見故，從
欲漏、有漏、無明漏中心得解脫。又諸經中說聖諦處，盡皆說四
諦，不但說滅。又佛說四智，苦智、集智、滅智、道智，皆為四諦
故有。行者法應遍見四諦，猶如良醫應知病、知病因、破病、破病
藥。如是行者欲脫諸苦，應知苦、苦因、苦滅、苦滅道。若不知
苦，何由當知苦因、苦滅及苦滅道？故知非但見滅。

答曰：諸有說
四聖諦利，皆於陰界入等中說，謂知此色等色等生滅，故得漏盡。
又佛自說：我於色等陰中不如實知味過出離，終不自謂得無上道。
若如實知，則自知得道。又《城喻經》說：我若未知老死、老死
生、老死滅、老死滅道，乃至諸行、諸行生、諸行滅、諸行滅道，
不自說我得無上道。若如實知，自說得佛。如是等見若是得道見
者，則十六心不名得道。
問曰：我不說此名得道見，是思惟時。

答曰：四諦中亦如是說，亦
可說是思惟時。若不爾，應說因緣，見四諦名得道時、見五陰等為
思惟時。
問曰：斷煩惱智名為得道，思惟五陰等不斷煩惱。

答曰：我先已說
五陰等智亦斷煩惱，如說知見色等故得漏盡。又說，見世間集則滅
無見、見世間滅則滅有見。又佛自觀因緣得道。又《甄叔伽經》中
說種種得道因緣，有人觀五陰得道，或觀十二入十八界十二因緣等
得道。故知非但以四諦得道。若汝意謂雖有是說，不以此觀能斷煩
惱，亦可說言雖觀四諦不斷煩惱。又要當以真諦得道，而解四諦中
說生苦、老苦、病苦、死苦、怨憎會苦、愛別離苦、所求不得苦，
取要言之五陰為苦。

又說：苦因所謂貪愛，常隨喜樂處處受身。觀
如是等不應盡漏，此皆世諦，非第一故。
問曰：雖觀生死等不應盡漏，略說五陰皆苦，是中有智能破煩惱。
答曰：餘三諦云何？故知汝自憶想分別。又觀五陰皆苦，是散亂
心，不應得道。
問曰：若不以四諦得道，當以何法得道？

答曰：以一諦得道，所謂
為滅。

如經中說：妄名虛誑，實名不顛倒。一切有為法皆虛誑妄
取，故知行者隨心在有為法中，皆非真實。

如經中說：諸有為法虛
誑，如幻如焰如夢如假借等。如《法句經》中說：虛妄繫世間，似
如有堅實，實無見如有，正觀則皆無。如實無男女法，但五陰和合
強名男女。凡夫倒惑，謂之實有。行者觀此五陰空無我故，即不復
見。如《法印經》中說：行者觀色無常、空虛、離相。無常者，謂
色體性無常。空虛者，如瓶中無水名曰空瓶。如是五陰中無神我，
故名為空。如是觀者者，亦名為空，亦名知見未淨，以未能見五陰
滅，故後乃見滅，所謂行者作如是念：我所見聞等，故知見滅諸煩
惱盡。
問曰：何故見滅則煩惱盡，非餘諦耶？

答曰：行者爾時苦想決定，
若未證滅相，於有為法中苦心未定。如人不得初禪喜樂，於五欲中
不生厭想。又如未得無覺觀定，於覺觀定不以為患。行者亦爾，未
證泥洹寂滅相時不得行苦，當知見滅諦故苦想具足，苦想具足故愛
等結斷。
問曰：若見滅諦故苦想具足，應見滅諦後煩惱方斷。

所以者何？見
滅諦已苦想具故。

答曰：非後時斷，隨於滅中得寂滅相，即時苦想
具足，後當現前。

如經中說：行者於集生相法知盡滅相，即於法中
得法眼淨。又人於諸陰中常有我心，雖觀諸陰無常苦等，未得永
滅；若見滅諦，以無相故我心永滅。
問曰：若見滅諦則我心盡，何故佛觀前人柔軟心等為說四諦，不但
說滅？

答曰：此中有順道行。何者以無常想無我想具足故，得此苦
觀以其近道，是故合說。
問曰：若得道時斷身見者，何故復說戒取疑耶？

答曰：行者得道，
現見諸法皆空無我，即不復疑。不同凡夫聞思等觀，若見道諦則知
唯此一實更無餘道，是故說三。
問曰：若得道時見諦所斷諸煩惱盡，何故但說三結盡耶？

答曰：一
切煩惱皆以身見為本。如佛問比丘：人以何事、因何事、見何事故
生如是見：唯有此身，死則斷滅。如是等一切見。比丘白佛：佛為
法王，唯願解脫。佛言：人以色、因色、見色是我，故起此見，乃
至識亦如是。當知因見我故生諸煩惱。

所以者何？若有身見則謂此
我若常無常，若定見常則是常見，定見無常則是斷見。若我是常，
則無業無報無苦解脫；我若無常，亦無業無報及苦解脫，不以修道
而得泥洹。若以此見為勝，即是見取。謂能得度，即是戒取。自見
中愛、他見中恚，以此見自高即是憍慢。皆以不如實知故起此結，
即是無明。是故身見斷故見諦結斷。
問曰：若身見斷餘亦斷者，何故別說戒取疑耶？

答曰：以其勝故。
行者現見法相則無有疑。此疑疑我為有為無，亦疑此道得清淨不？
令見苦諦則我見斷，亦知唯此一道更無有餘。是故說斷身見名真見
苦，斷戒取故名修行道，於知所知法中無疑。若以正智知所知法，
即斷集證滅名具四諦，故說此三示無疑相。此疑從我道生，如經中
說初得道相，謂見法、得法、知法、達法，度諸疑網不隨他教，於
佛法中得無畏力安，住果中。
content.en:
Question: You said that only one who sees the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya) is called a practitioner for the fruit. This is not so. Why is that? In a sūtra, the Buddha said: "Because I and you all did not see the Four Truths in accordance with reality, we have long remained in birth and death. Now, having seen these Four Truths, the condition for the body is severed, the root of birth and death is exhausted, and we will not take on another existence." One should know that it is because of seeing the Four Truths that one is called a practitioner for the fruit, not just by seeing cessation. Also, the Buddha said: "The supreme dharma is the so-called Four Truths." Therefore, the practitioner should know and see all of them. He also said: "If a person, wearing the dharma robes and having disfigured their form, goes forth from home with right faith, it is all for the sake of seeing the Four Truths. If a person wishes to attain the path of a stream-enterer (srotaāpanna), a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), or a non-returner (anāgāmin), it is all for the sake of seeing the Four Truths. If one attains the path of an Arhat, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Buddha, it is because they have already seen the Four Truths." Therefore, it is known that it is not only by seeing the truth of cessation. Also, the Buddha himself said that the Four Truths are attained in sequence.

Furthermore, in the Sūtra of Turning the Wheel of the Dharma (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, SN 56.11) it is said: "I contemplated this suffering, the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path to the cessation of this suffering. Therein arose the eye, knowledge, clarity, and realization." In this way, all three turnings speak of the Four Truths. It is also said in a sūtra: "A clean, white cloth, when thrown into a pool of dye, immediately takes the color. This person is like that; in a single sitting, they see the Four Noble Truths." It is also said: "The practitioner, with a pure mind, rightly contemplates the truth of suffering up to the truth of the path. Because of seeing in this way, their mind is liberated from the taint of desire (kāmāsrava), the taint of existence (bhavāsrava), and the taint of ignorance (avidyāsrava)." In all the sūtras where the Noble Truths are mentioned, all Four Truths are spoken of, not just cessation. The Buddha also spoke of four kinds of knowledge: knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of the origin (samudaya-jñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), all of which exist for the sake of the Four Truths. The practitioner should, by rights, see all Four Truths, just as a good physician should know the disease, know the cause of the disease, eliminate the disease, and know the medicine that eliminates the disease. In the same way, a practitioner who wishes to be free from all suffering should know suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path to the cessation of suffering. If one does not know suffering, how could one know the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path to the cessation of suffering? Therefore, it is known that it is not only by seeing cessation.

Answer: All the sūtras that speak of the benefits of the Four Noble Truths speak of them in the context of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana), that is to say, by knowing "this form, the arising and ceasing of this form," and so on, one attains the exhaustion of the taints (āsrava). Also, the Buddha himself said: "As long as I did not, in accordance with reality, know the gratification, the danger, and the escape concerning the aggregates of form and so on, I would never claim to have attained the unsurpassed path. When I knew them in accordance with reality, I then knew for myself that I had attained the path."

Furthermore, the City Simile Sūtra (cf. Nagaropama Sutta, SN 12.65) states: "If I did not yet know aging and death, the arising of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the path to the cessation of aging and death, all the way back to formations, the arising of formations, the cessation of formations, and the path to the cessation of formations, I would not declare that I had attained the unsurpassed path. When I knew them in accordance with reality, I declared that I had become a Buddha." If views such as these are the views that attain the path, then the sixteen moments of mind would not be what is called attaining the path.

Question: I do not say this is the seeing that attains the path; this is during the time of contemplation.

Answer: The Four Truths are also spoken of in this way. It could also be said that this is during the time of contemplation. If not, you should explain the reason why seeing the Four Truths is called the time of attaining the path, while seeing the five aggregates and so on is the time of contemplation.

Question: The knowledge that severs the afflictions is what is called attaining the path. Contemplating the five aggregates does not sever the afflictions.

Answer: I have already explained previously that knowledge of the five aggregates and so on also severs the afflictions, as it is said that by knowing and seeing form and so on, one attains the exhaustion of the taints. It is also said that by seeing the origin of the world, one eliminates the view of non-existence, and by seeing the cessation of the world, one eliminates the view of existence.

Furthermore, the Buddha himself attained the path by contemplating dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Also, in the Zhenshujia Sūtra, it speaks of various conditions for attaining the path. Some people attain the path by contemplating the five aggregates, or by contemplating the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, and so on. Therefore, it is known that one does not attain the path solely through the Four Truths. If you think that although these are mentioned, the afflictions cannot be severed through these contemplations, one could just as well say that although one contemplates the Four Truths, the afflictions are not severed.

Moreover, one must attain the path through the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). But in the explanation of the Four Truths, it says that birth is suffering, old age is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, the suffering of meeting with the hated, the suffering of parting from the loved, the suffering of not getting what one wants—in short, the five aggregates are suffering. It also says that the origin of suffering is craving (tṛṣṇā), which is accompanied by delight and passion and takes on a body in various places. By contemplating such things, one should not be able to exhaust the taints. These are all conventional truths (saṃvṛti-satya), not the ultimate.

Question: Although by contemplating birth and death and so on one may not exhaust the taints, in the summary statement that the five aggregates are suffering, there is a knowledge that can destroy the afflictions.

Answer: What about the other three truths? Thus, it is known that you are just engaging in your own ideation and discrimination.

Furthermore, to contemplate that the five aggregates are suffering is a scattered mind; it should not be able to attain the path.

Question: If one does not attain the path through the Four Truths, through what dharma does one attain the path?

Answer: One attains the path through a single truth, which is called cessation (nirodha). As it is said in a sūtra: "Falsehood is called delusory; the real is called non-inverted." All conditioned dharmas are delusory and are falsely grasped. Therefore, it is known that as long as the practitioner's mind is in conditioned dharmas, it is never in the real. As it is said in a sūtra: "All conditioned dharmas are delusory, like an illusion, like a mirage, like a dream, like a borrowed thing." As it is said in the Dhammapada: "The world is bound by falsehood, which seems to have solidity. What is unreal is seen as real, but under right contemplation, it is all non-existent." In reality, there is no dharma of 'man' or 'woman'; it is just the combination of the five aggregates to which the names 'man' and 'woman' are forcibly applied. The ordinary person (puthujjana, pṛthagjana) is deluded and confused and thinks they are real. The practitioner contemplates these five aggregates as empty and without an ātman, and immediately no longer sees them. As it is said in the Sūtra of the Seal of the Dharma: "The practitioner contemplates form as impermanent, empty, and separate from marks." 'Impermanent' means that the intrinsic nature of form is impermanent. 'Empty' is like an empty jar, so called because there is no water in the jar. In the same way, because there is no spiritual ātman in the five aggregates, they are called empty. One who contemplates in this way is also said to be empty, and it is also said that their knowledge and vision are not yet pure, because they have not yet been able to see the cessation of the five aggregates. Only later do they see cessation. That is, the practitioner thinks: 'What I have seen, heard, and so on…' and thereby knows that by seeing cessation all afflictions are exhausted.

Question: Why is it that when one sees cessation the afflictions are exhausted, and not with the other truths?

Answer: At that time, the practitioner's perception of suffering (duḥkha-saṃjñā) becomes decisive. If they have not yet realized the mark of cessation, their mind regarding suffering in conditioned dharmas is not yet settled. It is like a person who has not attained the joy and bliss of the first dhyāna and does not generate a perception of revulsion towards the five desires. And it is like one who has not yet attained the concentration without thought and examination (avitarka-avicāra-samādhi) and does not regard the concentration with thought and examination as a trouble. The practitioner is also like this; before realizing the mark of the tranquility of nirvāṇa, they do not attain [the perception of] the suffering of formations. One should know that it is because of seeing the truth of cessation that the perception of suffering is perfected. Because the perception of suffering is perfected, the fetters of craving and so on are severed.

Question: If it is because of seeing the truth of cessation that the perception of suffering is perfected, then the afflictions should be severed after seeing the truth of cessation. Why is that? Because after seeing the truth of cessation, the perception of suffering is perfected.

Answer: They are not severed at a later time. At the very moment that one attains the mark of tranquility in cessation, the perception of suffering is perfected; it becomes manifest later on. As it is said in a sūtra: "When a practitioner knows the mark of exhaustion and cessation in a dharma that has the nature of arising, they immediately attain the pure eye of the dharma in that very dharma." Also, a person always has the thought of an ātman in relation to the aggregates. Although they contemplate the aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and so on, they have not yet permanently destroyed it. If they see the truth of cessation, because it is without a mark (animitta), the thought of an ātman is permanently destroyed.

Question: If the thought of an ātman is exhausted when one sees the truth of cessation, why did the Buddha, after observing that a person's mind was pliant, teach them the Four Truths, and not just cessation?

Answer: In this there is the practice that accords with the path. Because the perception of impermanence and the perception of non-ātman are perfected, one attains this contemplation of suffering. Because it is near to the path, they are spoken of together.

Question: If identity view (satkāya-dṛṣṭi) is severed when one attains the path, why is it also said that adherence to rites and rituals (śīla-vrata-parāmarśa) and doubt (vicikitsā) are severed?

Answer: When the practitioner attains the path, they directly see that all dharmas are empty and without an ātman, and immediately they no longer have doubts. This is different from the contemplation of an ordinary person, which is based on hearing and thinking. If one sees the truth of the path, one knows that only this one path is real and there is no other path. This is why the three are mentioned.

Question: If at the time of attaining the path all the afflictions severed by seeing the truths are exhausted, why is it only said that the three fetters are exhausted?

Answer: All afflictions have identity view as their root. As when the Buddha asked a bhikṣu: "Regarding what thing, because of what thing, and seeing what thing does a person give rise to such views as: 'There is only this body; it is annihilated upon death'," and all other such views. The bhikṣu said to the Buddha: "The Buddha is the king of the dharma; I only pray for your explanation." The Buddha said: "A person, regarding form, because of form, and seeing form as an ātman, gives rise to this view. It is the same up to consciousness." One should know that it is because of seeing an ātman that the various afflictions arise. Why is that? If there is identity view, then one thinks that this ātman is either permanent or impermanent. If one definitely sees it as permanent, this is the view of eternalism. If one definitely sees it as impermanent, this is the view of annihilationism. If the ātman is permanent, then there is no karma, no retribution, no suffering, and no liberation. If the ātman is impermanent, there is also no karma, no retribution, no suffering, and no liberation; one does not attain nirvāṇa by cultivating the path. To hold this view as supreme is the adherence to views (dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa). To think that it can purify one is the adherence to rites and rituals (śīla-vrata-parāmarśa). Craving for one's own view and aversion towards others' views [arises]. To be conceited because of this view is conceit (māna). All these fetters arise because of not knowing in accordance with reality; this is ignorance (avidyā). Therefore, when identity view is severed, the fetters severed by seeing the truths are severed.

Question: If when identity view is severed the others are also severed, why are adherence to rites and rituals and doubt mentioned separately?

Answer: Because of their significance. The practitioner directly sees the nature of dharmas and thus has no doubt. This doubt is doubt about whether the ātman exists or not, and also doubt about whether this path brings purity or not. By seeing the truth of suffering, the view of an ātman is severed, and one also knows that there is only this one path and no other. Therefore, it is said that severing identity view is truly seeing suffering, severing adherence to rites and rituals is cultivating the path, and having no doubt about the knowable and the knowledge of the knowable. If one knows the knowable with right knowledge, this is severing the origin and realizing cessation, thus perfecting the Four Truths. Therefore, these three are mentioned to show the state of no doubt. This doubt arises from [wrong views about] the ātman and the path. As it is said in a sūtra, the mark of first attaining the path is: "having seen the dharma, attained the dharma, known the dharma, and penetrated the dharma, one has crossed over all networks of doubt, does not follow other teachers, and in the Buddha's teaching has attained fearlessness, abiding securely in the fruit."

Now, having seen these Four Truths, the condition for the body is severed, the root of birth and death is exhausted, and we will not take on another existence." He also said: "If a person, wearing the dharma robes and having disfigured their form, goes forth from home with right faith, it is all for the sake of seeing the Four Truths.
