Question: It is said in a sūtra that if a practitioner has seven skillful means and three kinds of contemplation, they will quickly attain the exhaustion of the taints (āsrava-kṣaya) in this dharma. What kinds of knowledge (jñāna) are these?

Answer: The seven skillful means are the wisdom from hearing (śrutamayī prajñā) and the wisdom from contemplating (cintāmayī prajñā). Why is that? One whose mind is not yet concentrated makes such a contemplation, namely: this is form (rūpa), the origin of form, the cessation of form, the path to the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form.

Question: If these are the wisdom from hearing and contemplating, why does it say they will "quickly attain the exhaustion of the taints"?

Answer: Although they are the wisdom from hearing and contemplating, by discriminating the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) in this way, one is able to destroy the thought of an ātman. Therefore, it is said that they will quickly attain the exhaustion of the taints. The knowledge of the three kinds of contemplation is to contemplate conditioned dharmas as impermanent (anitya), suffering (duḥkha), and non-ātman (anātman). If one were to contemplate conditioned dharmas through the gates of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana), there would be no meaning or benefit.

Question: If so, then in the [contemplation of the] danger, impermanence and suffering have already been spoken of, and in the [contemplation of the] escape, non-ātman has already been spoken of. Why are these three kinds of contemplation spoken of again?

Answer: One learns and practices the three kinds in sequence: first the wisdom from hearing and contemplating, and then the wisdom from cultivating (bhāvanāmayī prajñā). First, the seven kinds are spoken of in the context of the wisdom from hearing and contemplating; later, the three kinds are spoken of in the context of the wisdom from cultivating. Why is that? The mark of destruction in [the contemplation of] impermanence and suffering is the impermanence of destruction, not the impermanence of formations (saṃskāra). Although it speaks of eliminating the taint of desire, it does not say how to eliminate it. Only later does it speak of the three kinds of contemplation.

Question: What are the eight kinds of acceptance (aṣṭa-kṣānti)?

Answer: If a knowledge is able to break through provisional designation (prajñapti), it is called an acceptance (kṣānti). This acceptance is found in the stages of heat (uṣmagata), summit (mūrdhan), acceptance (kṣānti), and the supreme worldly dharma (laukikāgra-dharma).

Question: A practitioner also has acceptance in relation to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as the precepts (śīla) and so on. Why are only eight spoken of?

Answer: They are spoken of because of their excellence. "Excellence" means being near to the path. This wisdom acts on behalf of knowledge (jñāna), and therefore is called acceptance. For example, on behalf of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharma-jñāna), it is called the acceptance of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharma-jñāna-kṣānti), and so on. Why is that? One first uses the wisdom from contemplating which accords with the path, and afterward one attains direct knowledge, just as an elephant tracker first observes the elephant's tracks and knows by inferential knowledge that it is nearby, and afterward sees it directly. The practitioner is also like this: first with acceptance (kṣānti), they inferentially know and contemplate nirvāṇa, and afterward with knowledge (jñāna), they see it directly. Therefore, it is said in the sūtra that the "knower" and "seer" are able to attain the exhaustion of the taints.
content.pt:
Pergunta: É ensinado nos Sutras que se o praticante possuir sete modalidades de meios hábeis e três modalidades de discernimento ele realiza rapidamente a extinção das impurezas através destes dharmas. Que discernimento é este? 
Resposta: As sete modalidades dos meios hábeis são o nome dado às sabedorias do ouvir e da reflexão. Por que razão? Se a mente realizar este discernimento sem ainda ter adentrado na absorção meditativa (Dhyana) ele se constituirá na visão da forma, da origem da forma, da extinção da forma e do caminho da extinção da forma, de seu sabor, de sua passagem e de sua saída. 
Pergunta: Caso se trate das sabedorias do ouvir e da reflexão, por que razão se realiza rapidamente a extinção das impurezas? 
Resposta: Mesmo que se trate das sabedorias do ouvir e da reflexão, caso ocorra este discernimento dos cinco agregados isto conduz à dissolução da mente do ãtman. Em função disto se realiza rapidamente a extinção das impurezas. O discernimento associado às três modalidades de visão implicam na penetração da impermanência, da insatisfatoriedade e do vazio de ãtman dos dharmas condicionados. Caso venha a ocorrer o discernimento dos dharmas condicionados através dos agregados, das esferas e das entradas nada existe além disto. 
Pergunta: Se for desta forma, no processo inicial já terão sido ensinados a impermanência e a insatisfatoriedade e a partir daí se ensina o vazio de ãtman. Por que razão ainda se ensina a respeito das três modalidades de discernimento? 
Resposta: No aprendizado destas três modalidades surgem em primeiro lugar as sabedorias do ouvir e da reflexão e posteriormente a sabedoria do cultivo. Em meio as sabedorias do ouvir e da reflexão se ensinam sete modalidades. Posteriormente ensinam-se três modalidades em meio a sabedoria do cultivo. Por que razão? Caso a impermanência e a insatisfatoriedade estiverem associadas a desagregação das características, elas são chamadas de impermanência da desagregação, elas não consistem no cultivo da impermanência. Mesmo que seja ensinada a exclusão dos desejos obsessivos, não se ensina a maneira com que eles são excluídos. Assim sendo, as três modalidades do discernimento são ensinadas posteriormente. 
Pergunta: No que consistem as oito pacientes? 
Resposta: Se o discernimento tiver a capacidade de romper com o nominal ele é chamado de paciência. Esta paciência existe em meio aos estágios do calor (Usmagata), da culminância (Murdham), da paciência (Ksanti) e dos supremos dharmas mundanos (laukika dharma). 
Pergunta: Se o praticante ainda exerce a paciência em sua relação com o Buddha, o Dharma, a Sangha e o Vinaya, por que razão só se ensinam estas oito modalidades?
Resposta: Elas são ensinadas devido a sua excelência. A excelência é chamada de caminho próximo. Esta sabedoria consiste no discernimento. Em função disto, é chamada de paciência. É como o discernimento do dharma da insatisfatoriedade que é chamado de paciência do dharma da insatisfatoriedade e de outros fatores desta natureza. Por que razão? No início se emprega a sabedoria do discernimento em concordância com o caminho. Posteriormente se dá a realização presente deste discernimento. É como um pastor de elefantes que os procura encontrar através da visão de suas pegadas. É através do discernimento dedutivo que se dá em seu interior que surge posteriormente a visão presente. E é da mesma forma a respeito de sua prática. Ocorre inicialmente a paciência dedutiva através da qual se conhece o Nirvana através da reflexão, posteriormente este discernimento se realiza como a visão presente. Em função disto se ensina nos Sutras que aquele que possui o discernimento e a visão realiza a extinção das impurezas.

segments.label: 199 九智品 (On the Nine Discernments | Discernimentos)

content.zh:
問曰：有論師言，阿羅漢證盡智時得世俗九智，謂欲界繫善無記，
乃至非想非非想處善無記。是事云何？

答曰：非一切阿羅漢盡得諸
禪定，云何當得九智？
問曰：一切阿羅漢皆得禪定，但非一切皆能現入。

答曰：若不能現
入，云何名得？如人言知書而不識一字，是事亦爾。
問曰：若人離欲而未能現入初禪，是人命終不生彼耶？

答曰：經中
說，先此間入，後當生彼。今云何此間不入而能生彼？
問曰：若離欲時，過去未來諸禪皆本得得，以此報生。

答曰：未來
業無作無起，不應得報。過去諸禪曾於心生，若與果報則無所害。
又不應得未來諸業，若可得者，一切未來皆應可得，以何障故有得
不得？
問曰：若未來法不可得者，學人不應八分成就，無學不應十分成
就。

所以者何？若依第二禪等入正法位，是人未來得正思惟。又若
行者盡智現前，爾時未來得世正見。又人依無色定得羅漢果，是人
未來得正思惟、正語、正業、正命。又若人依第三禪等得聖道得，
未來喜。如是等法，則應皆無，故知有未來法。又若無未來修者，
云何當得諸果、諸禪定等？行者若在道比智中，悉得初果所攝諸智
諸定。若不爾，果等應數數得。

所以者何？諸果皆應現前時得。是
事不可，故知應有未來中修。

答曰：汝說無諸分者，此無所妨。所
以者何？我說戒等諸分，以次第得，非一時得，故非難也。汝言諸
得得其種類，行者得苦智時，餘苦智種皆名為得，如得人種故名得
人相，亦不名於念念中漸得人相，是事亦爾。
問曰：行者所有苦等諸智次第得者皆已捨離，更一時得須陀洹果所
攝諸智。

答曰：無漏諸智得則不失。
問曰：若先得不失，則得行無別。

所以者何？得果者即是行者，有
此等過。

答曰：若無差別，有何咎耶？如成就果者亦名行者，此亦
如是。又是人更得勝法，故有差別，是故無過。如受五戒者，更得
出家律儀，亦不失本戒。又得果者，不以見道故有差別，如人雖知
初事，更以勝事故有差別。此事亦爾，故知無未來得。又行者住空
無我智，爾時云何得世間法？故知得盡智時不得世智。
問曰：此諸世智共盡智得，與阿羅漢作入出定心。

答曰：阿羅漢心
相續生念念皆淨，若更得九智，眼等皆應更得。若不爾，不應但得
九智。又說未來修者，皆無因緣。

所以者何？此等說見諦道中但修
相似智，思惟道中亦修相似及不相似。見諦道中不修上地，思惟道
中修。道比智中不修世俗善，餘智中修。無礙道中不修他心智。信
解脫轉為見到時，一切無礙解脫道中不修世俗道。時解脫轉為不壞
解脫時，九無礙八解脫道中不修世俗道，第九解脫道中修，微細心
中不修一切無漏。如是等皆無因緣。是故汝今若說正因、若應信
受、若以學習為修，在煖等中時，上諸善根一切皆修，以悉增益
故。如誦習經書則皆明利，是故在煖等法時乃至盡智一切皆修。若
不爾，當說正因。

Question: A master of treatises has said that when an Arhat realizes the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), they attain nine kinds of worldly knowledge (laukika-jñāna), namely, the wholesome and indeterminate [knowledge] connected with the desire realm, up to the wholesome and indeterminate [knowledge] of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. What about this matter?

Answer: Not all Arhats attain all the meditative concentrations (dhyāna). How then could they attain the nine kinds of knowledge?

Question: All Arhats attain the meditative concentrations, but not all are able to enter them at will.

Answer: If they cannot enter them at will, how can it be called "attaining"? It is like a person who says they know how to write but does not recognize a single character. This matter is also like that.

Question: If a person is detached from desire but is not yet able to enter the first dhyāna at will, will they not be born there upon dying?

Answer: It is said in a sūtra that one first enters it here, and afterward will be born there. Now, how could one who does not enter it here be able to be born there?

Question: At the time one becomes detached from desire, one attains the original attainment of all past and future meditative concentrations, and is born through the force of this retribution.

Answer: Future karma has no activity and does not arise. It should not yield a retribution. Past meditative concentrations have previously arisen in the mind; if they were to give a retribution, there would be no harm in that.

Furthermore, one should not be able to attain future karma. If it could be attained, then all of the future ought to be attainable. Due to what obstruction is some attained and some not?

Question: If future dharmas are unattainable, then a learner (śaikṣa) should not be one who has perfected the eight aspects, and one beyond learning (aśaikṣa) should not be one who has perfected the ten aspects. Why is that? If a person enters the stage of the true dharma by relying on the second dhyāna and so on, this person in the future attains right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa). Also, if a practitioner's knowledge of exhaustion manifests, at that time they in the future attain worldly right view (laukika-samyag-dṛṣṭi). Also, a person who relies on a formless concentration to attain the fruit of Arhatship in the future attains right thought, right speech (samyag-vāc), right action (samyak-karmānta), and right livelihood (samyag-ājīva). Also, if a person relies on the third dhyāna and so on to attain the noble path, they in the future attain joy. These and other such dharmas ought then all to be non-existent. Therefore, it is known that future dharmas exist.

Furthermore, if there were no future cultivation, how could one attain the various fruits, meditative concentrations, and so on? If a practitioner is in the analogical knowledge of the path (mārge 'nvaya-jñāna), they attain all the kinds of knowledge and concentration included in the first fruit. If it were not so, the fruits and so on would have to be attained again and again. Why is that? All the fruits would have to be attained at the time they are manifest. This is impossible; therefore, it is known that there must be cultivation in the future.

Answer: Your statement about being without the various aspects is not an obstacle. Why is that? I say that the aspects of morality (śīla) and so on are attained in sequence, not at the same time. Therefore, this is not a valid objection. You say that by attaining, one attains its species. When a practitioner attains the knowledge of suffering, all other species of the knowledge of suffering are said to be attained. It is like how, by attaining the human species, one is said to have attained the human characteristic; one is not said to have gradually attained the human characteristic in moment after moment. This matter is also like that.

Question: The various kinds of knowledge of suffering and so on that a practitioner possesses and attains in sequence are all abandoned, and then one attains at one time the kinds of knowledge included in the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotaāpatti).

Answer: Untainted kinds of knowledge, once attained, are not lost.

Question: If what was previously attained is not lost, then there is no difference between the attainment and the practice. Why is that? One who has attained the fruit is the same as the practitioner. There are such faults.

Answer: If there is no difference, what is the fault in that? Just as one who has perfected the fruit is also called a practitioner, this is also like that.

Furthermore, this person attains a superior dharma, so there is a difference. Therefore, there is no fault. It is like one who has received the five precepts and then receives the monastic code of discipline; they do not lose the original precepts. Also, one who has attained the fruit is not different on account of the path of seeing. It is like a person who, although they know the first matter, is further distinguished on account of a superior matter. This affair is also like that. Therefore, it is known that there is no future attainment.

Furthermore, the practitioner abides in the knowledge of emptiness and non-ātman; at that time, how could they attain a worldly dharma? Therefore, it is known that at the time of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion, one does not attain worldly knowledge.

Question: These various kinds of worldly knowledge are attained together with the knowledge of exhaustion, to serve as the Arhat's mind when entering and leaving concentration.

Answer: The Arhat's mind arises in continuous succession, and every moment is pure. If they were to further attain the nine kinds of knowledge, the eye and other faculties ought also to be further attained. If not, they should not only attain the nine kinds of knowledge.

Furthermore, those who speak of future cultivation have no reason for it. Why is that? They say that in the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) one only cultivates similar knowledge, while in the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) one cultivates both similar and dissimilar knowledge. In the path of seeing, one does not cultivate the higher levels; in the path of cultivation, one does. In the analogical knowledge of the path, one does not cultivate worldly wholesome [states]; in the other kinds of knowledge, one does. In the unobstructed path (ānantarya-mārga), one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds. When one liberated by faith (śraddhā-vimukta) transforms into one who has attained to the view (dṛṣṭi-prāpta), in all the unobstructed paths and paths of liberation, one does not cultivate the worldly path. When one liberated in season (samaya-vimukta) transforms into one with the unshakable liberation (akopya-vimukti), in the nine unobstructed paths and eight paths of liberation, one does not cultivate the worldly path; in the ninth path of liberation, one does. In a subtle mind, one does not cultivate any untainted [state]. These and other such claims are all without reason. Therefore, if you now speak of a correct reason, you should accept this: if "cultivation" is taken as "learning," then at the time of the stages of heat (uṣmagata) and so on, all the higher wholesome roots are cultivated, because they are all enhanced. It is like how reciting and studying the sūtras makes them all clear and sharp. Therefore, at the time of the stages of heat and so on, up until the knowledge of exhaustion, everything is cultivated. If it is not so, you should state a correct reason.

segments.label: 200 十智品 (The Ten Discernments | Os Dez Conhecimentos)

content.zh:
235

十智，法智、比智、他心智、名字智、四諦智、盡智、無生智。知
現在法是名法智。如經中說，佛告阿難：汝於此法如是見知如是通
達，過去未來亦如是知。應言現法智，今不說現故但說法智。如經
中說：愚者貴現在法，智者貴未來。

又說：現在諸欲、未來諸欲，
皆是魔網魔繫魔縛。如是等中皆說現語，略現語故但說法智。知餘
殘法名曰比智，餘謂過去未來諸法，次現法後知，故名比智。所以
者何？先現知已，然後比知。法智名現智，隨此法智思量比知，名
為比智。
問曰：此智是無漏智，無漏智云何名比智？

答曰：世間亦有比智。
所以者何？法智、比智、他心智、苦智、集智、滅智、道智，皆有
有漏、無漏。是諸智在煖等法中是有漏，入法位中所得名無漏。
問曰：有人言，知欲界諸行、諸行集、諸行滅、諸行滅道，名為法
智。知色無色界諸行四種，名為比智。是事云何？

答曰：經中說，
佛告阿難：過去未來世中亦如是知。無有經說色無色界諸行中知名
為比智。

又經中說：行者應念，我今為現色之所侵食，過去亦曾為
色之所侵食，未來中色亦當侵食。

又經中說：生緣老死，去來世中
亦復如是。如馬鳴菩薩說偈：如現在火熱，去來火亦熱，現在五陰
苦，去來陰亦苦。如是等苦，諸大論師亦如是說。又知過去未來世
法名為比智，亦有道理。

所以者何？行者於去來現在苦中厭離，厭
離名於此法中生真智慧。如現在行苦，去來諸行亦如是苦。今以何
智知去來法？若是法智，色無色界諸行亦有去來，於彼中知亦應名
法智，然則唯是法智無比智也。若色無色界去來行中別有智者，欲
界去來行中亦應別更有智。以此義故，諸論師言：有得未得故次第
見諦。欲界苦名得，色無色界苦名未得，是故不可一時並知。若未
得苦，以比智知。今欲界中所未得苦，亦應以比智知。
問曰：以何智為斷結道？

答曰：但用法智、比智在方便道中。
問曰：用何法智？

答曰：用苦法智、滅法智。

所以者何？行者觀無
常苦時見空無我，爾時證諸行滅，餘智皆是方便。
問曰：觀何苦滅？

答曰：觀諸受苦，此中能生我心，亦於此中見
滅。如說，內解脫故，諸愛盡滅，自說得阿羅漢。
問曰：經中不說一切行斷名斷性耶？

答曰：此行者證內滅，故一切
厭離。又行者必當應證內滅，餘不必定。
問曰：於諸諦中云何生智？

答曰：知生苦等。
問曰：此非定心，何能生智？

答曰：有如是觀，亦有見陰無常等
過，生苦無我想。

如經中說：若法無常即是無我。

所以者何？眼等
諸根有生有滅，若是我者我即生滅，故知非我。是眼等生時無所從
來，以有所作故名為我。而經中說無有作者，故知若法無常即是無
我。如是行者善修無常及無我故，身心寂滅，所有行生皆覺其惱則
生苦想，如無皮牛小觸覺痛。行者如是，以無我想故成上苦想。愚
者以我想故，雖有大苦不覺其惱。是名苦智。見諸行生是名集智，
見諸行滅是名滅智，念道始終是名道智。
問曰：何謂盡智？

答曰：盡一切相故名盡智。

所以者何？學人相斷
還生，此畢竟斷故名盡智。

如經中說：若知妄想唯是妄想，諸苦則
盡。學人智但妄想是我，此心永斷，名為盡智。

如經中說：阿羅漢
於佛前自記，世尊所說諸結，我無此也。我於是結不復生疑，我常
一心攝念正行，貪等不善不漏於心。是中取相故生諸結，諸相斷故
諸結則滅。學人行於相無相故我心時發，如見杌樹疑謂是人。故阿
羅漢獨得無疑，以心常行無相中，故先以生空於五陰中不見神我，
後以法空不見色性乃至識性，故知一切相盡名為盡智，知諸相不生
名無生智。學人斷相盡已更生，無學相盡更不復生，若能令諸相盡
滅更不復生，爾時名無生智。
問曰：學人亦知有盡智、無生智，如念我三結盡更不復生，何故不
說十分成就？

答曰：學人不能斷一切相，故不說有盡智、無生智。
如人處處繫縛，雖一處解，不名得脫。亦有此義，舍利弗說給孤獨
氏十分成就。又阿羅漢得自在力故，自知結盡更不復生，學人不
爾。又阿羅漢得無學道時，自知一切生盡，名為盡智。梵行成者，

續。故知但阿羅漢於一切所作應得自在，成就盡智及無生智，非諸

如經中說：離一切處喜，
滅一切處憂，證一切法滅，常行無漏心。他心智如六通中說。五陰
和合假名眾生，此等中智名名字智。無漏智名真實智，此似無漏得
名為智，故曰名字智。
問曰：又人言，一切眾生成就等智。是事云何？

答曰：若佛弟子能
知諸法從眾緣生，是人能得，非餘眾生，以得智名故。一切眾生但
用想識，若得此智，名內凡夫。
content.en:
The ten kinds of knowledge (jñāna) are: knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna), analogical knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna), knowledge of designations (nāma-jñāna), knowledge of the four truths (catur-satya-jñāna), knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), and knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna). Knowing present dharmas is called knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna). As it is said in a sūtra, the Buddha told Ānanda: "You see, know, and penetrate this dharma in this way, and you should know the past and future in the same way." It should be called "knowledge of the present dharma," but as "present" is not stated here, it is simply called knowledge of the dharma. As it is said in a sūtra: "The foolish person values present dharmas; the wise person values the future." It is also said: "Present desires and future desires are all Māra's net, Māra's bonds, Māra's fetters" (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.1). In these and other such passages, the word "present" is used. By abbreviating the word "present," it is simply called knowledge of the dharma. Knowing the remaining dharmas is called analogical knowledge (anvaya-jñāna). The "remaining" refers to the dharmas of the past and future. Because they are known subsequent to the present dharma, it is called analogical knowledge. Why is that? First one knows the present, and then one knows by analogy. Knowledge of the dharma is called knowledge of the present (pratyakṣa-jñāna). To reflect upon and know by analogy in accordance with this knowledge of the dharma is called analogical knowledge.

Question: This knowledge is untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna). How can untainted knowledge be called analogical knowledge?

Answer: There is also worldly analogical knowledge. Why is that? Knowledge of the dharma, analogical knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of the origin (samudaya-jñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) are all either tainted (sāsrava) or untainted (anāsrava). These kinds of knowledge, when in the stages of heat (uṣmagata) and so on, are tainted. That which is obtained upon entering the stage of the dharma is called untainted.

Question: Some say that to know the formations (saṃskāra), the origin of formations, the cessation of formations, and the path to the cessation of formations in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is called knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna). To know these four aspects regarding the formations of the form and formless realms (rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu) is called analogical knowledge (anvaya-jñāna). What about this matter?

Answer: It is said in a sūtra that the Buddha told Ānanda: "You should know the past and future worlds in the same way." There is no sūtra that says the knowledge concerning the formations of the form and formless realms is called analogical knowledge. It is also said in a sūtra: "The practitioner should reflect: I am now being devoured by present form (rūpa); in the past, I was also devoured by form; and in the future, form will also devour me." It is also said in a sūtra: "Birth (jāti) is the condition for aging and death (jarā-maraṇa); it is the same in the past and future." As the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa said in a verse: "Just as present fire is hot, so too are past and future fire hot. Just as the present five aggregates (skandha) are suffering (duḥkha), so too are the past and future aggregates suffering." The great masters of treatises (śāstra) also speak of this kind of suffering (duḥkha).

Furthermore, there is a principle for calling the knowledge of the dharmas of the past and future worlds "analogical knowledge." Why is that? The practitioner feels revulsion towards suffering (duḥkha) in the past, future, and present. Revulsion means that true wisdom arises concerning this dharma. Just as present formations (saṃskāra) are suffering, so too are past and future formations suffering. Now, with what knowledge does one know the dharmas of the past and future? If it were with knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna), then since the formations of the form and formless realms also exist in the past and future, the knowledge of them should also be called knowledge of the dharma. In that case, there would only be knowledge of the dharma and no analogical knowledge. If there were a separate knowledge for the past and future formations of the form and formless realms, there should also be another, separate knowledge for the past and future formations of the desire realm. It is for this reason that the masters of treatises say: "Because some is attained and some is not yet attained, the truths (satya) are seen in sequence." The suffering of the desire realm is called "attained," and the suffering of the form and formless realms is called "not yet attained." Therefore, they cannot be known simultaneously. If the suffering that is not yet attained is known through analogical knowledge, then the suffering in the desire realm that is not yet attained should also be known through analogical knowledge.

Question: What knowledge serves as the path for severing the fetters (saṃyojana)?

Answer: Only knowledge of the dharma (dharma-jñāna) and analogical knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are on the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga).

Question: Which knowledge of the dharma?

Answer: The knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) and the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna). Why is that? When the practitioner contemplates impermanence (anitya) and suffering (duḥkha), they see emptiness (śūnyatā) and non-self (anātman). At that time, they realize the cessation of formations (saṃskāra). The remaining kinds of knowledge are all preparatory.

Question: The cessation of what suffering is contemplated?

Answer: One contemplates the suffering of the feelings (vedanā). It is in these that the thought of an ātman can arise, and it is also in these that one sees cessation. As it is said, "Through internal liberation, all cravings (tṛṣṇā) are exhausted and cease," thereby personally declaring the attainment of Arhatship.

Question: Is it not said in the sūtras that the cessation of all formations (saṃskāra) is called the nature of severance?

Answer: This practitioner realizes internal cessation, and therefore becomes disenchanted with everything.

Moreover, the practitioner must certainly realize internal cessation; the rest is not definite.

Question: How does knowledge (jñāna) arise concerning the truths (satya)?

Answer: By knowing that birth (jāti) is suffering (duḥkha), and so on.

Question: This is not a concentrated mind. How can it give rise to knowledge?

Answer: There is this kind of contemplation, and there is also seeing the faults of the aggregates (skandha), such as their impermanence, which gives rise to the perception of suffering (duḥkha-saṃjñā) and the thought of non-self (anātma-saṃjñā). As it is said in a sūtra: "Whatever dharma is impermanent (anitya) is non-self (anātman)" (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.59). Why is that? The sense faculties, such as the eye, arise and cease. If it were an ātman, that ātman would arise and cease; therefore, it is known not to be an ātman. When the eye and other faculties arise, they come from nowhere. Because there is an action, it is called an ātman. But it is said in the sūtras that there is no agent. Therefore, it is known that whatever dharma is impermanent is non-self. In this way, because the practitioner skillfully cultivates impermanence and non-self, their body and mind become tranquil. Whenever any formation arises, they feel its affliction and thus the perception of suffering arises, like a flayed cow feeling pain at the slightest touch. The practitioner is like this. Because of the thought of non-self, they perfect the higher perception of suffering. The foolish person, because of the thought of an ātman, does not feel affliction even when there is great suffering. This is called the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna). Seeing the arising of formations is called the knowledge of the origin (samudaya-jñāna). Seeing the cessation of formations is called the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna). Contemplating the path from beginning to end is called the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).

Question: What is meant by knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?

Answer: Because all signs (nimitta) are exhausted, it is called knowledge of exhaustion. Why is that? For a learner (śaikṣa), when the signs are severed, they can arise again. Here, they are completely severed, hence it is called knowledge of exhaustion. As it is said in a sūtra: "If one knows deluded thoughts to be merely deluded thoughts, all suffering (duḥkha) is exhausted." The learner's knowledge is merely that the deluded thought 'this is an ātman' arises. When this thought of an ātman is eternally severed, it is called knowledge of exhaustion. As it is said in a sūtra, an Arhat (arhat) declared himself before the Buddha, saying: "The fetters (saṃyojana) spoken of by the World-Honored One—I am without these. I no longer give rise to doubt concerning these fetters. I always, with a unified mind, maintain mindfulness and right practice. Unwholesome states like greed do not leak into my mind." Here, it is because of grasping at signs that the fetters arise. Because the signs are severed, the fetters are destroyed. The learner practices with regard to signs and signlessness, so the thought of an ātman sometimes arises, like seeing a tree stump and suspecting it is a person. Therefore, only the Arhat attains freedom from doubt, because their mind constantly abides in signlessness. First, through the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), one does not see a spiritual ātman within the five aggregates (skandha). Later, through the emptiness of dharmas (dharma-śūnyatā), one does not see the nature of form (rūpa) up to the nature of consciousness (vijñāna). Therefore, it is known that the exhaustion of all signs is called knowledge of exhaustion. Knowing that the signs will not arise is called knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna). For a learner, after the signs are exhausted, they arise again. For one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), when the signs are exhausted, they do not arise again. When one is able to cause the signs to be completely exhausted and cease, never to arise again, that is called knowledge of non-arising.

Question: A learner (śaikṣa) also knows they have knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising, for instance, when they reflect that 'my three fetters are exhausted and will not arise again.' Why is it not said that they have perfect accomplishment in the ten aspects?

Answer: Because the learner is unable to sever all signs (nimitta), it is not said that they have knowledge of exhaustion and knowledge of non-arising. It is like a person who is bound in many places; even if untied in one place, they are not called free. There is also this meaning, though Śāriputra said that Anāthapiṇḍada had perfect accomplishment in the ten aspects.

Furthermore, because the Arhat (arhat) has attained the power of sovereignty, they know for themselves that their fetters are exhausted and will not arise again. The learner is not like this. Also, when an Arhat attains the path of one beyond learning (aśaikṣa-mārga), they know for themselves that all arising is exhausted, and this is called knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna). 'The holy life (brahmacarya) is established' means that all the practices of a learner have been abandoned. 'What had to be done is done' means that all that ought to be done has been completed, and one knows that after this body there will be no further continuation. Therefore, it is known that only an Arhat has attained sovereignty over all that is to be done and has accomplished the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising, not the learners. It is like a person with malaria; even when the fever is not manifest, they are not said to be cured. As it is said in a sūtra: "Detached from delight in all places, having extinguished sorrow in all places, having realized the cessation of all dharmas, one constantly abides with an untainted (anāsrava) mind." Knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) is as explained in the section on the six supernormal powers (abhijñā). The provisional designation "sentient being" is based on the combination of the five aggregates (skandha). Knowledge concerning this is called knowledge of designations (nāma-jñāna). Untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) is called true knowledge. This other knowledge resembles untainted knowledge and so gets the name "knowledge," hence it is called knowledge of designations.

Question: Another person says that all sentient beings have accomplished equal knowledge. What about this matter?

Answer: If a disciple of the Buddha is able to know that all dharmas arise from a collection of conditions, that person can attain it, but not other sentient beings. Because they have attained what is called knowledge, all [other] sentient beings only use perception (saṃjñā) and consciousness (vijñāna). If one attains this knowledge, one is called an ordinary person on the inner path.

segments.label: 201 四十四智品 (The Forty-Four Discernments | Os Quarenta e Quatro Conhecimentos)

content.zh:
問曰：經中說四十四智，謂老死智、老死集智、老死滅智、老死滅
道智。生、有、取、愛、受、觸、六入、名色、識、行亦如是。何
故說此？

答曰：泥洹是真法寶，以種種門入。有以五陰門入，或觀
界入因緣諸諦如是等門，皆至泥洹。何以知之？

如經中說：王處城
中有雙使來，從一門入，到已向王說其事實，語已還去。諸門亦
爾。此中王喻行者，諸門謂觀陰界入等，雙使如止觀，說其事實謂
通達空。是諸使雖從諸門入，皆到一處，如是雖觀陰界入等諸門方
便，皆入泥洹。如羅睺羅說：於獨屏處思惟法時，知如是法皆隨順
趣向稱讚泥洹。

又佛於讚法中說：是法能滅諸煩惱火故名為滅，能
令行者心得安隱故名安隱，能令行者到正遍知故名為至。如是等義
皆讚泥洹。又梵行名八聖道，八聖道中正智為上，是正智果所謂泥
洹。又佛所說教皆為泥洹。故知五陰等門皆至泥洹。
問曰：有論師言，老死智名苦智。是事云何？

答曰：非也。所以者
何？是中不說苦行，故非苦智。
問曰：為是何智？

答曰：此名老死性智。
問曰：亦說知老死集、老死滅、老死滅道，故知應是苦智。

答曰：
此是因緣門，非真諦門，是故此中不應說苦行，應說集等以相順
故。
問曰：此中何故不說味、過、出等諸智耶？

答曰：此義皆攝，但集
經者略而不說。

Question: In the sūtras, forty-four kinds of knowledge (jñāna) are spoken of, namely: knowledge (jñāna) of aging and death (jarā-maraṇa), knowledge (jñāna) of the origin of aging and death, knowledge (jñāna) of the cessation of aging and death, and knowledge (jñāna) of the path to the cessation of aging and death. The same applies to birth (jāti), existence (bhava), grasping (upādāna), craving (tṛṣṇā), feeling (vedanā), contact (sparśa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍ-āyatana), name-and-form (nāma-rūpa), consciousness (vijñāna), and formations (saṃskāra). Why is this taught?

Answer: Nirvāṇa is the true jewel of the dharma, and it is entered through various gates. Some enter through the gate of the five aggregates (skandha), or through such gates as contemplating the elements (dhātu), the sense bases (āyatana), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), and the truths (satya). All of these lead to nirvāṇa. How is this known? As it is said in a sūtra: In a royal city, a pair of messengers arrived. They entered through one gate, and having arrived, they reported the facts of the matter to the king. Having spoken, they departed (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 35). It is the same with the various gates. Here, the king is an analogy for the practitioner; the various gates refer to the contemplation of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), and so on; the pair of messengers is like serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā); and reporting the facts of the matter refers to the penetration of emptiness (śūnyatā). Although these messengers enter through various gates, they all arrive at the one place. In the same way, although one contemplates through the various skillful gates of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), and so on, one enters nirvāṇa. As Rāhula said: When I was reflecting on the dharma in a secluded place, I knew that all such dharmas are concordant with, lead towards, and are praised as nirvāṇa (cf. Majjhima Nikāya 61-62).

Furthermore, in praising the dharma, the Buddha said: This dharma is called cessation because it can extinguish the fires of the afflictions (kleśa); it is called peace because it enables the practitioner's mind to attain peace; it is called attainment because it enables the practitioner to reach perfect, complete enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). Meanings such as these all praise nirvāṇa.

Moreover, the holy life (brahmacarya) is the Noble Eightfold Path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), and among the Noble Eightfold Path, right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) is supreme. The fruit of this right knowledge is what is called nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, all the teachings spoken by the Buddha are for the sake of nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is known that the gates of the five aggregates (skandha) and so on all lead to nirvāṇa.

Question: Some masters of treatises (śāstra) say that the knowledge (jñāna) of aging and death is called the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna). What about this matter?

Answer: It is not so. Why is that? Because the characteristic of suffering (duḥkha) is not mentioned here, it is not the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).

Question: What kind of knowledge (jñāna) is it then?

Answer: This is called the knowledge (jñāna) of the nature of aging and death.

Question: It also speaks of knowing the origin of aging and death, the cessation of aging and death, and the path to the cessation of aging and death. Therefore, one should know that it ought to be the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna).

Answer: This is the gate of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), not the gate of the true realities (satya). Therefore, the characteristic of suffering (duḥkha) should not be spoken of here; origin (samudaya) and so on should be spoken of because they are concordant with this gate.

Question: Why are the various kinds of knowledge (jñāna) concerning gratification (āsvāda), danger (ādīnava), and escape (niḥsaraṇa) not mentioned here?

Answer: These meanings are all included, but the compilers of the sūtras abbreviated and did not state them.

segments.label: 202 七十七智品 (On the Seventy-Seven Discernments | Os Setenta e Sete Conhecimentos)

content.zh:
問曰：經中說七十七智，謂生緣老死、不離生有老死，過去未來世
中亦如是。是法住智觀無常有為作起從眾緣生，盡相、壞相、離
相、滅相亦如是觀，乃至無明緣行亦如是。是中何故不說老死性及
滅道等耶？

答曰：為利智者故如是說，但開其門，可知餘亦如是。
又外道多於因緣中謬說世間萬物因世性等，故佛於此但說因緣。
問曰：已說生緣老死，何故更說不離？

答曰：為必定故，諸法中有
不定因，如施為福因，亦以持戒得福，如說持戒得生天上。或有生
念老死因生或不因生，故須定說。
問曰：何故去來世中復須定說？

答曰：現在與過去世或有異相，謂
過去眾生壽命無量勢同諸天，如是等。恐人謂壽命等異，老死因緣
亦當有異，故須定說。未來亦爾。此六種名法住智，餘名泥洹智。
能令老死相續，故說無常有為作起從眾緣生，盡相壞相即是無常
行，離相即是苦行，滅相即是空無我行。

所以者何？此中色性滅、
受想行識性滅，是名三種觀義。

如經中說：比丘！有七處方便三種
觀義，速得漏盡。皆是為泥洹智。如是等因緣智有百千無量，謂眼
智等。

如經中說：眼緣業業緣愛，愛緣無明，無明緣邪念，邪念緣
眼色，諸漏緣邪念，諸食緣愛，五欲緣揣食等，地獄短命緣殺生
等。若今苦先苦皆緣妄想，妄想緣身心憎愛，憎愛緣貪欲，貪欲緣
邪思惟。如是等諸因緣智無量無邊，自應當知。
content.en:
Question: In the sūtras, seventy-seven knowledges (jñāna) are spoken of, namely, that birth (jāti) conditions aging and death (jarā-maraṇa), and that aging and death are not separate from birth. It is also like this in the past and future worlds. This is the knowledge of the stability of dharmas (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), which contemplates dharmas as impermanent (anitya), conditioned (saṃskṛta), created, arisen, and produced from a collection of conditions (pratītyasamutpanna). The aspect of cessation (nirodha-lakṣaṇa), the aspect of destruction (bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa), the aspect of separation (virāga-lakṣaṇa), and the aspect of annihilation (vyaya-lakṣaṇa) are also contemplated in this way. This is so up to and including ignorance (avidyā) conditioning formations (saṃskāra). Here, why is the nature of aging and death, as well as cessation (nirodha), the path (mārga), and so forth, not discussed?

Answer: It is taught this way for the sake of those with keen faculties. It merely opens the gate, from which one may know that the rest is also like this.

Furthermore, the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) mostly err regarding causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya), saying that the myriad things of the world are caused by a worldly nature (prakṛti) and so forth. Therefore, the Buddha only spoke of causes and conditions here.

Question: Having already stated that birth conditions aging and death, why further state that they are 'not separate'?

Answer: It is for the sake of certainty. Among dharmas, there are uncertain causes; for example, giving is a cause for merit, and one also obtains merit by upholding the precepts (śīla), as it is said that by upholding the precepts one attains birth in heaven. Someone might think that aging and death are caused by birth, or that they are not caused by birth; therefore, a definitive statement is necessary.

Question: Why is it necessary to state this definitively for the past and future worlds as well?

Answer: The present may have different characteristics from the past world. That is to say, in the past, the lifespan of beings was immeasurable and their power was equal to that of the gods (deva), and so on. Fearing that someone might say that since lifespan and so forth are different, the causes and conditions for aging and death must also be different, a definitive statement is necessary. It is also so for the future. These six types are called the knowledge of the stability of dharmas (dharma-sthiti-jñāna); the remainder are called the knowledge of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-jñāna). Because they enable the continuation of aging and death, they are described as impermanent (anitya), conditioned (saṃskṛta), created, arisen, and produced from a collection of conditions (pratītyasamutpanna). The aspect of cessation and the aspect of destruction are the practice of contemplating impermanence. The aspect of separation is the practice of contemplating suffering (duḥkha). The aspect of annihilation is the practice of contemplating emptiness (śūnyatā) and not-self (anātman). Why is that? Herein, the nature of form (rūpa) is annihilated, and the natures of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are annihilated. This is what is meant by the three kinds of contemplation. As it is said in a sūtra: "O bhikṣu! There are seven skillful bases and three kinds of contemplation, by which one quickly attains the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya)." (cf. Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.67). All of this is for the sake of the knowledge of nirvāṇa. The knowledges of causes and conditions such as these are limitless, numbering in the hundreds and thousands, such as the knowledge of the eye, and so forth. As it is said in a sūtra: The eye (cakṣus) is conditioned by action (karman); action is conditioned by craving (tṛṣṇā); craving is conditioned by ignorance (avidyā); ignorance is conditioned by wrong mindfulness (mithyā-smṛti); wrong mindfulness is conditioned by the eye and form; the various outflows (āsrava) are conditioned by wrong mindfulness; the various nutriments (āhāra) are conditioned by craving; the five desires (pañca-kāmaguṇa) are conditioned by physical nutriment (kabalīkārāhāra), and so forth; and a short life in hell is conditioned by the taking of life, and so on. If present suffering (duḥkha) and past suffering are all conditioned by false discrimination (vikalpa), then false discrimination is conditioned by aversion and affection regarding body and mind, aversion and affection are conditioned by greed and desire (rāga), and greed and desire are conditioned by wrong thought (mithyā-vitarka). The knowledges of causes and conditions such as these are immeasurable and boundless, and should be known by oneself.
End of Scroll 16 of the Tattvasiddhi-śāstra.
